Computed NaNs use the canonical quiet pattern

Statement

The reference evaluator of module value (which the production apply_builtin and eval of panproto-expr are required to equal exactly) satisfies the following.

  1. (The canonical quiet pattern.) For each format F with precision p and exponent width w, computed_nan(F) is defined as exponent_mask << (p - 1) | 1 << (p - 2), that is (2w−1)2p−1+2p−2, which decode(F, ·) reads as NaN { negative: false, fraction: 2^(p-2) }: a positive NaN whose only set fraction bit is the quiet flag. Its values are 0x7e00, 0x7fc00000 and 0x7ff8000000000000 for binary16, binary32 and binary64, and computed_nan(Format::B64) equals CANONICAL_NAN_BITS.
  2. (Computed NaNs.) For every operation op among Add, Sub, Mul, Div, Neg, Abs, Clamp, IntToFloat and DecimalToFloat, and every argument slice args, every result Ok(Value::Float(b)) of apply_builtin(op, args) is of one of three kinds: (a) b = CANONICAL_NAN_BITS = computed_nan(Format::B64), returned exactly when the f64 datum the operation computes satisfies is_nan, or, for DecimalToFloat, when the operand is a NaN decimal; (b) b = x.to_bits() for the computed datum x, returned exactly when x.is_nan() is false; (c) for DecimalToFloat of an infinite decimal, b = 0x7ff0000000000000 or 0xfff0000000000000. So a computed NaN is always replaced by the one canonical quiet pattern, whatever the signs, quiet flags and payloads of the NaN operands. Under Assumption N below, a result b that decode(Format::B64, ·) reads as a NaN is thus computed_nan(Format::B64).
  3. (Pass-through NaNs.) For every 64-bit pattern b, every environment env (a map from names to values) and every name x: eval(Expr::Literal(Value::Float(b)), env) is Ok(Value::Float(b)); eval(Expr::Variable(x), env) is Ok(v) when env maps x to v; and eval(Expr::Let { name: x, value: Literal(Float(b)), body: Variable(x) }, env) is Ok(Value::Float(b)). A NaN that is written, bound or returned without computation keeps its sign, quiet flag and payload.
  4. (Read NaNs.) For every string t, every result Ok(Value::Float(b)) of apply_builtin(StrToFloat, [Value::Str(t)]) is computed from the datum x parsed from t as follows: when x.is_nan() holds, b is NEGATIVE_CANONICAL_NAN_BITS = 0xfff8000000000000 if t begins with - and CANONICAL_NAN_BITS = 0x7ff8000000000000 otherwise; when it does not, b = x.to_bits(). The two NaN patterns are computed_nan(Format::B64) with the sign bit set or clear, so a NaN spelling keeps its written sign, and no payload or signalling flag reaches the result, whatever datum the platform parser produces. Under Assumption N, a result b that decode(Format::B64, ·) reads as a NaN is one of these two patterns, chosen by the written sign.

Outside the domain

Item 2 constrains only results of the form Ok(Value::Float(_)). Successful non-float results, including integer arithmetic, are outside that item; failed calls return the following typed refusals. EvalError::ArityMismatch for a wrong number of arguments; EvalError::ExactArithmetic for an exact operand (Decimal, BigInt or Temporal) of Add, Sub, Mul, Div, Neg or Abs; EvalError::DivisionByZero for Div by an integer zero or a float equal to zero; EvalError::Overflow for integer overflow; EvalError::TypeError for operands of the wrong kind, and for Clamp with a NaN bound or a lower bound above the upper one; EvalError::InvalidDecimal when DecimalToFloat cannot read its decimal text. Item 3 concerns a name bound in env; an unbound name gives Err(EvalError::NotAFunction) when it names a builtin (builtin_named(x) is Some, so eval_runtime returns a Runtime::Builtin with no argument supplied, which Runtime::value refuses), and Err(EvalError::UnboundVariable) otherwise. Item 4 constrains only Ok(Value::Float(_)) results: StrToFloat refuses a string that the platform parser str::parse::<f64> rejects with EvalError::InvalidDecimal, a wrong argument count with EvalError::ArityMismatch, and a non-string argument with EvalError::TypeError. Which texts the platform parser reads as a NaN is the parser’s grammar, not part of this law; the law fixes the bits of every NaN it reads.

Definitions used

  • Format parameters (from Format): width W∈{16,32,64}, precision p∈{11,24,53}, exponent width w=W−p∈{5,8,11}, sign bit S=2W−1, exponent_mask =2w−1. A pattern of F is an integer 0≤b<2W, written uniquely as b=σS+E2p−1+f with σ∈{0,1}, exponent field 0≤E<2w and fraction 0≤f<2p−1.
  • decode(F, b): the reference definition; with these fields, E=2w−1 gives Infinite { negative } when f=0 and NaN { negative, fraction: f } when f=0; any other E gives Finite { negative, value }. In each case negative is σ=1.
  • A pattern “is a NaN” under F when decode(F, ·) returns FloatValue::NaN { .. }.
  • computed_nan(F): the reference definition exponent_mask << (p - 1) | 1 << (p - 2), in which << binds tighter than |.
  • CANONICAL_NAN_BITS and NEGATIVE_CANONICAL_NAN_BITS: the reference constants 0x7ff8000000000000 and 0xfff8000000000000.
  • StrToFloat, in conversion_builtin: on Value::Str(t), t.parse::<f64>(); a parse failure gives Err(InvalidDecimal(t)); a parsed x gives Value::Float(NEGATIVE_CANONICAL_NAN_BITS) when x.is_nan() and t starts with -, and Value::Float(canonical_float(x)) otherwise; any other argument gives Err(TypeError).
  • f64 primitives. x.to_bits() is the 64-bit pattern Rust returns for the datum x, and x.is_nan() is Rust’s NaN test. The law’s unconditional items use only the values these primitives return, through canonical_float; they assume nothing about which datum an f64 operation or the parser produces. The reference writes the infinity results of decimal_to_float as f64::INFINITY.to_bits() and f64::NEG_INFINITY.to_bits(). Rust defines f64::INFINITY and f64::NEG_INFINITY as the IEEE 754 binary64 infinities and to_bits as the identity on the bits of the datum, so these are the patterns 0x7ff0000000000000 and 0xfff0000000000000 (exponent field all ones, fraction zero); the proof uses only these patterns.
  • Assumption N (a property of the platform, not proved here): for every f64 datum x, x.is_nan() holds exactly when decode(Format::B64, x.to_bits()) is NaN { .. }. The page uses it only for the consequences stated after items 2 and 4.
  • canonical_float(x): the reference definition, CANONICAL_NAN_BITS when x.is_nan() and x.to_bits() otherwise.
  • apply_builtin, numeric_binop, float_binop, numeric_unary, collection_builtin, clamp, conversion_builtin, decimal_to_float, eval, eval_runtime and Runtime::value: the reference definitions in module value. eval(e, env) lifts each binding v of env to Runtime::Value(v) and returns eval_runtime(e, lifted)?.value(). Runtime::value returns Ok(v) on Runtime::Value(v) and Err(NotAFunction) on a closure or a Runtime::Builtin. eval_runtime on Expr::Variable(x) returns the binding of x when there is one, else Runtime::Builtin { op, supplied: [] } when builtin_named(x) is Some(op), else Err(UnboundVariable(x)).

Proof

  1. Item 1. By the definition, computed_nan(F) =(2w−1)2p−1+2p−2, the two summands having disjoint bits because 2p−2<2p−1. The sum is below 2w⋅2p−1=2W−1, so the sign bit is clear; its exponent field is 2w−1 and its fraction is 2p−2=0, so decode returns NaN { negative: false, fraction: 2^(p-2) }. With (w,p)=(5,11), (8,24) and (11,53) the values are 0x7c00 + 0x200 = 0x7e00, 0x7f800000 + 0x400000 = 0x7fc00000 and 0x7ff0000000000000 + 0x8000000000000 = 0x7ff8000000000000, the last being CANONICAL_NAN_BITS.
  2. canonical_float. By its definition, canonical_float(x) is CANONICAL_NAN_BITS when x.is_nan() holds and x.to_bits() when it does not. By step 1, CANONICAL_NAN_BITS = computed_nan(Format::B64).
  3. Add, Sub, Mul, Div. apply_builtin checks the arity (else ArityMismatch) and calls numeric_binop. Its arms: an exact operand gives Err(ExactArithmetic); two Ints give Ok(Value::Int(_)) or Err; an Int with a Float, a Float with an Int, or two Floats call float_binop; any other pair gives Err(TypeError). float_binop returns Err(DivisionByZero) for Div by a zero, Ok(Value::Float(canonical_float(value))) for the four operations, and Err(TypeError) in its remaining arm. So every Ok(Value::Float(b)) has b = canonical_float(·).
  4. Neg, Abs. numeric_unary: an exact operand gives Err(ExactArithmetic); an Int gives Ok(Value::Int(_)) or Err(Overflow); a Float gives Ok(Value::Float(canonical_float(computed))); anything else gives Err(TypeError).
  5. Clamp. collection_builtin calls clamp: three Ints give Ok(Value::Int(_)) or Err(TypeError); three Floats give Err(TypeError) for a NaN or reversed bound and otherwise Ok(Value::Float(canonical_float(value.clamp(minimum, maximum)))); anything else gives Err(TypeError).
  6. IntToFloat. conversion_builtin: an Int gives Ok(Value::Float(canonical_float(int_as_f64(value)))); anything else gives Err(TypeError).
  7. DecimalToFloat. decimal_to_float: an infinite decimal gives Ok(Value::Float(0x7ff0000000000000)) or Ok(Value::Float(0xfff0000000000000)), whose exponent field is all ones and fraction zero, so neither is a NaN pattern; a NaN decimal gives Ok(Value::Float(CANONICAL_NAN_BITS)); a finite decimal or a BigInt gives Err(InvalidDecimal) or Ok(Value::Float(canonical_float(parsed))); anything else gives Err(TypeError).
  8. Item 2. By steps 3 to 7, every Ok(Value::Float(b)) returned by one of the nine operations is canonical_float(x) of the datum x the operation computes, or CANONICAL_NAN_BITS for a NaN decimal, or one of the two infinity constants for an infinite decimal. By step 2, canonical_float(x) is kind (a) when x.is_nan() and kind (b) otherwise; the NaN-decimal case is kind (a) and the infinite-decimal case kind (c). No branch reads the sign, flag or payload of a NaN operand. Under Assumption N: in kind (b), x.is_nan() is false, so x.to_bits() does not decode as a NaN; in kind (c), the exponent field is 211−1 and the fraction 0, so decode gives Infinite; hence a result that decodes as a NaN is of kind (a), which is computed_nan(Format::B64).
  9. Item 3. eval lifts env to the map lifted with x bound to Runtime::Value(v) exactly when env binds x to v. For Expr::Literal(Value::Float(b)), eval_runtime returns Ok(Runtime::Value(Value::Float(b))) (cloning copies the u64 b), and Runtime::value gives Ok(Value::Float(b)). For Expr::Variable(x) with x bound to v in env, the first branch of the Variable case applies, giving Runtime::Value(v) and then Ok(v); the builtin_named branch and the UnboundVariable branch are taken only for a name with no binding (Outside the domain). For the Let, eval_runtime evaluates the literal to Runtime::Value(Value::Float(b)), inserts x bound to it into a copy of lifted, and evaluates Variable(x) there; x is now bound, so the first branch returns that binding, and Runtime::value gives Ok(Value::Float(b)). None of these paths calls canonical_float or any arithmetic, so b is returned unchanged for every pattern, NaN patterns included.
  10. Item 4. apply_builtin checks the arity (else ArityMismatch) and calls conversion_builtin. A non-string argument gives Err(TypeError) and a parse failure gives Err(InvalidDecimal), so an Ok(Value::Float(b)) comes from a parsed datum x. If x.is_nan() and t starts with -, the definition returns NEGATIVE_CANONICAL_NAN_BITS. Otherwise it returns canonical_float(x), which by step 2 is CANONICAL_NAN_BITS when x.is_nan() (and then t does not start with -) and x.to_bits() when not. This is item 4. NEGATIVE_CANONICAL_NAN_BITS = CANONICAL_NAN_BITS +263 has sign bit set, exponent field 211−1 and fraction 251, so it decodes to NaN { negative: true, fraction: 2^51 }, the pattern of step 1 with the sign bit set. Neither NaN result depends on the datum x beyond x.is_nan(), so no payload or signalling flag reaches the result. Under Assumption N, the branch x.to_bits() with x.is_nan() false never decodes as a NaN, which gives the final sentence of item 4.

NaN bit transport is exact at every reference width

Statement

Let F be Format::B16, Format::B32 or Format::B64, with precision p, width W and shift k=53−p (so k=42, 29, 0). The following three claims concern the reference operations widen_bits and narrow_bits at all three widths:

  1. (Widen, then narrow.) For every pattern b<2W with decode(F, b) = NaN { negative: s, fraction: f }, widen_bits(F, b) decodes under Format::B64 to NaN { negative: s, fraction: f · 2^k }, and narrow_bits(F, widen_bits(F, b)) is Some(b). The sign, the quiet flag (the top fraction bit, bit p−2 of F, which lands on bit 51, the binary64 quiet flag) and the rest of the payload are all preserved.
  2. (Narrow, then widen: admitted NaNs.) For every binary64 pattern c with decode(Format::B64, c) = NaN { negative: s, fraction: g }, narrow_bits(F, c) is Some(h) exactly when g is divisible by 2k; in that case decode(F, h) is NaN { negative: s, fraction: g / 2^k } and widen_bits(F, h) =c.
  3. (Infinities.) For every s, widen_bits sends the infinity of F with sign s to the binary64 infinity with sign s, and narrow_bits(F, ·) sends that back.

In particular, at F = Format::B32, every binary32 NaN survives widening and narrowing bit for bit, and a binary64 NaN is admitted by binary32 narrowing exactly when its low 29 fraction bits are zero, in which case narrowing and widening it again restores its bits.

The production correspondence has a narrower domain. At binary16, binary16_widen supplies the widening operation and binary16_bits supplies the exact narrowing operation. At binary32, the production carrier is binary64, binary32_bits supplies exact narrowing, and the differential constructs the unique bit-preserving embedding into that carrier without using the reference implementation. Binary64 is already the production carrier, so there is no separate production widening or narrowing operation at that width. Thus the binary64 clauses above are reference identities, not claims about a missing production API.

Outside the domain

  • A binary64 NaN with a non-zero fraction bit below bit k is not admitted: narrow_bits(F, c) is None. The coercion of an existing value into a float kind maps this None to the refusal FidelityReason::NonFinite.
  • Finite patterns are outside this law: widen_bits and narrow_bits treat them by value, through round_to and holds_exactly, not bit-wise.
  • A value b≥2W is not a pattern of F; the operations are stated only for patterns of their formats.

Definitions used

  • Format parameters (from Format): width W∈{16,32,64}, precision p∈{11,24,53}, exponent width w=W−p∈{5,8,11}, sign bit S=2W−1, exponent_mask =2w−1. A pattern of F is an integer 0≤b<2W, written uniquely as b=σS+E2p−1+f with σ∈{0,1}, exponent field 0≤E<2w and fraction 0≤f<2p−1.
  • decode(F, b): the reference definition; with these fields, E=2w−1 gives Infinite { negative } when f=0 and NaN { negative, fraction: f } when f=0; any other E gives Finite { negative, value }. In each case negative is σ=1.
  • For binary64, W=64, p=53, w=11, the sign bit is 263, the exponent field is bits 52 to 62 and the fraction is bits 0 to 51.
  • widen_bits(F, b) on NaN { negative, fraction }: with shift =53−p=k, the pattern sign | (0x7ff << 52) | (fraction << shift), where sign is 263 when negative holds and 0 otherwise. On Infinite { negative }: Rounded::Overflow { negative }.bits(Format::B64).
  • narrow_bits(F, c) on decode(Format::B64, c) = NaN { negative, fraction }: None when fraction & ((1 << k) - 1) is non-zero; otherwise Some(sign | (exponent_mask << (p - 1)) | (fraction >> k)) with sign the sign bit of F when negative holds and 0 otherwise. On Infinite { negative }: Some(Rounded::Overflow { negative }.bits(F)).
  • Rounded::Overflow { negative }.bits(F): the pattern of F with all-ones exponent field, zero fraction and sign bit set exactly when negative holds.
  • Quiet flag: the top fraction bit of a NaN pattern, bit p−2.

Proof

  1. Item 1, widening. Let b decode under F to NaN { negative: s, fraction: f }; by the definition of decode, b has sign bit s, exponent field 2w−1 and fraction f with 0<f<2p−1, and no other bits since b<2W. widen_bits returns c=σ263+(211−1)252+f2k with σ=1 exactly when s. Since 0<f2k<2p−1+k=252, the three summands occupy disjoint bit ranges, so c has sign bit s, all-ones exponent field and fraction f2k=0; decode(Format::B64, c) is NaN { negative: s, fraction: f · 2^k }. Bit p−2 of f moves to bit p−2+k=51.
  2. Item 1, narrowing back. The fraction f2k has its low k bits zero, so narrow_bits(F, c) returns Some(h) with h = sign bit of F when s, plus (2w−1)2p−1, plus (f2k)/2k=f. These are exactly the fields of b, so h=b.
  3. Item 2. Let c decode under Format::B64 to NaN { negative: s, fraction: g }, so 0<g<252. By the definition of narrow_bits, the result is None exactly when gmod2k=0. Otherwise g=g′2k with g′=g/2k, 0<g′<252−k=2p−1, and narrow_bits returns h with sign bit s, exponent field 2w−1 and fraction g′; since g′=0, decode(F, h) is NaN { negative: s, fraction: g' }. Step 1 applied to h gives widen_bits(F, h) with sign bit s, all-ones exponent and fraction g′2k=g, which is c.
  4. Item 3. The infinity of F with sign s decodes to Infinite { negative: s }; widen_bits returns Overflow { negative: s }.bits(Format::B64), the binary64 pattern with sign s, all-ones exponent and zero fraction, which decodes to Infinite { negative: s }; narrow_bits returns Overflow { negative: s }.bits(F), the infinity of F with sign s.
  5. Binary32. At F = Format::B32, p=24 and k=29, so items 1 and 2 read as stated in the final paragraph of the Statement. The case analysis of decode (finite, infinite, NaN) is complete: NaN patterns are covered by steps 1 to 3, infinite ones by step 4, and finite ones are outside the law.
  6. Production correspondence. For binary16, the differential compares widen_bits with binary16_widen and narrow_bits with binary16_bits. For binary32, it compares widen_bits with an independently constructed carrier pattern and narrow_bits with binary32_bits. It checks the binary64 zero-shift identities only in the reference model, in accordance with the production boundary stated above.

Closest-shortest printing breaks ties to even

Statement

The block has two parts. Part I is the rounding lemma: the properties of round_to on which the float laws of this page rest, stated here because this is the first block that uses them (the last block of the page restates them as its law). Part II is the closest-shortest printer law.

Part I. For every format F∈{Format::B16, Format::B32, Format::B64}, every rational q that satisfies Premise P and every boolean z, the reference operation round_to(F, q, z) returns a result, and the result satisfies the following six items R1 to R6, with S, VF​, MF​ and “even” as defined below.

  • R1. (Signed zero.) If q=0, the result is Finite(S) when z holds and Finite(0) otherwise.
  • R2. (Signed overflow.) If ∣q∣≥MF​, the result is Overflow { negative } with negative true exactly when q<0.
  • R3. (Nearest, ties to even.) If 0<∣q∣<MF​, the result is Finite(b), where the sign bit of b is set exactly when q<0, decode(F, b) is Finite { negative, value: v } with negative true exactly when q<0, and ∣v−q∣≤∣t−q∣ for every t∈VF​. If moreover some t∈VF​ with t=v has ∣t−q∣=∣v−q∣, then t is the only such element, b is even, and the pattern whose sign bit equals that of b and whose value is t is odd. In particular a non-zero q whose nearest value is zero gives the zero of the sign of q.
  • R4. (Grid.) The non-negative elements of VF​ are exactly the numbers n⋅2emin​−p+1 with 0≤n<2p−1 and n⋅2m−p+1 with emin​≤m≤emax​ and 2p−1≤n<2p. The map from the patterns 0,1,…,bmax​ to their values is strictly increasing, where bmax​=(2w−1)2p−1−1 is the largest pattern with a clear sign bit that decodes as finite, and maxVF​=2emax​+1−2emax​−p+1. For a finite pattern b<S, the pattern b+S decodes to the negation of the value of b and has the same lowest bit.
  • R5. (Sign symmetry.) For every rational r>0 and booleans z,z′: round_to(F, -r, z) is Finite(S + b) when round_to(F, r, z') is Finite(b), and is Overflow { negative: true } when round_to(F, r, z') is Overflow { negative: false }.
  • R6. (Round trip.) For every pattern b<2W with decode(F, b) equal to Finite { negative: s, value: v }, round_to(F, v, s) is Finite(b).

Part II. Let F be Format::B16, Format::B32 or Format::B64, and let b<2W be a pattern with decode(F, b) = Finite { negative: s, value: v }. Then the closest-shortest printer shortest(F, b) (the reference operation, which the production printers DecimalValue::from_f16_shortest, from_f32_shortest and from_f64_shortest are required to equal exactly, the sign of a zero included) returns Some(D) with D.negative =s, and:

  • P1. if v=0, then D is the zero Dec { negative: s, coefficient: 0, exponent: 0 };
  • P2. if v=0, let b+=b with its sign bit cleared, x=∣v∣, and R the set of rationals r≥0 with round_to(F, r, false) = Finite(b⁺). Then D.coefficient is positive and not divisible by 10, and ∣D.value∣∈R (the printed decimal reads back to b+);
  • P3. (fewest digits) no positive decimal in R has fewer significant digits than D;
  • P4. (closest) every positive decimal d∈R with as many significant digits as D satisfies ∣d−x∣≥​∣D.value∣−x​;
  • P5. (ties to even) if such a d=∣D.value∣ has ∣d−x∣=​∣D.value∣−x​, then d is the only one, the last significant digit of D.coefficient is even, and the last significant digit of d is odd.

Outside the domain

  • Part I: a rational that does not satisfy Premise P is outside the proved domain. The implementation still returns a Rounded value because its conversions have fallbacks, but this law makes no arithmetic claim about that fallback path. Under Premise P, round_to never refuses and none of those fallbacks is taken (steps 11 and 26). Rounded::Overflow { negative } is a result of the operation, not a refusal; the exact float reading turns it into FidelityReason::Overflow, and the nearest reading turns it into the infinity of its sign.
  • Part II: a NaN or infinite pattern: midpoints returns None and shortest returns None; no decimal is printed. This is a result of the operation, not a refusal; callers that need text for such a pattern use their own spelling.
  • Part II: a value b≥2W is not a pattern of F, and the operation is not defined on it. The case does not arise: every caller in the reference passes either a pattern of the format or the binary32 pattern returned by narrow_bits, which is below 232, and the production printers take a value of the format (from_f32_shortest an f32, from_f64_shortest an f64, and from_f16_shortest an f64 holding a binary16 value).

Definitions used

  • Format parameters. For a format F, width W∈{16,32,64}, precision p∈{11,24,53}, exponent_bits w=W−p∈{5,8,11}, bias =2w−1−1, emin emin​=1−bias and emax emax​=bias. fraction_mask is 2p−1−1, exponent_mask is 2w−1 and sign_bit is S=2W−1. In each format p≥2 and 2w−2=2bias.
  • Pattern. An integer b with 0≤b<2W, written uniquely as b=σS+E⋅2p−1+f with σ∈{0,1}, 0≤E<2w and 0≤f<2p−1 (unique because W=1+w+(p−1)). Its lowest bit is bmod2; the pattern is even when this bit is 0 and odd otherwise.
  • decode(F, b). As defined in the reference: with sign σ, biased exponent E and fraction f, an all-ones E gives Infinite { negative } when f=0 and NaN { negative, fraction: f } otherwise; otherwise it gives Finite { negative, value } with value (−1)σN2Q, where (N,Q)=(f, emin​−p+1) when E=0 and (N,Q)=(2p−1+f, E−bias−p+1) when E≥1. In every case negative is σ=1.
  • VF​. The set of values v such that decode(F, b) is Finite { value: v, .. } for some pattern b.
  • MF​. The overflow threshold 2emax​+1−2emax​−p, the midpoint of maxVF​ and 2emax​+1.
  • Nat, Int, Rat and their operations. The definitions in num.rs (Nat as base-109 limbs with add, checked_sub, mul_small, shift_limbs, shift10, mul, div_small, div_rem, cmp, gcd, pow, pow2; Int as sign and magnitude; Rat as a pair built by Rat::new; pow2_wide, pow2_by_halving, pow10_wide and pow10_by_halving). Steps 1 to 9 prove that these are exact natural, integer and rational arithmetic and order.
  • floor_log2, floor_log10, bit_length, digit_count, Nat::is_even, Rat::floor. The definitions in num.rs: floor_log2(r) is None for r≤0 and otherwise, with e the bit length of the numerator less that of the denominator, e−1 when 2e>r and e otherwise; floor_log10 is the same with decimal digit counts and powers of ten. Steps 10 to 13 prove that these compute ⌊log2​r⌋, ⌊log10​r⌋, the binary and decimal lengths, parity and the floor.
  • Rationals. Rat holds a rational in lowest terms with a positive denominator, so == and cmp on Rat are equality and order of rational numbers, and add, sub, mul, div, floor, abs and neg are the exact operations (steps 8 and 12).
  • Premise P (a property of the operands, not proved here): every Nat whose bit_length or digit_count floor_log2 or floor_log10 converts to i64 has bit length and digit count below 263, so those conversions succeed. Rationals decoded from the finite patterns and midpoint intervals of the supported binary formats satisfy this bound. A decimal numeral needs a bound on its expanded magnitude as well as its coefficient length: the 22-character numeral 1e10000000000000000000 denotes 101019, whose numerator has more than 3⋅1019>263 bits. Its written length thus does not establish Premise P.
  • round_to(F, q, z). The reference definition: negative is z when q=0 and q<0 otherwise, sign is S when negative holds and 0 otherwise; a zero q returns Finite(sign); otherwise, with e = floor_log2(|q|), qe =max(e,emin​)−p+1, scaled s=∣q∣/2qe, floor n0​=⌊s⌋ and rem r=s−n0​, the significand n is n0​+1 when r>1/2 or (r=1/2 and n0​ odd), else n0​; a significand of 2p becomes 2p−1 with qe increased by one; a zero significand returns Finite(sign); qe +p−1>emax​ returns Overflow { negative }; a significand below 2p−1 returns Finite(sign | n); otherwise the result is Finite(sign | (qe + p - 1 + bias) << (p - 1) | (n - 2^(p-1))).
  • shortest, midpoints, ceil_div (the ceiling of a.div(u), computed from floor and is_integer), lo_floor_div (the magnitude of the floor of a.div(u)), pick_closer, last_significant_digit, Dec::normalized, Dec::value and Dec::significant_digits: the reference definitions in module float.
  • Decimal. A rational of the form a⋅10k with a,k integers. A positive decimal is uniquely a⋅10k with a≥1 not divisible by 10; its significant digits are the decimal digits of this a, their number is written #(d), and its last significant digit is amod10, which is non-zero. last_significant_digit(c) returns the least-weight non-zero digit of c (Nat::digit(i) is the digit of weight 10i), which is the last significant digit of c⋅10k for every k.
  • Dec::normalized(neg, c, k): for c=0 the zero Dec { negative: neg, coefficient: 0, exponent: 0 }; otherwise c with its trailing zero digits removed and k increased by their number, so the value c⋅10k (with the sign) is unchanged and the coefficient is not divisible by 10.

Proof

Part I.

  1. Lemma (representation of Nat). Write B=109. A Nat is a vector of u32 limbs ℓ0​,…,ℓn−1​, least significant first, and denotes ∑i​ℓi​Bi. Call the vector normal when every limb is below B and the last limb is non-zero (the empty vector denotes 0). from_u128 pushes nmodB while n>0, so its last limb is the final non-zero n<B; parse pushes nine-digit chunks, each below B, and calls normalized; normalized pops most-significant zero limbs, which leaves the sum unchanged. Steps 3 to 7 take normal operands; that their results are normal again is shown at the end of step 9, so by induction on the construction every Nat is normal. A natural number has exactly one normal vector (its base-B expansion), so the derived == on limbs is equality of numbers, and limb(i), zero past the end, is the base-B digit of weight Bi.

  2. Lemma (Nat::cmp). cmp compares the numbers of limbs, then the limbs from the most significant down, returning the first difference. For normal vectors, x with more limbs than y has x≥Bn−1>y, since y<Bn−1 when y has at most n−1 limbs. With equal lengths and first difference at limb i, the higher limbs agree and the lower parts are below Bi, so the order of ℓi​ decides. Hence cmp is the order of natural numbers, and <, > and min/max are too.

  3. Lemma (Nat::add). With c0​=0, the loop sets si​=ai​+bi​+ci​, pushes si​modB and carries ci+1​=⌊si​/B⌋. By induction ci​∈{0,1} (as si​≤2B−1, far below 264) and ∑j<i​oj​Bj+ci​Bi=∑j<i​(aj​+bj​)Bj. After n=max of the two lengths, pushing the final carry gives a+b.

  4. Lemma (Nat::checked_sub). It returns None exactly when a<b (step 2). Otherwise, with borrow β0​=0, it sets ti​=bi​+βi​ and pushes ai​−ti​ with βi+1​=0 when ai​≥ti​, and ai​+B−ti​ with βi+1​=1 otherwise; each pushed limb lies in [0,B). By induction ∑j<i​oj​Bj−βi​Bi=∑j<i​(aj​−bj​)Bj. After the n limbs of a (b≤a has at most n limbs), ∑j<n​oj​Bj−βn​Bn=a−b≥0 with 0≤∑j<n​oj​Bj<Bn, so βn​=0 and the result is a−b.

  5. Lemma (mul_small, shift_limbs, shift10, mul). For 0≤d<B (every call has such d: a limb in mul, a quotient digit below B in div_rem by step 7, 10kmod9≤108 in shift10, and 2 in gcd), mul_small sets pi​=xi​d+ci​, pushes pi​modB and carries ci+1​=⌊pi​/B⌋; by induction ci​<B, so pi​<B2<264, and ∑j<i​oj​Bj+ci​Bi=d∑j<i​xj​Bj; the final loop writes the last carry in base B, so the result is dx. shift_limbs(k) prepends k zero limbs to a non-zero x (and returns 0 for x=0), giving xBk. shift10(k) is x⋅10kmod9⋅B⌊k/9⌋=x⋅10k. mul(x, y) accumulates ∑i​(xyi​)Bi=xy by step 3.

  6. Lemma (div_small, half). For 0<d≤232, div_small runs from the most significant limb with carry initially 0; by induction, before limb i the carry is c=Xi+1​modd, where Xi+1​=∑j>i​xj​Bj−i−1, and the limbs written so far are the base-B digits of ⌊Xi+1​/d⌋. Then cur =cB+xi​=Xi​−⌊Xi+1​/d⌋dB satisfies cur <dB≤232⋅109<262, the digit cur / d is below B, and the new carry is cur % d =Xi​modd; since Xi​=BXi+1​+xi​, the digits now spell ⌊Xi​/d⌋. At the end the result is (⌊x/d⌋,xmodd). half is ⌊x/2⌋.

  7. Lemma (div_rem). For a non-zero divisor v with k limbs, div_rem(x, v) performs long division in base B. Invariant: before processing limb i (from the top), rem =Xi+1​modv with Xi+1​ as in step 6, so rem <v. The new remainder r′=rem⋅B+xi​ (steps 3 and 5) satisfies r′<vB and r′=Xi​−⌊Xi+1​/v⌋vB. Let δ=⌊r′/v⌋, which is below B. The estimate is at most δ. For k=1, lead is v and top is r′ itself (the limbs 1,0 of r′<B2), so the estimate top / lead is δ. For k≥2, write v=V1​Bk−1+V2​Bk−2+v′ with v′<Bk−2; lead =V1​B+V2​+1, so v<lead⋅Bk−2, and since r′<vB<Bk+1, top (limbs k down to k−2 of r′) is ⌊r′/Bk−2⌋. Then top/lead≤(r′/Bk−2)/(v/Bk−2)=r′/v, so ⌊top/lead⌋≤δ. In both cases top <B3 fits u128 and the estimate, at most δ<B, fits u64, so the fallback of u64::try_from is not taken. The correction loop. Starting from q = the estimate and product =vq (step 5), the loop replaces (q,product) by (q+1,product+v) while product + v ≤r′ (step 2); it stops at the least q with v(q+1)>r′, which is δ, after at most δ passes. Then checked_sub gives r′−vδ=r′modv=Xi​modv (step 4; its None is impossible as vδ≤r′), and the quotient digit δ<B is stored. After the last limb, x=Qv+R with Q the digit vector (normalized) and 0≤R<v, so div_rem returns (⌊x/v⌋,xmodv); it returns None only for v=0.

  8. Lemma (Nat::gcd, Int, Rat). gcd(a, b) returns b for a=0 and a for b=0. Otherwise it halves both (half, step 6) while both are even (is_even tests the least limb, whose parity is that of the number because B is even), doubling an exact Nat factor f, initially 1, by mul_small(2) (step 5); then halves x while it is even; then, while y=0, halves y while it is even and replaces (x,y) by (min,max−min); it returns x⋅f. Invariant: gcd(x,y)⋅f=gcd(a,b). Halving both and doubling f preserves it because gcd(2x′,2y′)=2gcd(x′,y′). The factor never exceeds min(a,b) and needs no fixed-width exponent counter. After the first loop one of x, y is odd; halving an even x while y is odd preserves gcd(x,y) because 2 divides only one of them, and afterwards x is odd, which every later step keeps (x becomes the minimum of two odd numbers). Halving an even y while x is odd preserves gcd for the same reason, and gcd(min,max−min)=gcd(x,y). Each pass of the main loop with y=0 makes x, y odd and replaces x+y by max(x,y)<x+y, so the loop ends, with y=0 and gcd(x,0)=x. Hence gcd is the greatest common divisor. An Int is a sign and a Nat magnitude, and Int::new clears the sign of zero; add adds magnitudes of equal signs and otherwise subtracts the smaller magnitude from the larger (steps 2, 4), keeping the sign of the larger; neg, sub, mul and cmp are the sign rules on exact magnitudes. So Int is exact integer arithmetic and order. Rat::new(n, d) refuses d=0, and otherwise divides n and d by g=gcd(∣n∣,d) (exactly, div_rem with zero remainder) unless g=1, giving lowest terms with d>0; from_int, zero, abs, neg, pow2 and pow10 build pairs already in lowest terms with positive denominator; add, sub, mul and div apply the fraction formulas and Rat::new (div moves the sign of the divisor to the numerator); cmp compares nd′ with n′d, which is the order of rationals as d,d′>0. Since the lowest-terms form with positive denominator is unique, the derived == on Rat is equality of rationals.

  9. Lemma (powers). Nat::pow(base, e) keeps acc⋅be=baseexp (an odd e moves one factor b into acc, then b is squared and e halved) and stops at e=0, returning baseexp. Nat::pow2(k) returns a memoized value that was computed as pow(2, k) and stored unchanged, so it is 2k. pow2_by_halving(m, limit) is 2m for every m, by strong induction on m: when m≤ limit and m fits u32 it is Nat::pow2(m); otherwise m>0, the recursive call on h=⌊m/2⌋<m gives 2h by the induction hypothesis, its square is 22h, and a further factor 2 when m is odd gives 2m. pow2_wide(m) is pow2_by_halving(m, 2^32 - 1), so it is 2m for every u64 m, and Rat::pow2(k) is 1/2∣k∣ for k<0 and 2k/1 otherwise: exactly 2k for every i64 k, in lowest terms. Nat::pow10(k) is one().shift10(k) =10k (step 5). The same strong-induction argument proves pow10_by_halving(m, limit) = 10^m: its recursive case squares 10⌊m/2⌋ and multiplies by 10 exactly when m is odd. pow10_wide(m) chooses the largest exponent that the target’s usize can represent for its direct branch, so, under Premise A, Rat::pow10(k) builds 10∣k∣/1 or 1/10∣k∣ exactly for every i64 k, without saturating the exponent on a narrower target. Normal results. add, checked_sub, mul_small, div_small and the quotient of div_rem push limbs below B (steps 3 to 7) and end with normalized, which removes the most-significant zeros; shift_limbs prepends zeros to a normal non-zero vector; mul, pow, the remainder of div_rem and shift10 are built from these. So each u32::try_from(·).unwrap_or(0) in them converts a number below B<232 and its fallback is not taken, and every result is normal, which completes the induction of step 1.

  10. Lemma (bit_length and digit_count). Let x be a Nat (step 1). (a) For x≥1, x.bit_length() is the least c with x<2c: by step 6 (div_small by 232) the loop keeps n=⌊x/2bits⌋ (initially n=x, bits=0; each pass replaces n by ⌊n/232⌋ and adds 32), and stops when ⌊n/232⌋=0, that is n<232, returning bits+c0​ where c0​=64− leading_zeros(n) is the least c0​ with n<2c0​. Then x<(n+1)2bits≤2c0​+bits, and x≥n2bits≥2c0​−1+bits since n≥2c0​−1 (n≥1: on the first pass n=x≥1, and a later pass is entered only with ⌊n/232⌋≥1). So 2c−1≤x<2c for c = bit_length. (b) For x≥1 with ℓ limbs and top limb t≥1, digit_count is 9(ℓ−1)+d with d the length of the decimal text of t, so 10d−1≤t<10d; since x=t⋅109(ℓ−1)+y with 0≤y<109(ℓ−1), we get 10L−1≤x<10L for L = digit_count.

  11. Lemma (floor_log2, floor_log10). Let r>0 be a Rat with numerator a′≥1 and denominator b′≥1, and let a, b be their bit lengths. By step 10(a), 2a−1≤a′<2a and 2b−1≤b′<2b, so 2a−b−1<r<2a−b+1. Under Premise P the conversions of a and b to i64 succeed (the fallback i64::MAX is not taken) and e=a−b does not overflow. floor_log2(r) returns e−1 when Rat::pow2(e) > r and e otherwise; Rat::pow2(e) is exactly 2e (step 9) and the comparison is the exact order of rationals (step 8). In the first case 2e−1<r<2e; in the second 2e≤r<2e+1. Either way the result g satisfies 2g≤r<2g+1. For a zero or negative Rat it returns None. The same argument with digit counts (step 10(b)), 10ℓa​−ℓb​−1<r<10ℓa​−ℓb​+1, Premise P for the digit counts, and the exact comparison with Rat::pow10(e) =10e (step 9; here ∣e∣≤max(ℓa​,ℓb​) is at most the largest usize) shows that floor_log10(r) is the integer g with 10g≤r<10g+1.

  12. Lemma (Rat::floor on non-negative rationals, ceil_div, lo_floor_div). For a Rat r=a′/b′≥0, floor computes (Q,R) = div_rem(a', b') (step 7) with a′=Qb′+R, 0≤R<b′, and, r not being negative, returns Q=⌊r⌋. For a≥0 and u>0, a.div(u) is the exact quotient a/u≥0 (it is None only for u=0). lo_floor_div(a, u) returns the magnitude of ⌊a/u⌋, which is ⌊a/u⌋. ceil_div(a, u) returns ⌊a/u⌋ when a/u is an integer (is_integer tests denominator 1, which in lowest terms is exactly integrality) and ⌊a/u⌋+1 otherwise; both equal ⌈a/u⌉.

  13. Lemma (Nat::is_even). is_even tests limb(0) % 2 == 0, where limb(0) is the least limb, xmod109 (and 0 for x=0, which has no limbs). Since 109 is even, x≡xmod109(mod2), so is_even holds exactly when x is even.

  14. Lemma (Format constants). By the definitions in Format, p≥11≥2, w=W−p≥5, bias =2w−1−1, so 2w−2=2bias and emax​−emin​=2bias−1; fraction_mask, exponent_mask and sign_bit are 2p−1−1, 2w−1 and 2W−1 by their shift expressions.

  15. Decoding table. By the definition of decode, a pattern b=σS+E2p−1+f with E<2w−1 has value (−1)σN2Q with (N,Q) as in the definition. Since 2p−1 is even (p≥2), N≡f≡b(mod2), so the lowest bit of b is the parity of N. Changing σ changes neither E, f, N, Q nor the lowest bit (as S is even), and negates the value. This proves the last sentence of item R4.

  16. Grid and monotonicity (item R4). Take σ=0. For E=0 the values are n2emin​−p+1 with n=f∈[0,2p−1), all in [0,2emin​). For 1≤E≤2w−2 put m=E−bias; then emin​≤m≤2w−2−bias=emax​, and the values are n2m−p+1 with n=2p−1+f∈[2p−1,2p), all in [2m,2m+1). These are exactly the numbers listed in item R4. The intervals [0,2emin​) and [2m,2m+1) for m=emin​,…,emax​ are disjoint and increase with E, and for fixed E the value increases with f; since b=E2p−1+f orders patterns first by E and then by f, the value is strictly increasing in b on 0,…,bmax​, where bmax​ has E=2w−2 and f=2p−1−1, that is bmax​=(2w−1)2p−1−1, with value (2p−1)2emax​−p+1=2emax​+1−2emax​−p+1. Two consequences are used below: (a) for emin​≤m≤emax​, 2m=2p−1⋅2m−p+1∈VF​; (b) by step 15, a non-zero value of VF​ together with a sign bit determines its pattern.

  17. Zero (item R1). If q=0, negative is z and the definition returns Finite(sign) before any other computation; sign is S when z holds and 0 otherwise. Both patterns have E=0 and f=0 and decode to the value 0.

  18. Set-up for q>0. Let q>0; then negative is false, sign is 0, and z is not consulted. floor_log2(q) is e with 2e≤q<2e+1 (step 11). Put m=max(e,emin​), u=2m−p+1 (so qe =m−p+1), s=q/u, n0​=⌊s⌋ and r=s−n0​∈[0,1). If e≥emin​ then u=2e−p+1 and 2p−1≤s<2p, so 2p−1≤n0​≤2p−1. If e<emin​ then u=2emin​−p+1 and 0<s<2p−1, so 0≤n0​≤2p−1−1. The definition sets n=n0​+1 exactly when r>1/2 or (r=1/2 and !significand.is_even(), that is n0​ odd by step 13), and n=n0​ otherwise.

  19. The two candidates when e≤emax​. We show that n0​u∈VF​, that (n0​+1)u∈VF​ unless e=emax​ and n0​=2p−1, and that no element of VF​ lies strictly between n0​u and (n0​+1)u. Case e≥emin​: n0​u is a grid number of binade m=e (step 16); (n0​+1)u is one too when n0​+1<2p, and otherwise equals 2e+1, which lies in VF​ when e+1≤emax​ by step 16(a) and exceeds maxVF​ when e=emax​. The open interval (n0​u,(n0​+1)u) lies in [2e,2e+1), whose elements of VF​ are multiples of u (step 16), and contains no multiple of u. Case e<emin​: n0​u with n0​<2p−1 is a grid number with E=0; (n0​+1)u is one too when n0​+1<2p−1 and otherwise equals 2emin​∈VF​ by step 16(a); the open interval lies in [0,2emin​), whose elements of VF​ are multiples of u. Consequently every t∈VF​ other than the two candidates satisfies t<n0​u or t>(n0​+1)u (negative elements satisfy t<0≤n0​u), hence ∣t−q∣>q−n0​u=ru or ∣t−q∣>(n0​+1)u−q=(1−r)u. So the nearest elements of VF​ to q are among the two candidates, and a tie with an element outside them is impossible.

  20. The result when e≤emax​. The cases on n are exhaustive. (a) n=0. Then n0​=0, which forces e<emin​, and the definition returns Finite(0), whose value 0=nu. (b) 1≤n<2p−1. Then e<emin​ (when e≥emin​, n≥n0​≥2p−1), there is no carry, qe +p−1=emin​≤emax​, and the result is Finite(n): E=0, f=n, value n2emin​−p+1=nu. (c) 2p−1≤n<2p. There is no carry and qe +p−1=m≤emax​, so the result is the pattern with E=m+bias∈[1,2w−2] and f=n−2p−1, of value n2m−p+1=nu. (d) n=2p. Then e≥emin​, n0​=2p−1 and the definition rounded up. The carry gives significand 2p−1 and exponent e+1, the value 2p−12e−p+2=2e+1=nu. If e=emax​ the result is Overflow { negative: false }; otherwise E=e+1+bias≤2w−2, f=0, and the pattern decodes to 2e+1. In every case except the overflow of (d), the returned pattern has a clear sign bit and decodes to nu, and nu is the candidate at distance min(ru,(1−r)u): n0​u when r<1/2, (n0​+1)u when r>1/2, and the one with even multiplier when r=1/2. The overflow of (d) occurs exactly when e=emax​, n0​=2p−1 and r≥1/2 (r>1/2, or r=1/2 with n0​ odd), that is, since q<2emax​+1 here, exactly when q≥(2p−21​)2emax​−p+1=MF​. When e=emax​, n0​=2p−1 and r<1/2, the second candidate is not in VF​ and the result n0​u is the unique nearest element.

  21. The case e>emax​. Then q≥2emax​+1>MF​. Since n≥n0​≥2p−1>0, the zero-significand return is not taken, and the exponent qe +p−1 is e or (after a carry) e+1, both above emax​; the result is Overflow { negative: false }. With step 20, for q>0 the result overflows exactly when q≥MF​, which is item R2 for q>0.

  22. Ties and parity (item R3 for q>0). Let 0<q<MF​. By steps 19 and 20 the result is Finite(b) with a clear sign bit, decode gives negative: false, and its value v=nu is a nearest element of VF​. If r=1/2 the two candidates are at different distances, so by step 19 v is the unique nearest element. If r=1/2 the two candidates tie and no other element ties (step 19); the chosen multiplier n is even and the other multiplier n′ is odd, with 1≤n′≤2p−1. By step 15 the lowest bit of b is the parity of its N, which is n in cases (a) to (c) and 2p−1 in case (d), even in all of them; so b is even. The other candidate n′u has, by steps 16 and 20 (cases (b), (c)), the pattern with N=n′, which is odd. A non-zero q whose nearest value is 0 falls in case (a) and returns Finite(0), the zero of the sign of q.

  23. Negative q (R2, R3 and R5). Let q<0 and r=∣q∣. The definition computes magnitude =∣q∣ and every quantity of step 18 from it alone; it differs from the run on r (with any z′) only in that negative is true and sign is S. Hence round_to(F, q, z) is Finite(S | b) = Finite(S + b) when round_to(F, r, z') is Finite(b) (whose sign bit is clear by steps 20 and 22), and Overflow { negative: true } when that run overflows; this is item R5. The symmetry used is the map t↦−t, a bijection of VF​ onto itself (step 15) with ∣(−t)−q∣=∣t−r∣, under which the pattern b corresponds to S+b, of the same lowest bit (step 15). It carries the nearest elements, the unique tie partner and the parities for r (step 22) to those for q, and the overflow condition r≥MF​ (step 21) to ∣q∣≥MF​. This proves R2 and R3 for q<0.

  24. Round trip (item R6). Let decode(F, b) be Finite { negative: s, value: v }. If v=0 then E=0 and f=0, so b=S when s holds and b=0 otherwise, and item R1 gives round_to(F, 0, s) = Finite(b). If v=0 then 0<∣v∣≤maxVF​<MF​, and item R3 gives Finite(b') whose value v′ satisfies ∣v′−v∣≤∣v−v∣=0, so v′=v; the sign bit of b′ is set exactly when v<0, that is exactly when s holds (by step 15 the sign of a non-zero value is its sign bit). By step 16(b) a non-zero value and a sign bit determine the pattern, so b′=b.

  25. R1 to R6 hold together. R1, R2, R3, R4, R5 and R6 are proved in steps 17, 21 and 23, 22 and 23, 15 and 16, 23, and 24 respectively, and the cases q=0, q>0 and q<0 are exhaustive.

  26. No fallback is taken. For q=0, floor_log2(|q|) is Some since ∣q∣>0; the division by 2qe=0 is Some; the final significand is below 2p≤253, so to_u64 is Some; and the biased exponent qe +p−1+ bias is at least emin​+bias=1 when it is computed, so u64::try_from succeeds. Hence each unwrap_or and unwrap_or_else in the definition returns its Some or Ok value, and the operation is total, which is the claim for Part I in Outside the domain.

Part II.

  1. Zero. If v=0 then b+=0; midpoints(F, 0) is Some((0, lo, hi)), and since x is zero shortest returns Dec::normalized(s, 0, 0), the zero of P1, with D.negative =s because negative is computed as the sign bit of b.

  2. The interval. Let v=0, so 1≤b+≤bmax​ and decode(F, b⁺) is Finite { negative: false, value: x } (R4). midpoints takes below = the value of b+−1 (finite, since b+−1<bmax​) and above = the value of b++1 when b+<bmax​, and 2emax​+1 when b+=bmax​, because bmax​+1 has an all-ones exponent and zero fraction and decodes as Infinite (the NaN arm is never taken). It returns (x,lo,hi) with lo=(x+below)/2 and hi=(x+above)/2. By R4, 0≤below<x<above, no element of VF​ lies strictly between below and x or between x and above, and for b+=bmax​, hi=MF​.

  3. R is the interval from lo to hi. We show: R contains every r with lo<r<hi; it contains lo and hi exactly when b+ is even; and it contains no r outside [lo,hi]. Let r≥0. Elements of VF​ other than below, x and above are below below or above above (step 28), hence farther from any r∈[below,above] than below or above. (i) lo<r<hi: then ∣r−x∣<r−below and ∣r−x∣<above−r, so x is the unique nearest element and r<MF​ (for b+=bmax​ because hi=MF​, otherwise because r<above≤maxVF​); R3 returns a pattern of value x with clear sign bit, which is b+ by R4. (ii) r=lo: below and x tie and nothing is nearer; their positive patterns b+−1 and b+ have opposite parities, and R3 returns the even one, which is b+ exactly when b+ is even. (iii) r=hi: if b+<bmax​, x and above tie with patterns b+ and b++1, and the result is b+ exactly when b+ is even; if b+=bmax​, then r=MF​ and R2 gives Overflow, while bmax​ (fraction all ones) is odd, so again r∈R exactly when b+ is even. (iv) r<lo: if r=0, R1 gives Finite(0), which is not Finite(b⁺) because b+≥1. If 0<r<lo, then r<MF​ (as lo<x≤maxVF​<MF​), so R3 applies; below is strictly nearer to r than x (if r≤below trivially, and otherwise r−below<x−r because r<lo), so x is not a nearest element and the pattern returned, whose value is a nearest element, is not b+. (v) r>hi: if r≥MF​, R2 gives Overflow, not Finite(b⁺). If hi<r<MF​, then b+<bmax​ (for bmax​, hi=MF​), R3 applies, and above is strictly nearer to r than x (if r≥above trivially, and otherwise above−r<r−x because r>hi), so again the result is not b+. Consequently R is an interval (any number between two elements of R is in R), x∈R, and R⊆[lo,hi].

  4. What the search computes. Since x>0, floor_log10(x) is Some(e) with 10e≤x<10e+1 (step 11). At iteration k=1,2,… the loop sets uk​=10e−k+1 (computed by Rat::pow10, exact by step 9 because ∣e−k+1∣<232 for every iteration reached, as shown at the end of this step), first =⌈lo/uk​⌉ and last =⌊hi/uk​⌋ (ceil_div and lo_floor_div compute these for lo,hi≥0 by step 12), so it tests exactly the integers c with lo≤cuk​≤hi, all positive because lo>0, and keeps c exactly when round_to(F, c u_k, false) = Finite(b⁺), that is cuk​∈R. By step 29 the kept set is Wk​={c≥1:cuk​∈R}. The loop returns at the least k with Wk​=∅ the value Dec::normalized(s, c*, e - k + 1), where c∗ is the result of folding pick_closer over Wk​ in increasing order. The loop ends at the latest at k=#(x): x∈R, and x=a10e−#(x)+1 with a an integer, so x/uk​ is an integer for every k≥#(x) and lies in Wk​. Writing x=N2Q (R4) with N<253 and Q≥−1074, x is N5−Q times 10Q when Q<0, whose significant digits number at most those of N51074<253⋅51074<10767, and an integer below 21024<10309 otherwise; so #(x)<800. Also 10−324<2−1074≤x<21024<10309 gives ∣e∣≤324, so every unit exponent reached has ∣e−k+1∣≤324+800<232.

If one element a attains it, every element processed before a is strictly farther, so pick_closer returns a when a arrives (the Greater arm), and keeps a against every later, strictly farther element (the Less arm); c∗=a. If two elements a<a′ attain it, then auk​<x<a′uk​, every c with a<c<a′ has ∣cuk​−x∣<δ and so is not in Wk​, and every element before a is strictly farther; hence the fold holds a when a′ arrives, the Equal arm returns a when last_significant_digit(a) is even and a′ otherwise, and later elements are strictly farther; so c∗ is a if its last significant digit is even, else a′.

Finite decimals compare by exact numeric value

Statement

Under Assumption W, for every pair of finite decimals a,b (values of DecimalValue), a.cmp_numeric(&b) is the order of the rational numbers they denote:

a.cmp_numeric(&b)=cmp(ν(a),ν(b)).

Consequently cmp_numeric ignores scale and the sign of zero: two finite decimals that denote one number compare Equal whatever their exponents and sign flags (1.50 and 1.5; -0, 0 and 0E+3), and two that denote different numbers compare in their mathematical order. The same holds for Decimal::cmp_numeric on two Decimal::Finite values, which is defined as DecimalValue::cmp_numeric of their payloads. The production DecimalValue::cmp_numeric on two values of class DecimalClass::Finite is required to equal this definition exactly.

Outside the domain

Subject to Assumption W, every value of the reference type DecimalValue is in the domain: its digits are a Nat and its exponent an Int, and both types hold only canonical representations (facts N1 and N3 below), so no ill-formed finite decimal can be written. A target that violates Assumption W’s pointer-width condition, or a held value that violates its limb bound, is outside the proved domain. In production, a finite DecimalValue whose digits are empty, contain a byte other than an ASCII digit, or have a leading zero is outside the domain: DecimalValue::new and deserialization refuse it with ExactParseError of reason FidelityReason::NotANumber, and a value built from the public fields in violation of that invariant is not a decimal the law speaks about. The law concerns finite decimals only; a Decimal infinity or NaN is not a DecimalValue and so is not an input of DecimalValue::cmp_numeric.

Definitions used

  • N1. A Nat holds base-109 limbs, least significant first, each limb below 109, with no most-significant zero limb (zero is the empty vector). Every constructor in num.rs keeps both invariants: from_u128, add, checked_sub, mul_small, div_small and div_rem store each limb as a remainder modulo 109 (or a quotient digit below 109) or as a nonnegative difference below 109, parse stores nine-digit chunks, each at most 999999999; normalized strips top zeros, from_u128 stops at zero, and shift_limbs only prepends zero limbs below a nonzero top limb. We write [[n]]=∑i​ℓi​109i∈N for the number denoted by the limbs ℓi​. Since a base-109 representation with every digit below 109 and no leading zero digit is unique, two Nats are equal under the derived == exactly when they denote the same number, and Nat::cmp (fewer limbs is smaller; equal counts compare limbs from the top) is the order of N.
  • N2. Nat’s Display writes the top limb in decimal and every lower limb as exactly nine digits, so n.to_string() is the decimal numeral of [[n]] with no leading zero ("0" for zero); digit_count is its length (under Assumption W below), ⌊log10​[[n]]⌋+1 for [[n]]>0 and 0 for zero.
  • N3. An Int is a sign flag and a Nat magnitude, the flag set only on a nonzero magnitude (Int::new clears it on zero, and every constructor goes through Int::new or builds zero unsigned). It denotes (−1)negative[[magnitude]]∈Z; Int::cmp is the order of Z (a nonnegative is above a negative, two nonnegatives by magnitude, two negatives by reversed magnitude), and Int::add is integer addition.
  • Assumption W (a property of the build, not proved here): the target’s pointer width is at most 64 bits, so every usize is at most 264−1; hence u64::try_from of a usize succeeds and is injective, and usize::try_from of a u64 that came from a usize succeeds with that usize. In addition, every Nat that is held has fewer than usize::MAX / 9 limbs, so the computation (limbs - 1) * 9 + top digits in digit_count stays within usize and is the digit count of N2. On a 64-bit host the bound is about 2×1018 limbs, beyond any installed memory; on wasm32 it is about 4.8×108 limbs (about 1.9 GB), which is assumed here rather than derived. The 64-bit hosts and the wasm32 target panproto builds for satisfy the pointer-width part.
  • A finite decimal d = DecimalValue { negative, digits, exponent } denotes ν(d)=(−1)negative⋅D⋅10e∈Q, with D=[[digits]] and e the integer exponent denotes.
  • The sign class s(d)∈{−1,0,1} is the closure sign in cmp_numeric: 0 when digits is zero, else −1 when negative, else 1.
  • The position p(d)=L(d)+e, with L(d) = digits.digit_count(), is position(), which computes Int::new(false, Nat::from_u64(u64::try_from(L(d)).unwrap_or(0))).add(&exponent); under Assumption W the conversion u64::try_from(L(d)) succeeds, so the fallback 0 is never taken and the first summand is the integer L(d).
  • cmp_magnitude(a, b) compares p(a) with p(b) and, when they are equal, compares the strings pad(a.digits.to_string()) and pad(b.digits.to_string()), where pad appends '0' characters on the right up to the width w=max(L(a),L(b)) (the format specification {text:0<width$}). String comparison is lexicographic on bytes, and the bytes '0' through '9' are increasing.
  • cmp_numeric(a, b) returns s(a).cmp(&s(b)) when s(a)=s(b) or s(a)=0, else cmp_magnitude(a, b) when s(a)=1 and its reverse when s(a)=−1.

Proof

  1. For every finite decimal d, the sign of ν(d) is s(d). If digits is zero then D=0 (N1) and ν(d)=0. Otherwise D>0 and 10e>0, so ν(d) is nonzero with sign (−1)negative, which is s(d) by its definition.
  2. Case s(a)=s(b)=0. By step 1, ν(a)=ν(b)=0, so cmp(ν(a),ν(b)) is Equal, and cmp_numeric returns 0.cmp(&0), which is Equal.
  3. Case s(a)=s(b). cmp_numeric returns cmp(s(a),s(b)). The six cases are (s(a),s(b))∈{(−1,0),(−1,1),(0,1)}, where the result is Less, and {(0,−1),(1,−1),(1,0)}, where it is Greater. By step 1, in each of the first three ν(a)<0=ν(b), ν(a)<0<ν(b) or ν(a)=0<ν(b), so ν(a)<ν(b); in each of the last three the same inequalities hold with a and b exchanged, so ν(a)>ν(b). The result thus equals cmp(ν(a),ν(b)).
  4. Case s(a)=s(b)=0: both digit strings are nonzero. For such d, N2 gives 10L(d)−1≤D<10L(d), so ∣ν(d)∣=D⋅10e∈[10p(d)−1,10p(d)), using p(d)=L(d)+e, which position() computes because under Assumption W its conversion of L(d) to u64 succeeds (the fallback 0 is not taken) and by N3 Int::add is integer addition.
  5. Within the case of step 4, if p(a)<p(b) then ∣ν(a)∣<10p(a)≤10p(b)−1≤∣ν(b)∣, and cmp_magnitude returns p(a).cmp(&p(b)) = Less (N3); if p(a)>p(b), the same argument with a and b exchanged gives ∣ν(a)∣>∣ν(b)∣ and the result Greater. So in both subcases cmp_magnitude(a, b) =cmp(∣ν(a)∣,∣ν(b)∣).
  6. Within the case of step 4, if p(a)=p(b)=p, let w=max(L(a),L(b)). By N2 and the definition of pad, the padded string of a is the w-digit decimal numeral of A=Da​⋅10w−L(a), and likewise for B=Db​⋅10w−L(b). Since ea​=p−L(a), ∣ν(a)∣=Da​10w−L(a)10p−w=A⋅10p−w, and likewise ∣ν(b)∣=B⋅10p−w, so cmp(∣ν(a)∣,∣ν(b)∣)=cmp(A,B). Two decimal numerals of the same length w compare as numbers exactly as they compare lexicographically, because the first differing digit has the largest place value among the differing places and the digit bytes are increasing; this is the String comparison cmp_magnitude returns. So cmp_magnitude(a, b) =cmp(∣ν(a)∣,∣ν(b)∣) here as well.
  7. Still in the case of step 4, if s(a)=s(b)=1 then ν(a)=∣ν(a)∣ and ν(b)=∣ν(b)∣, and cmp_numeric returns cmp_magnitude(a, b), which is cmp(ν(a),ν(b)) by steps 5 and 6. If s(a)=s(b)=−1 then ν=−∣ν∣ for both, negation reverses the order of Q, and cmp_numeric returns the reverse of cmp_magnitude(a, b), which is cmp(ν(a),ν(b)).
  8. Steps 2, 3 and 7 cover every pair of sign classes, so a.cmp_numeric(&b) =cmp(ν(a),ν(b)) for all finite decimals. If ν(a)=ν(b) the result is Equal whatever the exponents and sign flags; in particular every zero (either flag, any exponent) is Equal to every other, and 1.50 (digits 150, exponent −2) is Equal to 1.5 (digits 15, exponent −1), both denoting 3/2.
  9. Decimal::cmp_numeric on (Decimal::Finite(a), Decimal::Finite(b)) takes its first match arm, which returns a.cmp_numeric(b), so step 8 applies to it unchanged.

Decimal compare-total orders representations

Statement

Under Assumption W of L-values-10, Decimal::compare_total is a total order on decimal representations, finite and special, whose equality is equality of representations. For all a,b,c of type Decimal:

  1. a.compare_total(&b) is Equal exactly when a=b under the derived ==, that is, when the two values agree in variant and in every field: sign flag, digits and exponent for a finite value; sign for an infinity; sign, signalling flag and payload for a NaN;
  2. b.compare_total(&a) is the reverse of a.compare_total(&b);
  3. if a.compare_total(&b) and b.compare_total(&c) are both Less, so is a.compare_total(&c).

So compare-total separates every pair of distinct representations, including those that differ only in exponent (1.50 and 1.5), in the sign of zero (-0 and 0), or in a NaN’s flag or payload (NaN, sNaN, NaN1). Its order is the one its definition states: every representation with the sign flag set lies below every one without it; for the clear flag, finite values by number and then, at equal number, by exponent (the larger exponent higher, so 1.2300 < 1.23), then the infinity, then the signalling NaNs, then the quiet NaNs, two NaNs of one flag by payload; for the set flag, that whole order reversed, so finite values by number and, at equal number, the larger exponent lower (-1 < -1.00, -0 < -0.000), and below them the infinity, the signalling NaNs and the quiet NaNs, two NaNs of one flag by reversed payload. The production DecimalValue::compare_total is required to equal this definition exactly.

Outside the domain

Subject to Assumption W, every value of the reference type Decimal is in the domain: a finite payload is a DecimalValue, whose Nat digits and Int exponent hold only canonical representations (facts N1 and N3 of L-values-10), an infinity is a sign, and a NaN is a sign, a flag and a Nat payload, so no ill-formed decimal can be written. A target that violates Assumption W’s pointer-width condition, or a held value that violates its limb bound, is outside the proved domain. In production, a DecimalValue that violates the field invariants (canonical finite digits; "0" digits, zero exponent and canonical payload digits for a special value) is outside the domain: deserialization refuses it with ExactParseError of reason FidelityReason::NotANumber, and DecimalValue::new refuses noncanonical finite digits with the same reason.

Definitions used

  • ν(x), the number a finite decimal denotes, and facts N1 and N3 on Nat and Int, as in L-values-10; e(x) is the integer x.exponent denotes.

  • sign(d) is the negative field of every variant.

  • cmp_total_positive(a, b) uses rank: 0 for finite, 1 for an infinity, 2 for a signalling NaN, 3 for a quiet NaN. Its arms, in order: two finite values compare by cmp_numeric of their absolute values and then by exponent; two NaNs with equal flags compare by p1.cmp(p2) on payloads; every other pair compares by rank.

  • compare_total(a, b): if the sign flags differ, Less when a has the flag set and Greater otherwise; else, if both are finite, a.cmp_numeric(b) when it is not Equal and, when it is, a.exponent.cmp(&b.exponent), reversed when the common sign flag is set; else cmp_total_positive(a, b), reversed when the common sign flag is set.

  • For a decimal d let σ(d)=0 if its flag is set and 1 otherwise, ε(d)=−1 if its flag is set and +1 otherwise. The total key T(d)∈Z×Z×Q×Z, ordered lexicographically, is

    • T(Finite(x))=(σ,0,ν(x),ε⋅e(x));
    • T(Infinite)=(σ,ε,0,0);
    • T(NaN{…,signalling,payload p})=(σ,ε⋅r,ε⋅[[p]],0), with r=2 for a signalling NaN and r=3 for a quiet one.

    In every case the second component is ε⋅rank(d).

Proof

  1. The lexicographic order on Z×Z×Q×Z is a total order, because each component order is total and the first differing component decides.
  2. For all a,b: a.compare_total(&b) =cmp(T(a),T(b)). Case the sign flags differ: compare_total returns Less when a has the flag set, and then σ(a)=0<1=σ(b); it returns Greater otherwise, and then σ(a)=1>0=σ(b).
  3. Case equal flags, both finite, a = Finite(x), b = Finite(y), with common ε: the first two components of T agree, so cmp(T(a),T(b)) compares ν(x) with ν(y) and, when they are equal, εe(x) with εe(y), which is cmp(e(x),e(y)) for ε=+1 and its reverse for ε=−1. By L-values-10, x.cmp_numeric(y) =cmp(ν(x),ν(y)), and by N3 Int::cmp is the order of Z, so this is exactly the value compare_total returns: the numeric comparison when it is not Equal, and otherwise the exponent comparison, reversed for the set flag.
  4. Case equal flags, not both finite, both NaNs with equal signalling flags and payloads pa​,pb​: cmp_total_positive takes its second arm and returns P=cmp([[pa​]],[[pb​]]) (N1). In T the first two components agree and the third are ε[[pa​]] and ε[[pb​]], which compare as P when ε=+1 and as the reverse of P when ε=−1; the fourth components are both 0. compare_total returns P for the clear flag and its reverse for the set flag, which agrees in both subcases.
  5. Case equal flags, not both finite, and not two NaNs of one signalling flag: the first arm of cmp_total_positive needs two finite values and the second two NaNs of one flag, so the third arm returns P=cmp(rank(a),rank(b)). If the ranks differ, the second components εrank(a) and εrank(b) differ and compare as P for ε=+1 and as its reverse for ε=−1, matching compare_total. If the ranks are equal, the rank is not 0 (both would be finite), not 2 or 3 (both would be NaNs of one flag), so it is 1: both are infinities of the same sign, T(a)=T(b)=(σ,ε,0,0), and both sides are Equal. Steps 2 to 5 cover every pair.
  6. T is injective. Suppose T(a)=T(b). Equal first components give equal sign flags, hence equal ε, and then equal second components give equal ranks, hence the same variant and, for NaNs, the same signalling flag. For two finite values, ν(x)=ν(y) and εe(x)=εe(y), hence e(x)=e(y), give [[x.digits]]=∣ν(x)∣⋅10−e(x)=[[y.digits]], so the digits are equal Nats (N1), the exponents are equal Ints (N3), and the flags are equal, so x=y. Two infinities of one sign are equal. For two NaNs, ε[[pa​]]=ε[[pb​]] gives equal payloads (N1), so the NaNs are equal.
  7. By steps 2 to 5, compare_total is cmp∘(T×T). Property 1: Equal holds exactly when T(a)=T(b), which by step 6 holds exactly when a=b (the converse direction because T is a function). Property 2: comparison in a total order reverses when its arguments are exchanged. Property 3: T(a)<T(b)<T(c) gives T(a)<T(c) by step 1.
  8. The described order is read off T: the first component places every set flag below every clear flag; for finite values the third component orders by number and the fourth, εe, orders equal numbers by exponent upward for the clear flag and downward for the set flag (so -1, of exponent 0, is below -1.00, of exponent −2, and -0 below -0.000); the second component εrank orders finite, infinity, signalling NaN, quiet NaN upward for the clear flag and downward for the set flag; and the third component ε[[p]] orders NaN payloads upward for the clear flag and downward for the set flag. For the set flag every component after the first is thus the clear-flag key with its rank, payload and exponent negated, while the number ν, already negative, carries its own reversal of magnitude: this is the clear-flag order reversed.

Comparable temporals follow chronological order

Statement

Let T be the set of values v: Temporal with v.well_formed(). For every a,b∈T:

  1. if comparable(a, b) is false, then cmp_chronological(a, b) = None;
  2. if comparable(a, b) is true, then cmp_chronological(a, b) is never None, and it equals Some of the lexicographic comparison of the chronological keys κ(a) and κ(b) defined below;
  3. for any two strings x,y of ASCII digits, cmp_fraction(x, y) is the comparison of the rationals val(x) and val(y);
  4. (leap seconds) let a be finite and not truncated, with second 60; this covers every finite value with second 60 that has a year, and every time-only value with an hour and second 60, with any offset. If b is comparable with a, finite, not truncated, and U(b)=U(a)+1 with U as below (the whole-second instant of b is the first second of the minute after the minute of a), then cmp_chronological(a, b) = Some(Less) whatever the two fractions; and if c agrees with a in every field and in its offset except that its second is 59, then cmp_chronological(c, a) = Some(Less) whatever the two fractions. A leap second is thus never identified with the next minute’s second 0 nor with second 59. A truncated value with second 60 (the time-only shapes written -mm:60 and --60, and the day-only date-time shape written ---DDThh:mm:60, each with any fraction and offset) is ordered by its field tuple, in which its second follows every second up to 59: a value comparable with it whose other fields are equal and whose second is at most 59 compares Less.

Outside the domain

  • A pair with comparable(a, b) false is refused with None by clause 1; this is the comparator’s only refusal, and production Temporal::cmp_chronological returns None for the same pairs.
  • A value with well_formed() false is outside the temporal carrier. Such a value can be built only by assigning public fields directly; lexical_form and canonical_bytes return None for it, and production deserialization refuses it with the error “a noncanonical temporal representation”. The law makes no claim about it.
  • Arithmetic overflow cannot arise in the domain: step 4 bounds every intermediate quantity of order_key.

Definitions used

  • Offset::seconds and Offset::minutes: σ(v) is v.offset.seconds() and μ(v) is v.offset.minutes(), both None for Local; is_zoned is true for every offset except Local.
  • Temporal::shape, Temporal::form, Temporal::is_truncated as defined in the reference module temporal. A finite value is truncated when it has a date without a year, or no date and a time without an hour.
  • comparable(a, b): false when exactly one of the two is local; otherwise, when either is an infinity, a.form() == b.form(); otherwise a.shape() == b.shape() and, when a is truncated, μ(a)=μ(b).
  • val(x) for a digit string x=d1​⋯dn​: the rational ∑i=1n​di​10−i, and 0 for the empty string.
  • The formatting directive {x:0<n$} writes x followed by copies of the fill character 0 until the result has n characters (fill 0, alignment <, width n), and writes x unchanged when it already has at least n characters. For an ASCII string, characters are bytes.
  • The order Ord of String and of Vec<i128> is lexicographic: at the first index where the two sequences differ, the elements decide (bytes, respectively integers, by size); if there is no such index, the shorter sequence is less, and sequences of equal length are equal. p.then_with(f) is p when p is not Equal, and f() otherwise.
  • The field tuple F(v) of a truncated finite value: the present fields among month, day, hour, minute, second, in that order.
  • For a finite value that is not truncated, with year y (if a date is present), month M, day D, hour h, minute m and second s, an absent month or day read as 1 and an absent hour, minute or second read as 0: N(v) is day_number(y, M, D) when a date is present and 0 otherwise; σ0​(v) is σ(v), or 0 for a local value; U(v)=86400N(v)+3600h+60m+min(s,59)−σ0​(v),I(v)=2U(v)+[s=60]. Here [P] is 1 when P holds and 0 otherwise.
  • The chronological key: κ(v)=(0) for a negative infinity, (2) for a positive infinity, (1,F(v),val(fv​)) for a truncated finite value and (1,(I(v)),val(fv​)) for any other finite value, where fv​ is the fraction of the time part (empty when there is none). Keys compare lexicographically: integers by size, tuples of integers lexicographically, rationals by size; two keys whose first components are 0, or both 2, are equal.

Proof

  1. Clause 3. Let n=max(∣x∣,∣y∣). By the definition of {x:0<n$}, cmp_fraction compares X=x0n−∣x∣ with Y=y0n−∣y∣ by the String order. Appending zeros does not change the value, so val(X)=val(x) and val(Y)=val(y). X and Y are digit strings of the same length n, so by the definition of the String order they are equal when no byte differs, and otherwise the first differing digit decides. The integers 10nval(X) and 10nval(Y) have these digit strings as their n-digit decimal expansions, and two such expansions compare as the integers do by the same rule: equal expansions give equal integers, and at the first differing position the larger digit gives the larger integer, because the remaining positions contribute less than one unit of that position. Hence cmp_fraction(x, y) is the order of val(x) and val(y).
  2. Clause 1 is the first line of cmp_chronological, which returns None when comparable(a, b) is false.
  3. Assume comparable(a, b). The match on (a.infinity, b.infinity) has four arms, two of which have two alternatives. (i) (Some, Some), both infinite: the result is Some(left.cmp(&right)) with the derived order Negative < Positive, which is the order of first key components 0<2, and equal signs give equal keys. (ii) (Some(Negative), None) | (None, Some(Positive)): Some(Less), and the first components satisfy 0<1, respectively 1<2. (iii) (Some(Positive), None) | (None, Some(Negative)): Some(Greater), with 2>1, respectively 1>0. (iv) (None, None), both finite: evaluation continues to step 4. The four arms cover every pair of Option values: two Some values are arm (i), one Some and one None is arm (ii) or (iii) according to the sign and position, and two None values are arm (iv).
  4. order_key(v) is Some for every v∈T. The truncated branch returns Some unconditionally. In the other branch the year is an i64, so ∣y∣≤263. days_before_year(y) is 365y+⌈y/4⌉−⌈y/100⌉+⌈y/400⌉, and each ceiling has absolute value at most ∣y∣/4+1≤263, so its absolute value is at most 365⋅263+3⋅263=368⋅263; adding the month lengths and the day, at most 366, gives ∣N(v)∣≤368⋅263+366<369⋅263<272, and this computation uses i128 without overflow. Then the minute index is below 272⋅1440+1440<283 in absolute value, its product by 120 is below 290, and the remaining terms are below 218 because hours, minutes and seconds are u8 and ∣σ(v)∣<86400 by well_formed. Every checked operation thus stays inside i128, whose bound is 2127, and returns Some. Hence the ? operators in cmp_chronological never return None on comparable finite pairs, which with steps 2 and 3 proves the first half of clause 2.
  5. Truncated branch. By definition of order_key, the key vector is the month and day of a present date (a truncated date has no year), followed by the hour, minute and second of a present time, each only when present: this is F(v). The returned fraction is fv​.
  6. Non-truncated branch. days is N(v) when a date is present; a finite non-truncated value with a date has a year by the definition of is_truncated, and a value without a date gives unwrap_or(0), which is N(v)=0. With the defaults of map_or(0, ...) for hour, minute and second and unwrap_or(0) for the shift of a local value, the vector is the single integer 120(1440N+60h+m)+2min(s,59)+[s=60]−2σ0​=2U(v)+[s=60]=I(v).
  7. Both finite and comparable. Since comparable(a, b) holds and neither is an infinity, its last branch gives a.shape() == b.shape(). Whether a finite value is truncated is determined by its shape (the presence of the date, of its year and of the hour), so a and b take the same branch of order_key. The result is ka.cmp(&kb).then_with(|| cmp_fraction(&fa, &fb)). By the definitions of the Vec<i128> order and of then_with, this is the comparison of the key vectors when they differ and the comparison of the fractions otherwise, which by step 1 is the order of val(fa​) and val(fb​). With the equal first components 1, this is the lexicographic comparison of κ(a) and κ(b), which completes clause 2.
  8. Clause 4, non-truncated a. By the definition of is_truncated, a finite value with a year is not truncated, and a time-only value with an hour is not truncated, so the cases named in clause 4 are exactly the non-truncated finite values with second 60. By step 6 the keys of a, b and c are single integers (c has the shape of a, so it is not truncated, and it is comparable with a: same zoning, same shape, and its offset is that of a). Since sa​=60, I(a)=2U(a)+1, and by hypothesis U(b)=U(a)+1, so I(b)≥2U(b)=2U(a)+2>I(a); the key vectors differ, so by step 7 the fractions are never consulted and the result is Some(Less). For c, the fields and offset agree with a except the second 59, so U(c)=U(a) (both use min(s,59)=59) and I(c)=2U(a)<2U(a)+1=I(a), giving Some(Less) whatever the fractions.
  9. Clause 4, truncated a. By well_formed, the truncated shapes with a second are the time-only shapes with minute and second or with the second alone, and the day-only date-time shape with hour, minute and second; a truncated date without a time has no second. By step 5 the key is the field tuple, whose last entry is the second in each of these shapes; with the other fields equal, the first differing entry is the second, and 60 exceeds every second up to 59, so by step 7 a value comparable with a (hence of the same shape and offset minutes) that agrees with a in its other fields and has second at most 59 compares Less than a whatever the fractions.
