Complete temporal forms retain their established order

Statement

The established order is the production comparator Temporal::cmp_chronological at commit b05a4ced^ (the parent of the commit that admitted reduced, truncated and infinite forms), in crates/panproto-expr/src/exact/temporal.rs at that commit: its rustdoc at lines 621 to 637 and its definition at lines 639 to 666. Write leg for that function and L for the values of that commit’s Temporal admitted by that commit’s constructors (defined below). Let φ be the map from L to the reference Temporal defined below. Then:

  1. φ is a bijection from L onto the set of reference values v with v.well_formed() and complete_layout(v);
  2. for all x,y∈L, cmp_chronological(φ(x), φ(y)) == leg(x, y);
  3. for all well-formed a,b with is_complete(), cmp_chronological(a, b) is None exactly when the forms differ or exactly one value is local, and otherwise Some of the lexicographic comparison of (I(a),val(fa​)) with (I(b),val(fb​)).

By clauses 1 and 2, relative to commit b05a4ced^, the extended comparator neither adds nor removes a comparable pair among the values that commit could hold, and orders every such pair as that commit did; in particular a leap second keeps its place strictly after second 59 and strictly before the next minute’s second 0, which is where b05a4ced^ places it (the earlier comparator of commit 3081d314, which placed second 60 on the next minute’s second 0, is not the referent). Clause 3 extends the same order to the complete values that commit could not hold.

Outside the domain

  • Values that are not complete (reduced, truncated or infinite) are outside all three clauses; their order is the subject of Comparable temporals follow chronological order. Complete values outside φ(L) (a zoned date, an offset written +hhmm, +hh, +hh:mm:00 or +hh:mm:ss, an unwritten zone, a year -0000) had no representation at b05a4ced^, so clauses 1 and 2 make no claim about them; clause 3 covers them.
  • A value of either type whose public fields violate its constructors is outside the carrier: at b05a4ced^ deserialization refuses it through the constructors named below, and in the reference well_formed is false, lexical_form and canonical_bytes return None, and production deserialization refuses it.
  • The refusal is None, returned in both orders exactly when the forms differ or exactly one value is local.

Definitions used

  • At b05a4ced^, crates/panproto-expr/src/exact/temporal.rs: Temporal (lines 35 to 43) has the variants Date(CivilDate), Time(CivilTime, Offset) and DateTime(CivilDate, CivilTime, Offset, DateTimeSeparator); DateTimeSeparator (line 52) is Upper, Lower or Space; ZuluCase (line 90) is Upper or Lower; CivilDate (line 121) has year: i64, month: u8, day: u8; CivilTime (line 138) has hour, minute, second: u8 and fraction: Fraction; Fraction (line 167) wraps a private string that every constructor (Fraction::new, line 176, the derived Default, and deserialization through new) requires to be ASCII digits; Offset (line 246) is Local, Zulu(ZuluCase), Fixed(i16) or NegZero.
  • L: the values of that Temporal whose dates pass CivilDate::new (line 337: 1≤ month ≤12 and 1≤ day ≤ days_in_month(year, month), lines 316 to 328), whose times pass CivilTime::new (line 395: hour ≤23, minute ≤59, second ≤60), and whose offsets Fixed(m) pass Offset::fixed (line 425: ∣m∣<1440). These are the constructors deserialization uses (serde(try_from = …) on CivilDate, CivilTime, Fraction and Offset, the last through TryFrom<OffsetRepr> at line 300).
  • At that commit, Offset::minutes (line 442) is m for Fixed(m) and 0 for Local, Zulu(_) and NegZero; is_zoned is false only for Local; CivilDate::days_since_epoch (line 349) and Fraction::cmp_numeric (line 199) are as quoted in steps 4 and 5.
  • φ: a date (y,M,D) maps to DateFields with year Year { value: y, negative_zero: false, width: max(4, digits of |y|) }, month M and day D; a time maps to TimeFields with all three fields present and the same fraction digits; the separator maps by name; the offset maps by ψ: Local to Local, Zulu(c) to Zulu(c), Fixed(m) to Fixed(m, Extended), NegZero to NegZero(Extended). Date(d) maps to a date-only value with offset Local, Time(t, o) to a time-only value with offset ψ(o), and DateTime(d, t, o, s) to a value with both parts, separator s and offset ψ(o); no image has an infinity.
  • Reference: well_formed, complete_layout, is_complete, form, shape, is_truncated, comparable, order_key, cmp_fraction, day_number, is_leap, month_length, Offset::seconds and Offset::minutes in the modules temporal and canonical. E= day_number(1970, 1, 1) =719528.
  • For a complete reference value with date (y,M,D) if present and time (h,m,s) if present (an absent part contributing 0), N(v) is day_number(y, M, D) or 0 without a date, σ0​(v) is v.offset.seconds() or 0 for a local value, I(v)=2(86400N(v)+3600h+60m+min(s,59)−σ0​(v))+[s=60], with [P] equal to 1 when P holds and 0 otherwise, and val(f) is the rational value of the fraction digits f (empty without a time).
  • ⌊⋅⌋ and ⌈⋅⌉ are the floor and ceiling; for nonnegative integers Rust’s / is the floor, and div_euclid by a positive divisor is the floor.
  • Clauses 1 to 4 of Comparable temporals follow chronological order.

Proof

  1. Clause 1. Leap rules: the legacy is_leap is 4∣y∧(100∤y∨400∣y) and the reference is_leap is (4∣y∧100∤y)∨400∣y; these agree because 400∣y implies 4∣y, so days_in_month and month_length agree on months 1 to 12. Image: for x∈L, φ(x) is well formed (each offset in the image of ψ passes offset_ok, since ∣m∣<1440 and the form Extended is not hour-only; the full date passes valid_date by the leap agreement and has the canonical width and no negative_zero; the time fields are in range and the fraction is digits; a date-time has a full date and an hour), and complete_layout holds (no infinity, is_complete, offset Local, Zulu(Upper | Lower) or of form Extended, canonical year, and a date-only image is local). Injective: φ keeps every field of x (the variant is recovered from which parts are present, ψ is injective). Onto: for a reference v with well_formed and complete_layout, the form is Date, Time or DateTime with full fields; the year has the canonical width and no negative_zero, so it is determined by its value; month and day pass CivilDate::new by the leap agreement; the time fields pass CivilTime::new and the fraction passes Fraction::new; a date-only value is local; the offset is Local, Zulu(Upper), Zulu(Lower), Fixed(m, Extended) with ∣m∣<1440 (passing Offset::fixed) or NegZero(Extended), each the ψ-image of one legacy offset. The legacy value with these fields lies in L and maps to v.
  2. Clause 3. No complete value is an infinity or truncated (is_complete requires infinity.is_none(); a present date has a year; a value without a date has a time with an hour). On complete values the shape is determined by the form (the three forms have the shapes with every field present), so comparable(a, b) reduces to: both local or both zoned, and equal forms, its offset-minutes conjunct holding because a is not truncated. When comparable, by clause 2 of L-values-12 the key vectors are (I(a)) and (I(b)) and by its clause 3 the tie break is the order of val(fa​) and val(fb​). With clause 1 of L-values-12 this proves clause 3.
  3. The structure of leg (body lines 639 to 666). Its match has four arms: (i) (Date(a), Date(b)) gives Some(a.days_since_epoch().cmp(&b.days_since_epoch())); (ii) (Time, Time) with equal zoning gives Some(instant(None, …)); (iii) (DateTime, DateTime) with equal zoning gives Some(instant(Some(da), …, Some(db), …)); (iv) every other pair, that is different variants or a Time or DateTime pair of different zoning, gives None. The function instant compares key(date, time, offset) and breaks ties by ta.fraction.cmp_numeric(&tb.fraction), with key =(1440⋅days+60h+m)⋅120+2min(s,59)+[s=60]−120⋅ offset.minutes(), where days is days_since_epoch of the date, or 0 without one.
  4. days_since_epoch(d) = day_number(y, M, D) − E for every date admitted by CivilDate::new. The code sets y′=y−[M≤2], era =⌊y′/400⌋, year_of_era =y′−400era∈[0,399], p=(M+9)mod12, day_of_year =⌊(153p+2)/5⌋+D−1, day_of_era =365yoe+⌊yoe/4⌋−⌊yoe/100⌋+day_of_year, and returns 146097era+day_of_era−719468. Let G(t)=365t+⌊t/4⌋−⌊t/100⌋+⌊t/400⌋. Writing y′=400era+yoe gives ⌊y′/4⌋=100era+⌊yoe/4⌋, ⌊y′/100⌋=4era+⌊yoe/100⌋ and ⌊y′/400⌋=era, so the result is G(y′)+day_of_year−719468. For p=0,…,11, ⌊(153p+2)/5⌋ is 0,31,61,92,122,153,184,214,245,275,306,337, the cumulative lengths of March to January in that order, which do not depend on the year. With B(t)=365t+⌈t/4⌉−⌈t/100⌉+⌈t/400⌉, day_number(y, M, D) =B(y)+∑k<M​ month_length(y, k) +D−1. Two identities: ⌊t/k⌋−⌈t/k⌉=−[k∤t], so G(y)−B(y)=−[4∤y]+[100∤y]−[400∤y]=[is_leap(y)]−1 (since [is_leap(y)]=[4∣y]−[100∣y]+[400∣y] by cases on divisibility); and ⌊t/k⌋−⌊(t−1)/k⌋=[k∣t], so G(y)−G(y−1)=365+[is_leap(y)]. Case M≥3: y′=y, day_of_year =∑k=3M−1​ month_length(k) +D−1, and day_number =B(y)+31+28+[is_leap(y)]+∑k=3M−1​ month_length(k) +D−1, so the difference is G(y)−B(y)−59−[is_leap(y)]−719468=−1−59−719468=−719528. Case M≤2: y′=y−1, day_of_year =306+∑k<M​ month_length(y, k) +D−1 (January contributes 31 before February, which is the same in both counts), so the difference is G(y−1)+306−B(y)−719468=G(y)−365−[is_leap(y)]+306−B(y)−719468=−1−59−719468=−719528. In both cases the difference is −E, as E=B(1970)=719050+493−20+5=719528.
  5. cmp_numeric equals cmp_fraction on digit strings. cmp_numeric compares, for i=0,…,max(∣a∣,∣b∣)−1, the i-th bytes with a missing byte read as 0, and returns the first unequal comparison or Equal. This is the comparison of the two strings padded on the right with 0 to the common length n=max(∣a∣,∣b∣), which is what cmp_fraction compares (clause 3 of L-values-12 and its definition of {x:0<n$} and of the String order: equal-length strings are decided at the first differing byte).
  6. Clause 2, comparability. Let x,y∈L. By step 2 the reference result for φ(x),φ(y) is None exactly when the forms differ or exactly one is local. The forms of φ(x), φ(y) are those of the variants of x, y, and ψ preserves locality (only Local maps to Local). Two Date values are both local under φ, so the reference compares them, as arm (i) does. Two Time or two DateTime values are compared by both exactly when the zonings agree, as in arms (ii), (iii) and (iv). Different variants give None in both.
  7. Clause 2, order. For two dates, I(φ(x))=2⋅86400N and both fractions are empty, so the reference result is the order of N(φ(x)) and N(φ(y)), which by step 4 is the order of days_since_epoch, as in arm (i). For two times or two date-times, the offsets satisfy 120⋅ minutes() =2σ0​(ψ(o)), since seconds() is 60m for Fixed(m, Extended) and 0 for Zulu and NegZero, and σ0​ is 0 for Local. By step 4, for a date-time key =I(φ(x))−2⋅86400E, and for a time key =I(φ(x)); subtracting the same constant from both keys preserves their comparison. The tie break is the same by step 5, since φ keeps the fraction digits. Hence cmp_chronological(φ(x), φ(y)) == leg(x, y) in every arm.
  8. The leap-second sentence. In leg the term 2min(s,59)+[s=60] places second 60 at 2⋅59+1, strictly between second 59 at 118 and the next minute’s second 0 at 120; the reference does the same by clause 4 of L-values-12, and step 7 shows the two orders agree on φ(L).

Extended temporal forms have distinct canonical bytes

Statement

Let T be the set of values v: Temporal with v.well_formed(). Then:

  1. canonical_bytes(v) is Some exactly when v∈T;
  2. for all a,b∈T, canonical_bytes(a) == canonical_bytes(b) implies a == b.

So canonical bytes are injective on the whole carrier: on reduced, truncated, infinite and unwritten-offset values, on the complete values encoded under the historical layout, and across the two layouts. The witness is read_temporal, which returns v from the bytes write_temporal writes for v.

Outside the domain

  • A value with well_formed() false gets canonical_bytes(v) = None by clause 1; this is the reference refusal. Production Temporal::canonical_bytes returns bytes for every value of its type, and production deserialization refuses an ill-formed value with the error “a noncanonical temporal representation”, so no ill-formed value reaches it through the parsers or deserialization.
  • No well-formed value is refused.

Definitions used

  • canonical_bytes(v): value_bytes(&Value::Temporal(v)), which is the tag byte 15 followed by the bytes W(v) that write_temporal writes, or None when write_temporal returns None.
  • write_temporal, complete_layout, write_separator, write_option_u8, write_date_form, write_time_form, offset_form_tag, write_offset_form, and their readers read_temporal, read_date, read_time, read_offset, read_option_u8, read_date_form, read_time_form, read_offset_form_tag, read_offset_form, read_separator, read_bool, as defined in the reference module canonical.
  • The primitives of Writer and Reader: a tag is one byte; i64 and u64 are eight little-endian bytes; a string is its byte length as a u64 followed by its bytes. Reader reads the same layouts from the front of its input.

Proof

  1. Clause 1. write_temporal first returns None when !well_formed(). For a well-formed value the remaining None exits are unreachable: in the complete layout branch, complete_layout excludes FixedSeconds, so the arm Offset::FixedSeconds(_) => return None is not taken; in the infinity branch, well_formed excludes a time infinity, so TemporalForm::Time => return None is not taken; and t.form()? is Some for a finite well-formed value, because well_formed returns false when form() is None. write_value adds the tag 15 and returns Some.
  2. Primitive inverses. A tag byte is read back unchanged; i64::from_le_bytes inverts to_le_bytes, and likewise for u64. A string written by Writer::str is read by Reader::str: the length is written by u64::try_from(len), which succeeds because a usize has at most 64 bits, and Reader::count converts it back to the same usize; the bytes are those of a String, so the UTF-8 check succeeds. read_bool inverts u8::from(bool), and read_option_u8 inverts write_option_u8 (0 for None, 1 then the byte for Some).
  3. Offsets in the new layout. read_offset_form inverts write_offset_form on every variant: 0 is Local; 1 then 0, 1, 2 are Zulu(Upper), Zulu(Lower), Zulu(Unwritten); 2 then the minutes as i64 and the form tag is Fixed(m, f), with i16::try_from(i64::from(m)) = m and read_offset_form_tag inverting offset_form_tag on all five forms; 3 then the form tag is NegZero(f); 4 then the seconds as i64 is FixedSeconds(x), with i32::try_from(i64::from(x)) = x.
  4. Complete layout (v with complete_layout(v), tags 0, 1, 2). is_complete and the absence of an infinity hold, so the date (if any) is full and the time (if any) is full. Tag 0 (date only): the writer emits the year as i64, then month and day; complete_layout requires the offset of a date only to be Local and the year to have negative_zero false and the canonical width; read_date returns exactly these fields with negative_zero false and the canonical width, and read_temporal sets the offset Local. Tag 1 (time only): hour, minute, second and the fraction string, then the offset; read_time reads them, and its digit check passes because well_formed requires the fraction to be digits. Tag 2: date, separator byte (read by the inline match on T, t, space), time, offset. The historical offset bytes are inverted by read_offset on every offset complete_layout admits: Local is 0; Zulu(Upper) and Zulu(Lower) are 1 with Z or z (Zulu(Unwritten) is excluded); Fixed(m, Extended) is 2 with m, read back as Fixed(m, Extended) (both arms of the m == 0 test give that value); NegZero(Extended) is 3. complete_layout admits only the form Extended for Fixed and NegZero. The rebuilt value equals v and is well formed, so read_temporal returns Some(v).
  5. Infinity layout (tags 6, 7). The writer emits 6 for a date infinity and 7 for a date-time infinity, the sign byte, and the offset in the new layout. The reader maps the tag back to the form and the byte to the sign, reads the offset by step 3, and builds Temporal::infinite(sign, form, offset), which has no date, time or separator. A well-formed infinity has none either, so the rebuilt value is v.
  6. New finite layout (tags 3, 4, 5). The tag is that of v.form(). By the definition of form, a date is present exactly for Date and DateTime, a time exactly for Time and DateTime, and well_formed makes the separator present exactly for DateTime; the reader reads a date form, a separator and a time form under exactly these conditions. read_date_form inverts write_date_form: the year presence tag, then the value, the negative_zero byte and the width as u64, which is exact because a well-formed width is at most 19, the number of digits of 263; then month and day by step 2. read_time_form inverts write_time_form by step 2. read_separator inverts write_separator. The offset is inverted by step 3. The value is well formed, so read_temporal returns Some(v).
  7. Every v∈T takes exactly one of the branches of steps 4 to 6, so read_temporal applied to a reader over W(v) returns Some(v). Clause 2: if canonical_bytes(a) == canonical_bytes(b) with a,b∈T, both are Some by clause 1, and removing the common first byte 15 gives W(a)=W(b). Since read_temporal is a function of its input bytes, Some(a) is its result on W(a) and Some(b) is its result on the same bytes, so a=b.

Discriminator tables select tagged coercions

Statement

Let t be a lexeme text, c a lexical class, g an optional tag, T a discriminator table (a finite map from tag names to scalar kinds) and s a value specification. Write op(g,t) for the opaque value Opaque { type_: g, fields: { "value": Str(t) } }. The discriminated coercion coerce_tagged(t, c, g, T, s) (the manifest name of coerce_discriminated) satisfies:

  1. No tag. If g is None, the result is coerce(t, c, s).
  2. Known tag. If g = Some(h) and h∈domT, the result is coerce(t, c, s') with s′ equal to s except s'.kind = T(h). The lexeme keeps its own class and every other parameter of s (precision, scale, offset requirement, integer width, signedness, float reading and numeral dialect); in particular a Number lexeme tagged with a tag whose entry is Str is refused exactly as an untagged one is under Str with the same parameters, with NotANumberForKind when no numeral dialect is declared.
  3. Unknown tag. If g = Some(h) and h∈/domT, the result is Some(Ok(op(h, t))), for every class c and every specification s, admissible or not. The tag and the text are kept byte for byte, and the result is never a refusal. A present table thus overrides the open-tag reading of clause 4: under the empty table every tagged lexeme is opaque, whatever its tag names.
  4. Absent table (open tags). Without a table, a tagged lexeme is the class Tagged(h) passed to coerce, and coerce(t, Tagged(h), s) is: coerce(t, String, s) when s.kind is not Any; and when s.kind is Any, with n the tag name obtained from h by removing a leading tag:yaml.org,2002: or else a leading !!, the value Null when n = null, coerce(t, c', ValueSpec::of(k')) when n names a scalar kind k′ read in class c′ by the table below, and Some(Ok(op(h, t))) (with h as written, prefix included) for every other name. The names are: bool, boolean for (Bool, Bool); int, integer, numberLong, numberInt for (BigInt, Number); float, double, numberDouble for (Float { bits: 64 }, Number); decimal, numberDecimal for (Decimal, Number); str, string for (Str, String); binary, base64 for (Bytes(Base64), Bytes); hex for (Bytes(Hex), Bytes); timestamp, datetime, date-time for (DateTime, DateTime); date for (Date, DateTime); time for (Time, DateTime). Under Any the result is never None, so the tag is never dropped: it selects Null, selects the kind it names, or is kept in the opaque value.

The production coerce_discriminated in crates/panproto-inst/src/value/coerce.rs, with spec.discriminators = Some(T), is required to equal clauses 1 to 3, and with spec.discriminators = None to equal coerce (clause 4 for a tagged lexeme), as the named differential tests check.

Outside the domain

  • In clause 2, when s′ is not admissible (L-values-2), for instance when T(h) is a float kind of width other than 16, 32 or 64, the result is whatever coerce gives there, which may be None; in clauses 1 and 4 under a declared kind, likewise for s.

Definitions used

  • coerce and its rows, admissibility, and ValueSpec::of, as in L-values-2.
  • coerce_discriminated(t, c, g, T, s) is g.map_or_else(|| coerce(t, c, s), |h| T.get(h).map_or_else(|| Some(Ok(opaque_of(h, t))), |k| coerce(t, c, &ValueSpec { kind: *k, ..*s }))); coerce_tagged is a re-export of it under another name.
  • opaque_of(h, t) is op(h,t).
  • tag_name(h) is h.strip_prefix("tag:yaml.org,2002:").or_else(|| h.strip_prefix("!!")).unwrap_or(h).
  • tagged_kind(n) is the table of clause 4, and None for every other name.
  • coerce_tagged_open(t, h, s) is the function coerce calls for the class Tagged(h): coerce(t, String, s) when s.kind != Any, else Null for the name null, else coerce(t, c', ValueSpec::of(k')) when tagged_kind(tag_name(h)) = Some((k', c')), else Some(Ok(opaque_of(h, t))).

Proof

  1. Clause 1. With g = None, map_or_else evaluates its default closure, coerce(t, c, s).
  2. Clauses 2 and 3. With g = Some(h), map_or_else applies its second closure to h, which looks h up in T. When the lookup is Some(k), the inner map_or_else returns coerce(t, c, ValueSpec { kind: k, ..s }); the struct-update syntax copies every field of s other than kind, and c is passed unchanged, which is clause 2. For the example, the tagged call is literally the call an untagged lexeme of class Number makes under the specification of kind Str with the other parameters of s; with no numeral dialect it reaches row 4 of L-values-2, whose Str arm returns NotANumberForKind for Number. When the lookup is None, the inner map_or_else returns Some(Ok(opaque_of(h, t))), which reads neither c nor s, which is clause 3; with the empty table every lookup is None.
  3. Clause 4, declared kind. Row 2 of L-values-2 sends the class Tagged(h) to coerce_tagged_open(t, h, s), whose first line returns coerce(t, String, s) when s.kind is not Any.
  4. Clause 4, open kind. When s.kind is Any, coerce_tagged_open computes tag_name(h), which removes the first prefix present in the stated order. It returns Some(Ok(Null)) for the name null; otherwise it matches tagged_kind on the name, whose arms are exactly the listed names and pairs, returning coerce(t, c', ValueSpec::of(k')) for a listed name and Some(Ok(opaque_of(h, t))), built from the unstripped h, for any other.
  5. Never None under Any. The kinds k′ of the table are Bool, BigInt, Float { bits: 64 }, Decimal, Str, Bytes(Base64), Bytes(Hex), DateTime, Date and Time; none is an Int kind and the only float width is 64, so each ValueSpec::of(k') is admissible, and by L-values-2 (Domain) the call is not None. The other two outcomes of step 4 are Some. So under Any the result is Null for the null tag, the reading under the named kind, or an opaque value carrying h; no outcome discards the tag without one of these three effects.

Numeral dialects agree with their declared grammars

Statement

The dialect coercion coerce_dialect(t, c, s) is coerce(t, c, s). Let s.numeral = Some(d), k = s.kind, let s0​ be s with numeral set to None, and let c∗ be the effective class of L-values-2: String when c = Tagged(h) and k= Any, and c otherwise. A tagged lexeme under a declared kind is thus read as a string: coerce(t, Tagged(h), s) = coerce(t, String, s) for k= Any. The dialect is relevant when c∗ = Number, or c∗ = String and k is Int, BigInt, Float or Decimal. If it is relevant, coerce(t, c, s) is Some(Err(NotANumber)) when t∈/Ld​, and is coerce(N_d(t), c*, s_0) when t∈Ld​ (the default exact reading of L-values-2 row 4). If it is not relevant, it is ignored: coerce(t, c, s) = coerce(t, c, s_0). The language Ld​ (which may depend on c∗ and on whether k is a float kind) and the normal form Nd​ are as follows. Here, P is the permissive numeral grammar [+-]?([0-9]+(\.[0-9]*)?|\.[0-9]+)([eE][+-]?[0-9]+)?, X is [+-]?([0-9]+(\.[0-9]*)?|\.[0-9]+) (no exponent), J is the JSON number grammar -?(0|[1-9][0-9]*)(\.[0-9]+)?([eE][+-]?[0-9]+)?, and T is [+-]?(0|[1-9][0-9]*)(\.[0-9]+)?([eE][+-]?[0-9]+)?. Also, ⟨r⟩ρ​ is the decimal numeral, without leading zeros (0 for zero), of the value of the digit string r in radix ρ, and u(r) is r with every _ removed.

  1. Json. L=J and N(t)=t.
  2. ProtoJson. For c∗ = String and a float kind, L=J∪{NaN, Infinity, -Infinity}; otherwise L=J. N(t)=t.
  3. Java. For a float kind, L=P∪{NaN, Infinity, -Infinity}; otherwise L=P. N(t)=t.
  4. Sql. For a float kind or Decimal, L is P together with the texts whose ASCII lowercase is nan, infinity, inf, -infinity or -inf, normalized to NaN, Infinity (the two positive spellings) and -Infinity (the two negative ones); otherwise L=P. Texts in P are their own normal form.
  5. Xsd. For a float kind, L=P∪{INF, +INF, -INF, NaN, -NaN}, with INF and +INF normalized to Infinity, -INF to -Infinity, and the others unchanged; otherwise L=X and N(t)=t.
  6. Toml. L is the union of: the six texts inf, +inf, -inf, nan, +nan, -nan, normalized to Infinity, Infinity, -Infinity, NaN, NaN, -NaN; the prefixed integers 0xr, 0or, 0br (no sign), where u(r) is a nonempty string of digits of radix ρ = 16, 8, 2 and every _ of r has a radix digit immediately before and after it, normalized to ⟨u(r)⟩ρ​; and the texts t in which every _ has an ASCII digit immediately before and after it and u(t)∈T, normalized to u(t).
  7. Yaml12. L is the union of: the special floats σ.inf, σ.Inf, σ.INF for σ∈{ε,+,−}, normalized to Infinity (for ε and +) or -Infinity, and .nan, .NaN, .NAN and their forms with a leading -, normalized to NaN or -NaN; 0o[0-7]+ and 0x[0-9a-fA-F]+, normalized to ⟨r⟩8​ and ⟨r⟩16​ of the digits r after the prefix; and P, normalized to itself.
  8. Yaml11. L is the union of the special floats of Yaml12 and the texts σb with σ∈{ε,+,−} and σ′ = - when σ = - and empty otherwise, where the body b is one of the following, tried in this order (cases 1 to 3 are selected by the prefix 0b, the prefix 0x and the presence of :, and a body so selected that does not have the case’s form is refused; cases 4 and 5 are selected only by their full form, and a body failing them goes on to case 6):
    1. 0br with r∈ [01_]* containing a binary digit, normalized to σ′⟨u(r)⟩2​;
    2. 0xr with r∈ [0-9a-fA-F_]* containing a hexadecimal digit, normalized to σ′⟨u(r)⟩16​;
    3. a body containing :: without ., it must match [1-9][0-9_]*(:[0-5]?[0-9])+, normalized to σ′ followed by the decimal numeral of the base-60 value of its fields (the first field read as u of it in decimal); with a ., the part before the first . must match [0-9][0-9_]*(:[0-5]?[0-9])+ and the part after it [0-9_]*, normalized to σ′, the base-60 value of the first part, . and u of the second part;
    4. 0r with r∈ [0-7_]+, normalized to σ′⟨u(r)⟩8​ (0 when u(r) is empty);
    5. 0 or [1-9][0-9_]*, normalized to σ′u(b);
    6. m or mex or mEx, split at the first e or E, where m contains a digit and is w.f with w empty or matching [0-9][0-9_]*, f∈ [0-9_]*, and x∈ [+-][0-9]+, normalized to σ′, u(w) (or 0 when empty), ., u(f) (or 0 when empty), and ex when an exponent was written.

The cells of Java and Sql that the definitions above leave open are fixed by these sources, and a text no cited rule admits is refused.

  • Java, finite numerals. The Java SE 21 API documentation of Double.valueOf(String) gives the grammar FloatValue: Signopt NaN, Signopt Infinity, Signopt FloatingPointLiteral, Signopt HexFloatingPointLiteral or SignedInteger, with the productions “as defined in the lexical structure sections of The Java Language Specification, except that underscores are not accepted between digits”. The Java Language Specification, Java SE 21 Edition, Sec 3.10.2 gives DecimalFloatingPointLiteral as Digits . [Digits] [ExponentPart] [FloatTypeSuffix], . Digits [ExponentPart] [FloatTypeSuffix], Digits ExponentPart [FloatTypeSuffix] and Digits [ExponentPart] FloatTypeSuffix, with ExponentPart an e or E and a SignedInteger [Sign] Digits, and Sign one of + and -. Every text of P is a signed SignedInteger or a signed DecimalFloatingPointLiteral without a suffix, so P is admitted by this grammar; its hexadecimal literals and type suffixes are not admitted by the dialect, which reads decimal numerals only.
  • Java, special values. The same documentation of Double.toString(double): “If the argument is NaN, the result is the string “NaN”“, and “positive infinity produces the result “Infinity” and negative infinity produces the result “-Infinity”“. These three exact spellings are the dialect’s specials; no case variant is admitted.
  • Sql, finite numerals. PostgreSQL 16, Sec 4.1.2.6 (Numeric Constants): “Numeric constants are accepted in these general forms: digits, digits.[digits][e[+-]digits], [digits].digits[e[+-]digits], digits e[+-]digits”, and “any leading plus or minus sign is not actually considered part of the constant; it is an operator applied to the constant”. P is exactly these forms with an optional sign, read as that operator applied to the constant. The same section also admits the non-decimal integer forms 0x, 0o, 0b and underscores between digits; the dialect does not admit them, so they are refused with NotANumber.
  • Sql, special values and their case rule. PostgreSQL 16, Secs 8.1.2 (Arbitrary Precision Numbers) and 8.1.3 (Floating-Point Types) list the special values Infinity, -Infinity and NaN, and each says: “On input, these strings are recognized in a case-insensitive manner. The infinity values can alternatively be spelled inf and -inf.” The dialect admits exactly these five spellings, in any ASCII case, under a float kind (Sec 8.1.3) and under Decimal (Sec 8.1.2); neither section names +inf, +infinity or a signed NaN, so those texts are refused.

Every normal form denotes, under the default reading, the number the dialect’s text denotes: a radix or sexagesimal integer becomes the decimal numeral of the same integer, separators are removed between digits, empty integer parts and empty fractions in ordinary decimal forms become 0, an empty YAML 1.1 sexagesimal fraction remains empty after ., and a special float keeps its written sign. The production coerce with a declared NumeralDialect is required to equal this definition exactly, as the named differential tests check.

Outside the domain

  • When the dialect is not relevant (effective classes Bool, Null, DateTime, Bytes; effective class String under a kind that is not numeric; and Tagged(_) under Any, whose open-tag reading uses ValueSpec::of(k') and never consults s.numeral), the numeral dialect plays no part and coerce is described by L-values-2.
  • A text outside Ld​ is refused with NotANumber; a normal form that the default reading then refuses (for instance an integer normal form under a fixed-width Int kind that it overflows) is refused with that reading’s typed reason.
  • An inadmissible specification (L-values-2) yields None after a successful normalization.

Definitions used

  • coerce and its row 3, as in L-values-2; coerce_dialect is defined as coerce.
  • normalize_numeral(t, c, k, d) dispatches on d to json_number, normalize_toml, normalize_yaml12, normalize_yaml11, normalize_xsd, normalize_java, the ProtoJson arm and normalize_sql, passing whether k is a float kind (and, for Sql, whether it is a float kind or Decimal).
  • decimal_number(t, G) reads an optional sign (+ only when G permits it), a maximal digit run, then, when G permits a point, . and a maximal digit run, refuses when both runs are empty, refuses a nonempty integer run with a leading zero and more than one digit unless G permits leading zeros, then, when G permits an exponent, reads e or E, an optional sign and a nonempty digit run, and accepts exactly when the text is exhausted. The grammars are JSON (point, exponent), TOML (plus, point, exponent), PERMISSIVE (plus, leading zero, point, exponent) and XSD_DECIMAL (plus, leading zero, point).
  • json_number(t) is decimal_number(t, JSON) with the part before the first e or E neither starting with . or -. nor ending with ..
  • strip_separators(t, δ) refuses when t starts or ends with _ or some _ lacks a byte satisfying δ immediately before or after it, and otherwise returns u(t).
  • radix_decimal(r, ρ) reads each byte of r as a digit 0 to 9, a to f, A to F of value below ρ (refusing otherwise), keeps the decimal digits of the running value most significant first, starting from [0], multiplies by ρ and adds the digit at each step, and refuses an empty r.
  • base60(b, z) refuses unless the first :-field starts with a digit (1 to 9 when z is false) and consists of digits and _, and every later field is one or two digits of value below 60, with at least one later field; it returns the decimal numeral of v0​60m+∑i​vi​60m−i with v0​ the decimal value of the first field’s digits.
  • yaml_special, normalize_xsd, normalize_java, normalize_sql, normalize_toml, normalize_yaml12, normalize_yaml11 and prefixed_integer are the reference functions of those names.

Proof

  1. Reduction. coerce_dialect returns coerce(t, c, s). By L-values-2 row 2, a Tagged(h) lexeme under k= Any becomes coerce(t, String, s), so in every case except Null and Tagged under Any the call reaches row 3 with class c∗. When the dialect is relevant, row 3 returns Some(Err(NotANumber)) if normalize_numeral(t, c*, k, d) is None and otherwise coerce(N, c*, s_0), which row 4 decides. When it is not relevant: for c = Null, row 1 gives Null under s and s0​ alike; for Tagged(h) under Any, the open-tag reading of row 2 reads only the tag and calls coerce with ValueSpec::of(k'), so it is the same under s and s0​; otherwise row 3 is skipped, and since s and s0​ differ only in numeral, the parameter dependence of L-values-2 gives coerce(t, c, s) = coerce(t, c, s_0). It remains to show, for each dialect, that normalize_numeral(t, c*, k, d) is Some exactly on Ld​ with value Nd​(t).
  2. The four grammars. Following decimal_number byte by byte: the accepted texts are an optional sign, then either a nonempty digit run optionally followed by . and a possibly empty digit run, or . and a nonempty digit run (the two runs are not both empty), then an optional exponent, and nothing else. With PERMISSIVE this is P and with XSD_DECIMAL, which has no exponent, it is X (a remaining e is not consumed, so the text is not exhausted). With JSON the sign is - only (a leading + is refused) and a nonempty integer run has no leading zero unless it is 0; the extra conditions of json_number on the mantissa exclude an empty integer run (the mantissa would start with . or -.) and a point with an empty fraction (it would end with .), which gives J. With TOML the sign may be + or -, and the mantissa conditions of normalize_toml on the unsigned text give T.
  3. Radix conversion. radix_decimal(r, ρ) keeps the invariant that after j digits the vector is the decimal numeral of Vj​=∑i≤j​ri​ρj−i without leading zeros ([0] for zero). Initially V0​=0 and the vector is [0]. A step replaces each decimal digit, from the least significant, by (aρ+κ)mod10 with carry ⌊(aρ+κ)/10⌋, starting from κ=rj+1​, and prepends the remaining carry digit by digit. This is schoolbook multiplication by ρ with rj+1​ added, so the vector denotes Vj​ρ+rj+1​=Vj+1​ (all intermediate values stay below 9⋅16+15=159). The new leading digit is nonzero unless Vj+1​=0. From [0], a digit r gives [r] or [1, r - 10]. From a leading digit a≥1, the top position holds aρ+κ≥2, which is either a nonzero digit or produces a carry whose last prepended digit is its nonzero most significant digit. Bytes outside the digit set or of value at least ρ are refused, and an empty r is refused at the end. So radix_decimal(r, ρ) is Some exactly when r is a nonempty string of radix-ρ digits, with value ⟨r⟩ρ​. The same schoolbook argument with multiplier 60 and fields below 60 (intermediate values below 9⋅60+59) shows that base60 returns the numeral of the stated base-60 value. The final trimming of leading zeros produces a numeral without leading zeros (0 for zero).
  4. Json, ProtoJson, Java, Sql, Xsd. Json returns t when json_number(t), so L=J by step 2. ProtoJson returns t for the three named spellings when the class passed, c∗, is String and k is a float kind, and otherwise when json_number(t). normalize_java returns t for the three named spellings when k is a float kind, and otherwise when t∈P. normalize_sql with specials admitted matches the ASCII lowercase of t against the five spellings and returns the stated normal forms, and otherwise (and always when specials are not admitted) returns t when t∈P. normalize_xsd for a float kind matches t exactly against INF, +INF, -INF, NaN, -NaN with the stated results and otherwise returns t when t∈P; for any other kind it returns t when t∈X and t contains no e or E, which every text of X satisfies.
  5. Toml. normalize_toml first matches the six special texts exactly, with the stated results. Next, for a text not starting with + or -, prefixed_integer(t, true) takes the prefix 0x, 0o or 0b, applies strip_separators with hexadecimal neighbours to the rest r and radix_decimal to u(r); by step 3 it succeeds exactly when u(r) is a nonempty string of radix digits, and since every byte of r other than _ is then a radix digit, the neighbour condition is that every _ of r lies between two radix digits. On success it returns ⟨u(r)⟩ρ​. On failure, and for every other text, the function continues with strip_separators with decimal neighbours, which succeeds exactly when every _ of t lies between two ASCII digits, and accepts u(t) exactly when u(t)∈T (step 2). A prefixed text that failed the prefixed reading contains x, o or b, so it is not in T after separator removal, and is refused; the three parts of L are thus accepted exactly as stated.
  6. Yaml12 and the special floats. yaml_special splits off a leading - or + (or none) and compares the rest with .inf, .Inf, .INF (accepted with any sign, negative only for -) and .nan, .NaN, .NAN (accepted with no sign or with -, giving NaN or -NaN), returning None otherwise, for instance for +.nan. normalize_yaml12 returns the special result when there is one; then for a text starting with 0o or 0x it returns radix_decimal of the rest in radix 8 or 16, without falling through, which by step 3 is the stated form; otherwise it returns t when t∈P. A text starting with 0o or 0x is not in P, so the three parts are accepted exactly as stated.
  7. Yaml11. normalize_yaml11 returns the special result first. It then removes a leading - (recording σ′ = -) or + (recording nothing) to get the body b and tries the cases in the stated order. Each case returns without falling through once its selecting condition holds. A body starting with 0b or 0x is accepted exactly when the rest consists of radix digits and _ with at least one digit, and then radix_decimal of u of the rest succeeds (step 3). A body containing : is read by base60(b, false) when it has no ., and otherwise split at the first . into a part read by base60(·, true) and a fraction that must consist of digits and _, which is the stated case 3 with the base-60 value of step 3. A body 0r with r nonempty in [0-7_]+ gives 0 when u(r) is empty and ⟨u(r)⟩8​ otherwise. A body equal to 0, or accepted by underscored with a first byte 1 to 9 (all bytes digits or _), gives σ′u(b). Every remaining body is split at its first e or E into m and an optional exponent x. The mantissa m must contain a . (split at the first one into w and f), w must be empty or accepted by underscored with a digit first, f must consist of digits and _, m must contain a digit, and x must be a sign followed by at least one digit; the result is the stated normal form. A body selected by case 1, 2 or 3 that fails that case’s form is refused without reaching the later cases, and a body that fails case 6 is refused, as stated.
  8. Denotation. For the identity cases there is nothing to show. A prefixed or sexagesimal integer is replaced by the decimal numeral of the same integer (step 3), with the written minus sign kept as σ′ and a written plus sign dropped, which changes no value. Removing _ keeps the sequence of digits. Supplying 0 for an empty integer part or an empty fraction in an ordinary decimal form and writing the exponent marker as e keep the value of the decimal numeral. A YAML 1.1 sexagesimal text with an empty fraction retains the point with no following digits; the default reading assigns that form the same integer value. The special spellings are mapped to Infinity, -Infinity, NaN and -NaN with the sign written in the source, and the default reading reads those four through parse_non_finite (float kinds and Any) or parse_decimal (Decimal) with that sign.

Latin-1 decoding followed by encoding is identity

Statement

For every byte string b=b1​⋯bn​ with n≥0, latin1_encode(&latin1_decode(b)) = Ok(b); equivalently, latin1_decode_encode(b) is true. In particular latin1_encode never refuses a string in the image of latin1_decode. Production reading under BytesText::Latin1 is required to equal the reference coercion reading coerce::decode_bytes, which for this form is bytes::latin1_encode(text).ok(), with None reported as FidelityReason::InvalidEncoding; on the text latin1_decode(b) it thus returns the bytes b with no refusal.

Outside the domain

The domain is every byte string, so no input lies outside it. The only refusal latin1_encode can return, NonLatin1, cannot arise on this domain, because every code point that latin1_decode produces is at most U+00FF (step 3 below); for the same reason the production reading never reports FidelityReason::InvalidEncoding here.

Definitions used

  • A byte string is a finite sequence b1​⋯bn​ of integers 0≤bi​≤255; a string is a finite sequence of Unicode scalar values, read in order by chars().
  • latin1_decode(b) is the string c1​⋯cn​ with ci​= char::from(b_i), the scalar value whose code point is bi​ (the reference definition: map each byte b to U+0000 + b), collected in order.
  • latin1_encode(t) maps each character c of t, in order, to u8::try_from(u32::from(c)): the byte equal to the code point of c when that code point is at most 255, and the refusal NonLatin1 otherwise. Collecting into a Result returns Ok of the sequence of bytes when every character maps to a byte, and the first refusal otherwise.
  • The reference coercion reading coerce::decode_bytes, the function every coercion differential compares with production, reads BytesText::Latin1 text as bytes::latin1_encode(text).ok(); its caller reports None as FidelityReason::InvalidEncoding.
  • latin1_decode_encode(b) is the predicate latin1_encode(&latin1_decode(b)) == Ok(b).

Proof

  1. Let b=b1​⋯bn​ be a byte string. By the definition of latin1_decode, t= latin1_decode(b) is the string c1​⋯cn​ of length n with ci​ the scalar value of code point bi​, in the order of b.
  2. By the definition of a string’s characters, t.chars() yields exactly c1​,…,cn​ in that order.
  3. For each i, u32::from(c_i) is the code point of ci​, which is bi​ by step 1, and 0≤bi​≤255 by the definition of a byte. Hence u8::try_from(b_i) succeeds and returns the byte bi​; no character of t maps to NonLatin1.
  4. By the definition of collecting into a Result, there are two cases. If some character maps to a refusal, the result is that refusal; by step 3 this case does not occur. Otherwise the result is Ok of the mapped bytes in order, which by steps 2 and 3 is Ok(b1​⋯bn​) = Ok(b). The case n=0 is included: t is empty, no character is mapped, and the result is Ok of the empty sequence, which is Ok(b).
  5. By step 4 and the definition of latin1_decode_encode, the predicate is true for every b.
  6. Production reading under BytesText::Latin1 is required to equal the reference coercion reading coerce::decode_bytes, which for this form is bytes::latin1_encode(text).ok(), with None reported as FidelityReason::InvalidEncoding. By steps 3 and 4, latin1_encode returns Ok(b) on t, so the reference reading, and with it the production reading, returns the bytes b for the text t.

Accepted padded base64 text is canonical

Statement

For every string t and byte string b, if decode_base64(t, true) = Ok(b) then encode_base64(b) = t; equivalently, padded_text_encode_decode(t) is true for every t that required-padding decoding accepts. Consequently required-padding decoding is injective on the texts it accepts: two accepted texts that decode to the same bytes are equal. Production reading under each base64 form is required to equal the reference coercion reading coerce::decode_bytes, with None reported as FidelityReason::InvalidEncoding. That reading is bytes::decode_base64(text, false) for BytesText::Base64 and bytes::decode_base64(text, true) for BytesText::Base64Padded; for BytesText::Base64Url and BytesText::Base64UrlPadded it refuses a text that contains + or / and otherwise is bytes::decode_base64(τ(text), r) with r false and true respectively, where τ replaces each - by + and each _ by /. Consequently every text that the BytesText::Base64Padded reading accepts is encode_base64 of the bytes it returns, and every text that the BytesText::Base64UrlPadded reading accepts is the URL-safe canonical padded encoding of the bytes it returns.

Outside the domain

The domain is the set of texts that decode_base64(·, true) accepts; on every other text the law makes no claim and padded_text_encode_decode is false. Such a text is refused, at the first failing check of the definition, with: InvalidPadding when the suffix from its first = contains a byte other than = or has more than two bytes; InvalidBase64 when a byte before its first = lies outside the standard alphabet S (every byte of a character above U+007F is such a byte); InvalidPadding when the part before the first = has byte length ≡1(mod4), when padding is present with a length other than the required one, or when the required padding is absent; and InvalidBase64 when the last quantum carries nonzero unused bits. NonLatin1 cannot arise, since no base64 operation returns it. Production reading under BytesText::Base64Padded reports each of these as FidelityReason::InvalidEncoding; under BytesText::Base64UrlPadded a text containing + or / is refused with FidelityReason::InvalidEncoding, and any other text s is refused exactly when τ(s) is refused above.

Definitions used

  • ∣t∣ is the length of t in bytes (its UTF-8 encoding); optional and decode_base64 inspect t bytewise.
  • S is the standard alphabet, the 64 bytes A through Z, a through z, 0 through 9, + and /. The table α(i)= ALPHABET[i] for 0≤i<64 lists them in that order: α(i) is A+i for i<26, a+(i−26) for 26≤i<52, 0+(i−52) for 52≤i<62, + for i=62 and / for i=63. The map σ= sextet sends each byte of S to the integer given by the same four ranges and +, /, and every other byte to None.
  • For an integer 0≤w<224, its sextets are fk​(w)=⌊w/218−6k⌋mod64 for k=0,1,2,3, the values (w >> 18) & 63, (w >> 12) & 63, (w >> 6) & 63 and w & 63; base-64 positional notation gives w=∑k​fk​(w)218−6k, and w is determined by its sextets.
  • optional(t) splits t at its first = into a body u and a padding suffix p (p empty when t has no =), then checks, in order: (a) p consists of = only and ∣p∣≤2, else InvalidPadding; (b) every byte of u is in S, else InvalidBase64; (c) with e=(4−∣u∣mod4)mod4, e≤2 and (p empty or ∣p∣=e), else InvalidPadding. It then returns Ok of u followed by e copies of =.
  • decode_base64(t, r) computes m= optional(t)?, returns InvalidPadding when r holds and m=t, and otherwise splits m into consecutive 4-byte quanta. For each quantum q0​q1​q2​q3​ it counts the trailing = bytes d, sets vj​=σ(qj​) for qj​= = (refusing InvalidBase64 when σ(qj​) is None) and vj​=0 for qj​= =, refuses InvalidBase64 when d=2 and v1​mod16=0 or when d=1 and v2​mod4=0, forms w=∑k​vk​218−6k, and appends the bytes ⌊w/216⌋mod256, then ⌊w/28⌋mod256 when d<2, then wmod256 when d=0. It returns Ok of the appended bytes.
  • encode_base64(b) splits b into consecutive chunks of three bytes, the last possibly shorter. For a chunk x0​x1​x2​ of length ℓ∈{1,2,3} it forms w=x0​216+x1​28+x2​ with each absent byte taken as 0, and writes α(f0​(w))α(f1​(w)), then α(f2​(w)) if ℓ>1 and = otherwise, then α(f3​(w)) if ℓ>2 and = otherwise.
  • The reference coercion reading coerce::decode_bytes, the function every coercion differential compares with production, reads BytesText::Base64 as bytes::decode_base64(text, false) and BytesText::Base64Padded as bytes::decode_base64(text, true). For BytesText::Base64Url and BytesText::Base64UrlPadded it returns None when the text contains + or /, and otherwise bytes::decode_base64(τ(text), r) with r false and true respectively; its caller reports None as FidelityReason::InvalidEncoding.
  • τ replaces each byte - of a text by + and each _ by /; υ replaces each + by - and each / by _. All four are single ASCII bytes, and no byte of a UTF-8 encoded character above U+007F is ASCII, so both maps preserve byte length and every other byte. Hence υ(τ(s))=s for a text s without + or /, and τ(υ(x))=x with υ(x) free of + and / for a text x without - or _. The URL-safe canonical padded encoding of b is υ(encode_base64(b)).
  • padded_text_encode_decode(t) is decode_base64(t, true).is_ok_and(|bytes| encode_base64(&bytes) == t).

Proof

  1. Alphabet inversion. By comparing the four ranges and the two single bytes in the definitions of α and σ, σ(α(i))=i for every 0≤i<64 and α(σ(c))=c for every c∈S; and σ(c) is None exactly when c∈/S.
  2. Shape of an accepted text. Suppose decode_base64(t, true) = Ok(b). Then optional(t) = Ok(m) and, since r holds, m=t. By the definition of optional, t=u=e where u contains no = (it precedes the first =), every byte of u is in S by check (b), and e=(4−∣u∣mod4)mod4≤2 by check (c). Hence ∣u∣mod4∈{0,2,3}, with e=0,2,1 respectively, and ∣t∣=∣u∣+e≡0(mod4), so the quanta of t cover it exactly. Write ∣t∣=4N and t=Q1​⋯QN​.
  3. Padding count per quantum. When N=0, t is empty, there is no quantum, and b is empty. When N≥1, the e≤2 bytes = are the last e bytes of t, so they lie in QN​; each Qj​ with j<N consists of four bytes of u, all in S, and has d=0. In QN​, counting positions from 0, the byte at position 3−e≥1 is a byte of u and so is not =, while positions after it are =; hence QN​ has d=e. Every non-= byte of every quantum lies in u⊆S, so by step 1 no InvalidBase64 from σ arises, and vj​=σ(qj​) for those bytes.
  4. Case d=0 (every Qj​ with j<N, and QN​ when e=0). The decoder forms w=∑k​vk​218−6k with vk​<64, so 0≤w<224 and fk​(w)=vk​ by base-64 positional notation, and it appends the three bytes x0​=⌊w/216⌋mod256, x1​=⌊w/28⌋mod256, x2​=wmod256, whose base-256 recombination x0​216+x1​28+x2​ is w. Encoding the chunk x0​x1​x2​ forms that same w and writes α(v0​)α(v1​)α(v2​)α(v3​), which is Qj​ by step 1.
  5. Case d=2 (QN​ when e=2). Here v2​=v3​=0, the check gives v1​mod16=0, and w=v0​218+v1​212. Since v1​=16⌊v1​/16⌋, w=(4v0​+⌊v1​/16⌋)216 with 4v0​+⌊v1​/16⌋≤255, so the single appended byte is x0​=4v0​+⌊v1​/16⌋ and x0​216=w. Encoding the one-byte chunk x0​ forms w and writes α(v0​)α(v1​)==, which is QN​ by step 1.
  6. Case d=1 (QN​ when e=1). Here v3​=0, the check gives v2​mod4=0, and w=v0​218+v1​212+v2​26, whose value modulo 28 is (v2​mod4)26=0. Hence w=x0​216+x1​28 for the two appended bytes x0​,x1​. Encoding the two-byte chunk x0​x1​ forms w and writes α(v0​)α(v1​)α(v2​)=, which is QN​ by step 1. The case d=3 does not occur by step 3, and d=4 does not occur since e≤2.
  7. Chunk alignment. By steps 4 through 6, the decoded bytes b are the concatenation of three bytes for each Qj​ with j<N followed by 3−e bytes for QN​ (no bytes when N=0, that is, t empty). Splitting b into chunks of three thus reproduces exactly these groups, because every group but the last has three bytes and the last has 3−e∈{1,2,3} bytes. By the definition of encode_base64 and steps 4 through 6, encode_base64(b) is Q1​⋯QN​=t; when t is empty, b is empty and the encoding is empty.
  8. By step 7 and the definition of is_ok_and, padded_text_encode_decode(t) is true on the domain. If two accepted texts t,t′ decode to the same b, then t= encode_base64(b) =t′ by step 7, which is the injectivity claim.
  9. Production. Under BytesText::Base64Padded the reference coercion reading is decode_base64(·, true), so a text it accepts with bytes b satisfies the hypothesis of step 7 and equals encode_base64(b). Under BytesText::Base64UrlPadded, a text s it accepts with bytes b contains no + or /, and decode_base64(τ(s), true) = Ok(b); by step 7, τ(s)= encode_base64(b), and by the translation identity υ(τ(s))=s of the definitions, s=υ(encode_base64(b)). Production reading is required to equal this reference reading, with None reported as FidelityReason::InvalidEncoding, so both conclusions hold for it.

Optional-padding base64 decodes canonical encodings

Statement

For every byte string b, let t= encode_base64(b) be its canonical padded encoding and t∘ the text t with its trailing = bytes removed. Then (i) optional(t) = Ok(t); (ii) optional(t∘) = Ok(t); and (iii) decode_base64(t, false) = decode_base64(t∘, false) = Ok(b). Optional-padding decoding thus returns the source bytes from the canonical encoding written with or without its padding. Production reading under each base64 form is required to equal the reference coercion reading coerce::decode_bytes, with None reported as FidelityReason::InvalidEncoding. That reading is bytes::decode_base64(text, false) for BytesText::Base64 and bytes::decode_base64(text, true) for BytesText::Base64Padded; for BytesText::Base64Url and BytesText::Base64UrlPadded it refuses a text that contains + or / and otherwise is bytes::decode_base64(τ(text), r) with r false and true respectively, where τ replaces each - by + and each _ by /. Consequently the BytesText::Base64 reading returns b from t and from t∘, and the BytesText::Base64Url reading returns b from υ(t) and from υ(t∘).

Outside the domain

The domain is every byte string, and the texts read are t and t∘, so no input lies outside it. No refusal can arise on these texts: InvalidPadding and InvalidBase64 are excluded by steps 3, 4, 7 and 8 below, and NonLatin1 is never returned by a base64 operation. Optional-padding decoding of texts that are neither t nor t∘ for any b is not the subject of this law; its padding behaviour is stated by the optional-padding law that follows on this page.

Definitions used

  • ∣t∣, the standard alphabet S, the table α, the map σ= sextet, the sextets fk​(w) of a 24-bit integer w, optional, decode_base64 and encode_base64 are as defined in the padded-canonicity law. In particular optional(t) splits t at its first = into a body u and a suffix p and checks (a) p is = only with ∣p∣≤2, (b) u⊆S, (c) e=(4−∣u∣mod4)mod4≤2 and (p empty or ∣p∣=e), returning u followed by e copies of =.
  • The reference coercion reading coerce::decode_bytes, the function every coercion differential compares with production, reads BytesText::Base64 as bytes::decode_base64(text, false) and BytesText::Base64Padded as bytes::decode_base64(text, true). For BytesText::Base64Url and BytesText::Base64UrlPadded it returns None when the text contains + or /, and otherwise bytes::decode_base64(τ(text), r) with r false and true respectively; its caller reports None as FidelityReason::InvalidEncoding.
  • τ replaces each byte - of a text by + and each _ by /; υ replaces each + by - and each / by _. All four are single ASCII bytes, and no byte of a UTF-8 encoded character above U+007F is ASCII, so both maps preserve byte length and every other byte. Hence υ(τ(s))=s for a text s without + or /, and τ(υ(x))=x with υ(x) free of + and / for a text x without - or _. The URL-safe canonical padded encoding of b is υ(encode_base64(b)).
  • =e is the text of e bytes =; t∘ is the longest prefix of t that does not end in =.

Proof

  1. Alphabet inversion. By comparing the ranges in the definitions of α and σ, σ(α(i))=i for 0≤i<64, and α(i)∈S, so α(i) is never =.
  2. Shape of the encoding. Write ∣b∣=3M+ρ with ρ∈{0,1,2}. By the definition of encode_base64, t consists of M quanta of four bytes α(⋅), one per full chunk, followed when ρ=1 by α(f0​)α(f1​)== and when ρ=2 by α(f0​)α(f1​)α(f2​)=. Hence t=u=e, where u consists of bytes of S only (step 1), (∣u∣mod4,e) is (0,0), (2,2) or (3,1) for ρ=0,1,2, and in each case e=(4−∣u∣mod4)mod4. Since u contains no =, t∘=u.
  3. Claim (i). If e=0, t has no =, so the body is t=u and p is empty; check (a) holds, (b) holds by step 2, and (c) holds since the computed e is 0. If e∈{1,2}, the first = is at byte ∣u∣, so the body is u and p==e; check (a) holds since e≤2, (b) holds by step 2, and (c) holds since e≤2 and ∣p∣=e. In both cases optional(t) returns u=e=t.
  4. Claim (ii). t∘=u contains no =, so its body is u and p is empty; checks (a) and (b) hold as in step 3, and (c) holds since e≤2 by step 2 and p is empty. Hence optional(t∘) returns u=e=t.
  5. Reduction. By the definition of decode_base64, with r false the comparison with the input is skipped, and every later operation reads only m= optional(·). By steps 3 and 4, m=t for both inputs, so both decodings equal the quantum loop run on t. It remains to show that this loop returns Ok(b). When b is empty, t is empty, the loop has no quantum, and the result is Ok of the empty sequence; assume b nonempty below.
  6. Full chunks. Let x0​x1​x2​ be a full chunk with w=x0​216+x1​28+x2​<224. Its quantum α(f0​(w))⋯α(f3​(w)) contains no = (step 1), so d=0 and vk​=σ(α(fk​(w)))=fk​(w) by step 1. The decoder forms ∑k​fk​(w)218−6k=w by base-64 positional notation and appends the base-256 digits ⌊w/216⌋mod256=x0​, ⌊w/28⌋mod256=x1​ and wmod256=x2​.
  7. Case ρ=1, last chunk x0​. Here w=x0​216, so f1​(w)=16(x0​mod4) and f2​(w)=f3​(w)=0. The quantum α(f0​)α(f1​)== has d=2, because its byte at position 1 is in S; v0​=f0​(w), v1​=f1​(w), v2​=v3​=0, so v1​mod16=0 and the unused-bit check passes. The decoder forms f0​(w)218+f1​(w)212=w, since the omitted sextets are 0, and appends the single byte ⌊w/216⌋mod256=x0​.
  8. Case ρ=2, last chunk x0​x1​. Here w=x0​216+x1​28, so f3​(w)=0 and f2​(w)=4(x1​mod16). The quantum α(f0​)α(f1​)α(f2​)= has d=1, because its byte at position 2 is in S; v2​=f2​(w) has v2​mod4=0, so the check passes. The decoder forms f0​218+f1​212+f2​26=w−f3​(w)=w and appends x0​ and x1​. Case ρ=0 has no last partial chunk, and the cases ρ∈{0,1,2} are exhaustive.
  9. By steps 6 through 8, no quantum is refused (no σ lookup fails by step 1, and both unused-bit checks pass), and the appended bytes are the chunks of b in order, which concatenate to b. With step 5 this proves decode_base64(t, false) = decode_base64(t∘, false) = Ok(b), claim (iii).
  10. Production. Under BytesText::Base64 the reference coercion reading is decode_base64(·, false), which returns b from t and t∘ by step 9. Under BytesText::Base64Url: t and t∘ consist of bytes of S and = by step 2, so they contain no - or _; by the translation identity of the definitions, υ(t) and υ(t∘) contain no + or /, and τ(υ(t))=t, τ(υ(t∘))=t∘. The reading is thus decode_base64(t, false) and decode_base64(t∘, false), which return b by step 9. Production reading is required to equal this reference reading, with None reported as FidelityReason::InvalidEncoding, so it returns b in all four cases.

Optional base64 padding preserves decoded bytes

Statement

Let u be any string that contains no = and whose byte length satisfies ∣u∣mod4=1, and let n(u)=(4−∣u∣mod4)mod4, its required padding count, so that n(u)∈{0,1,2}. Then optional(u) = optional(u=n(u)), and hence decode_base64(u, false) = decode_base64(u=n(u), false), as results: both return the same bytes, or both return the same refusal variant. Adding the required terminal padding to an unpadded text, or removing it from a padded one, thus leaves optional-mode decoding unchanged, whether or not the text is well formed. Production reading under each base64 form is required to equal the reference coercion reading coerce::decode_bytes, with None reported as FidelityReason::InvalidEncoding. That reading is bytes::decode_base64(text, false) for BytesText::Base64 and bytes::decode_base64(text, true) for BytesText::Base64Padded; for BytesText::Base64Url and BytesText::Base64UrlPadded it refuses a text that contains + or / and otherwise is bytes::decode_base64(τ(text), r) with r false and true respectively, where τ replaces each - by + and each _ by /. Consequently, under BytesText::Base64 and under BytesText::Base64Url, the reading of u and of u=n(u) return the same bytes, or both return FidelityReason::InvalidEncoding.

Outside the domain

Two cases fall outside the domain. First, when ∣u∣mod4=1 no padding completes a quantum: n(u)=3, and optional(u=3) is refused with InvalidPadding by check (a), while optional(u) is refused with InvalidBase64 when a byte of u lies outside S and with InvalidPadding otherwise, so both texts are refused, with possibly different variants (for u= @, the variants are InvalidBase64 and InvalidPadding); production refuses both with FidelityReason::InvalidEncoding under BytesText::Base64, and under BytesText::Base64Url likewise, since τ preserves byte length and introduces no =. Second, a suffix other than the required padding is not the operation this law describes. For u=k with k≥1 and k=n(u), optional refuses with InvalidPadding at check (a) when k>2; when 1≤k≤2 it refuses with InvalidBase64 at check (b) if a byte of u lies outside S, and otherwise with InvalidPadding at check (c), since the suffix length k differs from n(u) (or n(u)=3>2). The case k=0 is u itself, which is the unpadded side of the law. A text whose = bytes are not confined to a terminal run has a suffix, from its first =, that contains a byte other than =, and optional refuses it with InvalidPadding at check (a). NonLatin1 cannot arise, since no base64 operation returns it.

Definitions used

  • ∣u∣, the standard alphabet S, optional with its checks (a), (b) and (c), and decode_base64 are as defined in the padded-canonicity law. In particular optional(t) splits t at its first = into a body and a suffix p, checks (a) p is = only with ∣p∣≤2, else InvalidPadding; (b) every body byte is in S, else InvalidBase64; (c) with e=(4−∣body∣mod4)mod4, e≤2 and (p empty or ∣p∣=e), else InvalidPadding; and returns the body followed by =e.
  • The reference coercion reading coerce::decode_bytes, the function every coercion differential compares with production, reads BytesText::Base64 as bytes::decode_base64(text, false) and BytesText::Base64Padded as bytes::decode_base64(text, true). For BytesText::Base64Url and BytesText::Base64UrlPadded it returns None when the text contains + or /, and otherwise bytes::decode_base64(τ(text), r) with r false and true respectively; its caller reports None as FidelityReason::InvalidEncoding.
  • τ replaces each byte - of a text by + and each _ by /; υ replaces each + by - and each / by _. All four are single ASCII bytes, and no byte of a UTF-8 encoded character above U+007F is ASCII, so both maps preserve byte length and every other byte. Hence υ(τ(s))=s for a text s without + or /, and τ(υ(x))=x with υ(x) free of + and / for a text x without - or _. The URL-safe canonical padded encoding of b is υ(encode_base64(b)).
  • =k is the text of k bytes =, and u=k is u followed by it.

Proof

  1. Range of n(u). Since ∣u∣mod4∈{0,2,3}, the definition gives n(u)=0,2,1 respectively, so n(u)≤2.
  2. Case n(u)=0. Then u=n(u)=u, and both sides of each equation are the same expression.
  3. Case n(u)∈{1,2}: the split. Since u contains no =, optional(u) has body u and empty suffix. In u=n(u) the first = is at byte ∣u∣, so its body is also u and its suffix is =n(u).
  4. Check (a). For u the suffix is empty and (a) holds. For u=n(u) the suffix is = only and has length n(u)≤2 by step 1, so (a) holds. Neither text is refused at (a).
  5. Check (b). Both texts have body u by step 3, so (b) holds for both or fails for both; when it fails, both results are Err(InvalidBase64) and the equation holds.
  6. Check (c), when (b) holds. Both bodies are u, so both compute e=n(u), and e≤2 by step 1. For u the suffix is empty, and for u=n(u) the suffix length is n(u)=e; (c) holds for both. Both results are Ok(u=n(u)).
  7. Steps 5 and 6 cover both outcomes of check (b), so in every case optional(u) = optional(u=n(u)).
  8. Decoding. By the definition of decode_base64 with r false, the result is the refusal of optional when it refuses, and otherwise a function of m= optional(·) alone, the comparison with the input being skipped. By step 7 (and step 2 in the remaining case) the two texts have equal optional results, so their optional-mode decodings are equal results.
  9. Production. Under BytesText::Base64 the reference coercion reading is decode_base64(·, false), which agrees on the two texts by step 8. Under BytesText::Base64Url there are two cases. If u contains + or /, so does u=n(u), and conversely, since the added bytes are =; both are refused. Otherwise τ(u=n(u))=τ(u)=n(u), and τ(u) contains no = and has byte length ∣u∣ by the definition of τ, so n(τ(u))=n(u) and step 8 applied to τ(u) gives equal results. Production reading is required to equal this reference reading, with None reported as FidelityReason::InvalidEncoding, so it returns the same result for both texts under both forms.

Epoch counts round-trip through temporals

Statement

For every count c (i128), unit u (TimeUnit) and flag instant, let du​∈{0,3,6,9} be the number of fraction digits of u and τu​=10du​. Write S=⌊c/τu​⌋, Δ=⌊S/86400⌋ (floors toward −∞), E= day_number(1970, 1, 1) =719528, and let Y be the unique integer with B(Y)≤E+Δ<B(Y+1). Then:

  1. from_epoch_count(c, u, instant) is Some exactly when Y lies in the range of i64 (the count is in range);
  2. for every in-range count, from_epoch_count(c, u, instant) = Some(t) with t.well_formed(), and to_epoch_count(&t, u, instant) == Some(c).

Outside the domain

  • A count whose year Y leaves i64 is refused with None by the reference, and production Temporal::from_epoch_count refuses it with ExactParseError of reason FidelityReason::Overflow.
  • Every i128, every unit and both flags are otherwise in the domain; there is no other refusal.

Definitions used

  • B(y) for an integer y: days_before_year_wide(y), that is 365y+⌈y/4⌉−⌈y/100⌉+⌈y/400⌉, computed by div_ceil; for i64 years days_before_year is the same formula.
  • is_leap, month_length, day_number, date_from_day, TimeUnit::digits, TimeUnit::ticks, from_epoch_count and to_epoch_count as defined in the reference module temporal.
  • [P] is 1 when P holds and 0 otherwise.

Proof

  1. Calendar facts. (a) For integers y and k>0, ⌈(y+1)/k⌉−⌈y/k⌉=[k∣y]: with y=qk+r, 0≤r<k, the left ceiling is q+1 because 1≤r+1≤k, and the right one is q+[r>0]. (b) Hence B(y+1)−B(y)=365+[4∣y]−[100∣y]+[400∣y], and the bracket sum is is_leap(y) as 0 or 1 in each of the four cases: 4∤y gives 0; 4∣y, 100∤y gives 1; 100∣y, 400∤y gives 0; 400∣y gives 1. So B is strictly increasing and Y in the statement is unique. (c) B(400k)=146000k+100k−4k+k=146097k. (d) The twelve values month_length(y, 1..=12) sum to 365+[is_leap(y)].
  2. date_from_day(x) for an integer x. cycle is ⌊x/146097⌋, so by (c) B(400cycle)≤x<B(400cycle+400). The first loop starts at 400cycle and increments year while B(year+1)≤x, so it stops at the unique Y of fact (b), after at most 399 steps, keeping B(year)≤x; the second loop’s condition is then false. The checked operations do not overflow for the counts considered, since ∣x∣<2111 gives ∣Y∣<2103. The function returns None at i64::try_from(year) exactly when Y leaves i64. Otherwise within =x−B(Y)∈[0,365+[is_leap(Y)]), and by (d) the month loop finds the unique M∈1..12 with ∑k<M​month_length(Y,k)≤within<∑k≤M​month_length(Y,k) and returns D=within−∑k<M​month_length(Y,k)+1∈[1,month_length(Y,M)], so the final None is unreachable. Then day_number(Y, M, D) =B(Y)+∑k<M​month_length(Y,k)+D−1=x.
  3. Clause 1. In from_epoch_count, seconds is S and fraction is f=c−τu​S∈[0,τu​); days is Δ and in_day is r=S−86400Δ∈[0,86400); epoch is E=B(1970)=365⋅1970+493−20+5=719528, and ∣Δ∣≤2127/86400<2111, so epoch.checked_add(days) succeeds. By step 2, date_from_day(E + Δ) is None exactly when Y leaves i64. The remaining conversions succeed: the hour ⌊r/3600⌋≤23, the minute ⌊(rmod3600)/60⌋≤59 and the second rmod60≤59 fit u8, and the width du​ fits usize.
  4. The value. For an in-range count, t has the date (Y,M,D) of step 2 with negative_zero false and width the maximum of 4 and the number of digits of ∣Y∣, the time with those hour, minute and second, the fraction {f:0d_u$} (empty when du​=0), which has exactly du​ ASCII digits because f<10du​, the separator Upper, and the offset Zulu(Upper) when instant and Local otherwise, with no infinity. Every condition of well_formed holds: the offset is admitted, the date shape is full and valid_date holds by step 2, the width is canonical, the time shape is full with fields in range, the fraction is digits after a second, and a date-time has a full date and an hour.
  5. The checks of to_epoch_count(&t, u, instant) all pass: date, time and year are present; negative_zero is false; the separator is Upper; the offset is the one instant selects; month, day, hour, minute and second are present; the width is canonical; 1≤M≤12 and 1≤D≤ month_length(Y, M) by step 2; hour, minute and second are at most 23, 59, 59; the fraction has du​ digits.
  6. The count. The fraction parses to f (for du​=0 the code takes 0, and then τu​=1 gives f=0). By step 2, day_number(Y, M, D) −E=Δ. The seconds are 86400Δ+3600⌊r/3600⌋+60⌊(rmod3600)/60⌋+rmod60=86400Δ+r=S, and the result is τu​S+f=c by Euclidean division. No checked operation overflows: ∣E+Δ∣<366⋅263+366<272 because Y is an i64 year, so ∣86400Δ∣<289, the seconds are below 290 in absolute value, and their product by τu​≤109<230 plus f<230 stays below 2121. Hence to_epoch_count(&t, u, instant) == Some(c).

Canonical epoch temporals round-trip through counts

Statement

For every value t: Temporal with t.well_formed(), every unit u (TimeUnit) and flag instant: if to_epoch_count(&t, u, instant) = Some(c), then from_epoch_count(c, u, instant) == Some(t).

With Epoch counts round-trip through temporals, the image of from_epoch_count(·, u, instant) is exactly the set of well-formed t with to_epoch_count(&t, u, instant) ≠ None, and the two functions are inverse bijections between the in-range counts and that set. In particular every temporal in the image returns to itself through its count.

Outside the domain

  • A well-formed value outside the image (not a date-time with a full date and a full time, another separator than T, another offset than Z for an instant column or than none for a wall-clock column, a -0000 year, second 60, or another number of fraction digits than the unit fixes) is refused by to_epoch_count with None; production Temporal::to_epoch_count returns None for the same values.
  • A value with well_formed() false is outside the carrier. The hypothesis of well-formedness is used: a value built by assigning public fields with a full date-time, separator T, offset Z and also infinity = Some((Positive, DateTime)) passes every check of to_epoch_count, which does not read infinity, yet from_epoch_count returns a finite value. Production cannot hold such a value, since its to_epoch_count accepts only the DateTime variant, and its deserialization refuses ill-formed values.

Definitions used

  • B(y)=365y+⌈y/4⌉−⌈y/100⌉+⌈y/400⌉, computed by days_before_year and days_before_year_wide; E= day_number(1970, 1, 1) =B(1970)=719528.
  • is_leap, month_length, day_number, date_from_day, TimeUnit::digits, TimeUnit::ticks, from_epoch_count, to_epoch_count and well_formed as defined in the reference module temporal; du​ is the digit count of u and τu​=10du​.
  • [P] is 1 when P holds and 0 otherwise.

Proof

  1. What the checks give. Since to_epoch_count returned Some, t has a date with year Y, month M, day D, negative_zero false and the canonical width, 1≤M≤12 and 1≤D≤ month_length(Y, M); a time with hour h≤23, minute m≤59, second s≤59 and a fraction of exactly du​ ASCII digits with value f∈[0,τu​); the separator Upper; and the offset Zulu(Upper) when instant, Local otherwise. Because t is well formed and has a date, it has no infinity (the infinity branch of well_formed requires date.is_none()). These are all the fields of a Temporal.
  2. The count. With Δ= day_number(Y, M, D) −E and r=3600h+60m+s∈[0,86399], the function returns c=τu​(86400Δ+r)+f.
  3. Calendar facts. For integers y and k>0, ⌈(y+1)/k⌉−⌈y/k⌉=[k∣y] (write y=qk+r′ with 0≤r′<k: the left ceiling is q+1 and the right one q+[r′>0]). Hence B(y+1)−B(y)=365+[is_leap(y)], checked over the four cases of divisibility by 4, 100, 400, so B is strictly increasing; B(400k)=146097k; and the twelve month lengths of year y sum to 365+[is_leap(y)].
  4. date_from_day(E + Δ) = Some((Y, M, D)). Let x=E+Δ= day_number(Y, M, D) =B(Y)+w with w=∑k<M​month_length(Y,k)+D−1; by step 1 and step 3, 0≤w<365+[is_leap(Y)], so B(Y)≤x<B(Y+1), and Y is the unique year with this property. date_from_day starts at 400⌊x/146097⌋, where B is at most x, and its first loop stops at the unique year with B(year)≤x<B(year+1), which is Y; the second loop does not run, and Y fits i64 because it is the year of t. Its month loop finds the unique month whose cumulative range contains w, which is M because D−1< month_length(Y, M), and returns the day D.
  5. from_epoch_count(c, u, instant). Since 0≤f<τu​, seconds is 86400Δ+r and fraction is f; since 0≤r<86400, days is Δ and in_day is r. epoch.checked_add(days) is x, and step 4 gives the date (Y,M,D), written with negative_zero false and the width the maximum of 4 and the digit count of ∣Y∣, which is the canonical width of t by step 1. The hour is ⌊r/3600⌋=h, the minute ⌊(rmod3600)/60⌋=m and the second rmod60=s, because m,s≤59. The fraction is {f:0d_u$}, the unique string of du​ decimal digits with value f, which is the fraction of t (empty when du​=0). The separator is Upper and the offset is the one instant selects, as in t, and there is no infinity. Every field agrees with t by step 1, so the result is Some(t).
  6. The bijection remark. By L-values-28, every t = from_epoch_count(c, u, instant) is well formed with to_epoch_count(&t, u, instant) = Some(c); by steps 1 to 5, every well-formed t with to_epoch_count(&t, u, instant) = Some(c) is from_epoch_count(c, u, instant). The two functions are thus inverse bijections between the in-range counts and that set.

Binary16 lexical mapping is exact

Statement

For every rational q satisfying Premise P of L-values-9 and every boolean z, the binary16 lexical mapping binary16(q, z) satisfies the following. The production binary16 rounding in crates/panproto-expr/src/exact/binary16.rs is required to agree on the exact rationals denoted by its finite decimal inputs.

  1. if q=0 it returns Finite(0x8000) when z holds and Finite(0x0000) otherwise, so the sign of an exact zero is kept;
  2. if ∣q∣≥65520 it returns Overflow { negative } with negative true exactly when q<0;
  3. if 0<∣q∣<65520 it returns Finite(h) where decode(Format::B16, h) is Finite { negative, value: v } with negative true exactly when q<0, v is an element of V16​ nearest to q, and when two elements of V16​ are nearest, h is even and the other one’s pattern of the same sign is odd (ties to even); a non-zero q whose nearest value is zero gives the zero of the sign of q;
  4. for each pattern h<216 for which decode(Format::B16, h) is Finite { negative: s, value: v } (the 2×31×1024=63488 patterns whose exponent field is not all ones), binary16(v, s) is Finite(h): the mapping is exact on binary16 values.

Outside the domain

A rational that does not satisfy Premise P is outside the proved arithmetic domain. binary16 still returns a Rounded value because round_to has conversion fallbacks, but this law makes no nearest-value claim about that path. An overflow is the result Rounded::Overflow { negative }, not a refusal; the routes that use the mapping turn it into FidelityReason::Overflow (exact reading) or into the infinity of its sign (nearest reading). Patterns whose exponent field is all ones decode as Infinite or NaN and are outside item 4 by its hypothesis; they are not readings of a rational.

Definitions used

  • binary16(q, z): the reference definition round_to(Format::B16, q, z).
  • round_to, decode, pattern, even and odd patterns, VF​, MF​ and the format parameters: as defined in Part I of L-values-9.
  • V16​: VF​ for F = Format::B16.
  • The binary16 parameters, from Format: W=16, p=11, w=5, bias =15, emin​=−14, emax​=15, S=215= 0x8000.

Proof

  1. By the definition of binary16, binary16(q, z) equals round_to(Format::B16, q, z) for all q and z, so every property of round_to at F = Format::B16 is a property of binary16.
  2. With the binary16 parameters, M16​=2emax​+1−2emax​−p=216−24=65520, and S=215= 0x8000.
  3. Item 1 is item R1 of L-values-9 at F = Format::B16, with Finite(S) = Finite(0x8000).
  4. Item 2 is item R2 of L-values-9 at F = Format::B16, using step 2 for M16​.
  5. Item 3 is item R3 of L-values-9 at F = Format::B16, using step 2 for M16​.
  6. Item 4 is item R6 of L-values-9 at F = Format::B16; its hypothesis ranges over all patterns h<216 with a finite decoding, which by the definition of decode are those whose exponent field E is one of the 31 values 0,…,30, with either sign and any of the 210 fractions. Each such rational has a numerator and denominator of fewer than 263 bits, so it satisfies Premise P. The cases q=0, 0<∣q∣<65520 and ∣q∣≥65520 are exhaustive on the stated domain, so items 1 to 3 cover every rational in that domain.
