Nearest reading accepts finite rounded numerals

Statement

Let F be Format::B16, Format::B32 or Format::B64, of width W∈{16,32,64}, and let spec be any ValueSpec with kind: ScalarKind::Float { bits: W }, float_reading: FloatReading::NearestKeepingLexeme and numeral: None (its other fields are arbitrary). For every text t and every class c∈{LexClass::Number, LexClass::String}, the reference coercion coerce(t, c, spec) (which the production coerce is required to equal exactly) is as follows.

  1. If parse_non_finite(t) is Some(nf), the result is Some(Ok(Value::Float(non_finite_bits(nf)))): 0x7ff8000000000000 or 0xfff8000000000000 for a NaN spelling without or with a minus sign, and the binary64 infinity of the written sign for an infinity spelling.
  2. Otherwise, if parse_numeral(t) is Some(n), let d = DecimalValue::of_numeral(n) and q=val(d). The result is Some(Ok(Value::Float(x))) with x = widen_bits(F, nearest(F, d).bits(F)); the nearest reading never refuses a numeral. When q satisfies Premise P of L-values-9, nearest(F, d) equals round_to(F, q, n.negative). Then decode(Format::B64, x) is Infinite { negative: n.negative } when ∣q∣≥MF​, and otherwise Finite { negative: n.negative, value: v } where v is the element of VF​ nearest to q with ties to even, in the sense of item R3 of L-values-9 (and v=0 when q=0). The sign of the result is always the written sign.
  3. Otherwise the result is Some(Err(FidelityReason::NotANumber)).

Two facts used by later laws are part of this statement. (a) For every finite DecimalValue d that satisfies Premise D of L-values-3 and whose exact value satisfies Premise P, nearest(F, d) equals round_to(F, val(d), d.negative). (b) For every pattern b<2W of F with decode(F, b) equal to Finite { negative: s, value: v }, decode(Format::B64, widen_bits(F, b)) is Finite { negative: s, value: v }; for an infinite pattern it is the binary64 infinity of the same sign.

Outside the domain

  • A class other than Number or String: LexClass::Bool, LexClass::Bytes and LexClass::DateTime are refused with FidelityReason::NotANumber (the numeric_class check); LexClass::Null gives Some(Ok(Value::Null)); LexClass::Tagged(_) is read by the tagged coercion of L-values-22.
  • A spec with numeral: Some(dialect): the text is first normalized by the dialect (L-values-23); a text the dialect rejects is refused with FidelityReason::NotANumber, and a normalized text is then read by this law.
  • A float width other than 16, 32 or 64: Format::of_width is None and the reference returns None, outside its domain; no rule is stated for such a width.
  • Coercing an existing value (rather than a lexeme) under NearestKeepingLexeme: the reference coerce_value returns None, outside its domain. The source text kept by the reading route (the nearest-reading complement of the page introduction) is not an operation of this law.
  • A parsed numeral whose exact rational does not satisfy Premise P remains operationally inside item 2 and is accepted, but the equation with round_to and the nearest-value characterization are outside the proved arithmetic domain.
  • An arbitrary finite DecimalValue that violates Premise D is outside fact (a). A value built from a parsed numeral automatically satisfies that premise, as proved in step 5.

Definitions used

  • coerce, coerce_float, nearest, non_finite_bits, nan_bits, inf_bits, parse_non_finite, parse_numeral, DecimalValue::of_numeral, DecimalValue::scaled, pow10_exact and DecimalValue::position: the reference definitions in pages/values.rs, modules coerce and exact.
  • val(d): for d = DecimalValue { negative, digits, exponent }, the rational (−1)negative⋅digits⋅10exponent. digits is a Nat, so it has no leading zero; its digit_count L satisfies 10L−1≤digits<10L when it is non-zero. position is L+exponent.
  • widen_bits(F, b): on Finite { negative, value }, round_to(Format::B64, value, negative).bits(Format::B64); on Infinite { negative }, Rounded::Overflow { negative }.bits(Format::B64); on a NaN, the bit-wise widening of L-values-8.
  • Rounded::bits(F): Finite(b) gives b, Overflow { negative } gives the pattern with all-ones exponent, zero fraction and sign bit set exactly when negative holds.
  • round_to, decode, pattern, VF​, MF​, S and the format parameters: as defined in Part I of L-values-9.
  • BOUND =400.

Proof

  1. Dispatch. coerce returns early only for LexClass::Null and LexClass::Tagged, neither of which is c. With numeral: None the dialect branch is skipped. The kind is Float { bits: W }, so Format::of_width(W) is Some(F), numeric_class() is Ok(()) for Number and String, and the result is Some(coerce_float(t, F, NearestKeepingLexeme)).
  2. Items 1 and 3. coerce_float first tries parse_non_finite(t); on Some(nf) it returns Ok(Value::Float(non_finite_bits(nf))), where nan_bits gives 0x7ff8000000000000 or 0xfff8000000000000 by the written sign and inf_bits gives Overflow { negative }.bits(Format::B64); this is item 1. Otherwise it applies parse_numeral(t) and maps None to Err(FidelityReason::NotANumber), which is item 3.
  3. Fact (a): nearest is round_to of the exact value. Let d be finite, satisfy Premise D, and have q=val(d). If d is zero, scaled returns Value(0) and nearest returns round_to(F, 0, d.negative). Otherwise let P = position =L+exponent, so 10P−1≤∣q∣<10P. Three cases, exhaustive by the definition of scaled(-400, 400): (i) P>400: scaled is AtLeastHi and nearest returns Overflow { negative: d.negative }. Here ∣q∣≥10400>8400=21200>21024≥2emax​+1>MF​, so item R2 of L-values-9 gives round_to(F, q, d.negative) = Overflow { negative: q < 0 }, and q<0 exactly when d.negative since digits is non-zero. (ii) P≤−400: scaled is BelowLo and nearest returns Finite(S) when d.negative holds and Finite(0) otherwise (sign_bit(F) =2W−1=S). Here 0<∣q∣<10−400<2−1200<2−1075≤2emin​−p (the exponent emin​−p is −25, −150, −1075 for the three formats). Every non-zero t∈VF​ has ∣t∣≥2emin​−p+1 by item R4 of L-values-9, so ∣t−q∣≥∣t∣−∣q∣>2emin​−p>∣q∣=∣0−q∣; hence 0 is the unique nearest element, and item R3 of L-values-9 gives Finite(b) with value 0 and sign bit set exactly when q<0, that is, b=S when d.negative and b=0 otherwise. (iii) −400<P≤400: scaled returns Value(q') with q′ = Int::new(d.negative, digits) × pow10_exact(exponent). Premise D and L-values-3, step 10, give pow10_exact(k) =10k on this call, so q′=(−1)d.negative⋅digits⋅10exponent=q; nearest returns round_to(F, q, d.negative). In all cases, when q satisfies Premise P, nearest(F, d) = round_to(F, q, d.negative).
  4. Fact (b): widening is exact. Let decode(F, b) be Finite { negative: s, value: v }. We show v∈V64​. If F is Format::B64 this is the definition of V64​. Otherwise, if v=0 it is the value of the binary64 pattern 0. If v=0, by item R4 of L-values-9 write ∣v∣=N2Q with 1≤N<2p, p≤24 and an integer Q, and let m = floor_log2(|v|). By item R4 of L-values-9, 2emin​−p+1≤∣v∣<2emax​+1, so −149≤m≤127, inside [−1022,1023]. From 2m≤N2Q<2Q+p we get m≤Q+p−1≤Q+52, so n=∣v∣/2m−52=N2Q−m+52 is an integer, and 252≤n<253 because 2m≤∣v∣<2m+1. By item R4 of L-values-9 at Format::B64, ∣v∣ and thus v lie in V64​. Choose the binary64 pattern b′ of value v whose sign bit is set exactly when s holds (for v=0 this is the sign of v; for v=0 both signs exist). Item R6 of L-values-9 at Format::B64 gives round_to(Format::B64, v, s) = Finite(b'), so widen_bits(F, b) =b′ and decode(Format::B64, b') is Finite { negative: s, value: v }. For an infinite pattern, widen_bits returns Overflow { negative }.bits(Format::B64), whose exponent field is all ones and fraction zero, so decode(Format::B64, ·) is Infinite { negative }.
  5. Item 2, the value. After parse_numeral(t) = Some(n), coerce_float sets d = of_numeral(n), so d.negative = n.negative, computes rounded = nearest(F, d), and under NearestKeepingLexeme returns Ok(Value::Float(widen_bits(F, rounded.bits(F)))) with no further test, independently of Premise P. The digit Nat has at most ⌈∣t∣/9⌉ limbs. A Rust string has length at most isize::MAX, and on either supported pointer width ⌈isize::MAX/9⌉<⌊usize::MAX/9⌋, so this parsed d satisfies Premise D. When q satisfies Premise P, step 3 gives rounded = round_to(F, q, n.negative), and no branch of this path returns Err.
  6. Item 2, the decoding under Premise P. If ∣q∣≥MF​, item R2 of L-values-9 gives Overflow { negative } with negative the sign of q, which is n.negative because q=0 and the sign of val(d) is d.negative; bits(F) is the infinity of F of that sign, and step 4 widens it to the binary64 infinity of that sign. If 0<∣q∣<MF​, item R3 of L-values-9 gives Finite(b) decoding to Finite { negative: q < 0, value: v } with v the nearest element, ties to even, and step 4 gives decode(Format::B64, x) = Finite { negative: n.negative, value: v }. If q=0, item R1 of L-values-9 gives the zero pattern of sign n.negative, which step 4 widens to the binary64 zero of that sign.
  7. Items 1 to 3 are exhaustive over t: either parse_non_finite accepts it (item 1), or it does not and parse_numeral accepts it (item 2), or neither does (item 3). Facts (a) and (b) are steps 3 and 4.

Closest-shortest text round-trips without a complement

Statement

Let F be Format::B16, Format::B32 or Format::B64, of width W, and let b<2W be a pattern with a finite decoding. Then shortest(F, b) is Some(D), and:

  1. round_to(F, D.value(), D.negative) is Finite(b): the closest-shortest decimal reads back by nearest rounding to its source pattern, sign of zero included;
  2. the text T = D.to_scientific() is a numeral whose reading is that decimal: parse_non_finite(T) is None, parse_numeral(T) is Some(n) with n.negative = D.negative, and val of DecimalValue::of_numeral(n) equals D.value();
  3. consequently, for c∈{LexClass::Number, LexClass::String} and every spec with kind: ScalarKind::Float { bits: W }, float_reading: FloatReading::NearestKeepingLexeme and numeral: None, coerce(T, c, spec) is Some(Ok(Value::Float(widen_bits(F, b)))). No complement is needed to return from the printed text to the pattern.

These are statements about the reference operations, which the production printer and reader are required to equal exactly.

Outside the domain

  • A NaN or infinite pattern: shortest returns None (Outside the domain of L-values-9, Part II), so there is no closest-shortest text; such values are written with their non-finite spellings, read by L-values-31, item 1.
  • A value b≥2W is not a pattern of F; the case does not arise, as recorded in L-values-9.
  • Classes other than Number and String, specs with a numeral dialect, and other float widths: as in L-values-31.

Definitions used

  • shortest, Dec, Dec::value, Dec::to_scientific: the reference definitions in module float. D.value() is (−1)negative⋅coefficient⋅10exponent, built with Int::new, which makes a negative zero equal to zero. to_scientific writes - when negative holds, then the decimal digits g1​g2​…gL​ of coefficient (Nat display: no leading zero, and 0 for zero), with a point after g1​ when L>1, then e, then the i64 decimal text of exponent +L−1 (a leading - when negative).
  • parse_numeral, parse_non_finite, DecimalValue::of_numeral, val, coerce, widen_bits: as defined in L-values-31.
  • round_to, decode, pattern, S: as defined in Part I of L-values-9.

Proof

  1. Zero. If the value is 0 then b=0 or b=S, and by P1 of L-values-9, D is Dec { negative: s, coefficient: 0, exponent: 0 } with s true exactly when b=S. D.value() is 0, and item R1 of L-values-9 gives round_to(F, 0, s) = Finite(b). This is item 1 for zero.
  2. Non-zero. Otherwise, with b+ the pattern b with its sign bit cleared, P2 of L-values-9 gives Some(D) with D.negative equal to the sign bit s of b and round_to(F, |D.value()|, false) = Finite(b⁺), where ∣D.value∣>0. If s is false, D.value() =∣D.value∣; since the value is non-zero, round_to ignores its third argument, and the result is Finite(b⁺) = Finite(b). If s is true, D.value() =−∣D.value∣, and item R5 of L-values-9 gives Finite(S + b⁺) = Finite(b). This is item 1.
  3. The text is not a non-finite spelling. After an optional -, T begins with the digit g1​, so neither stripping a point nor comparing with nan, inf or infinity matches, and parse_non_finite(T) is None.
  4. Parsing T (item 2). split_sign reads the leading - exactly when D.negative holds, so n.negative = D.negative. The remainder contains exactly one e (the digits, the point and the exponent’s sign contain none), so the mantissa is g1​ or g1​.g2​…gL​ and the exponent text is the decimal of k=exponent+L−1. The mantissa gives integer part g1​, fraction g2​…gL​ (empty when L=1), both non-empty in total and all digits; the exponent text has an optional - and at least one digit, so parse_numeral returns Some(n) with exponent k. of_numeral gives digits = the natural with decimal digits g1​…gL​, that is D.coefficient, and exponent k−(L−1) = D.exponent. Hence val of of_numeral(n) is the signed product of D.coefficient and 10 to the power D.exponent, which is D.value() (both are zero when the coefficient is zero).
  5. Reading T (item 3). By L-values-31, item 2, and steps 3 and 4, coerce(T, c, spec) is Some(Ok(Value::Float(widen_bits(F, round_to(F, D.value(), D.negative).bits(F))))). By step 1 or 2 the inner result is Finite(b), whose bits(F) is b, so the result is Some(Ok(Value::Float(widen_bits(F, b)))).
  6. Steps 1 and 2 cover every finite pattern (zero or not), which completes the proof.

The exact float reading is the fidelity law

Statement

Under the exact reading FloatReading::Exact, the coercion of a numeral is the fidelity law. Let F∈{Format::B16, Format::B32, Format::B64} be the format of Float { bits }, mF​ = 5, 9, 17 its significant-digit bound, s a specification with s.kind = Float { bits } and s.float_reading = Exact, and t a lexeme of effective class Number or String (L-values-2) that the declared dialect, if any, accepts, with t∘ its normal form (L-values-23), not a NaN or infinity spelling. Then:

  1. if parse_numeral(t°) is None, coerce(t, c, s) is Some(Err(NotANumber));
  2. otherwise, with n the numeral, d = DecimalValue::of_numeral(n), x=val(d) and π = nearest(F, d) (the round-to-nearest-even pattern LF​(x), the sign of a zero kept), the result is Some(Err(Overflow)) when π is Overflow; Some(Ok(Float(widen_bits(F, π)))) when π is finite and either its value is x or shortest(F, π) (the closest-shortest text CF​(LF​(x))) is a decimal equal to x numerically; and Some(Err(PrecisionExceeded { max: m_F })) otherwise.

So the exact reading accepts a finite numeral exactly when LF​(x)=x or CF​(LF​(x))=x, and then returns LF​(x) unchanged; it is not the representability test alone: "0.1" under Float { bits: 64 } is accepted as Float(0x3fb999999999999a), because the closest-shortest text of that pattern is 0.1, although 1/10∈/V64​. This is the converse half of clause 6 of L-values-4, stated here for each width.

Lemma (exact membership). For every format F and every rational q satisfying Premise P of L-values-9, the reference exact_reading(F, q) holds if and only if q∈VF​, that is, if and only if some pattern of F decodes to the finite value q. It is false for every rational of magnitude at least MF​ and true for 0 (of either written sign). The value of the finite pattern π of item 2 equals x if and only if x∈VF​, so the first disjunct of item 2 is the exact-membership test of the Lemma.

The production correspondence of the Lemma has a narrower carrier. For every finite binary64 datum x, let qx​ be the exact rational in decode(Format::B64, x.to_bits()). Then binary16_bits(x).is_some() holds if and only if qx​∈V16​. No conversion from an arbitrary rational to f64 is part of this claim. The production coerce under the exact reading is required to equal items 1 and 2 at each width, as the supplemental exhaustive tests named below check.

Outside the domain

A rational that does not satisfy Premise P is outside the proved reference domain. exact_reading still returns a boolean because round_to has conversion fallbacks, but the equivalence is not asserted for that path. A text that parse_numeral rejects has no rational value and never reaches the operation (the coercion that reads it refuses it with FidelityReason::NotANumber before any float decision). NaN and infinity spellings are not rationals and are read by parse_non_finite, not by this operation. The production correspondence concerns finite binary64 data only; infinities and NaNs are outside its rational carrier and are governed by L-values-8.

Definitions used

  • exact_reading(F, q): the reference alias of holds_exactly(F, q), defined as: match round_to(F, q, false); on Finite(bits), true exactly when decode(F, bits) is Finite { value, .. } with value == q; on Overflow { .. }, false.
  • round_to, decode, VF​, MF​: as defined in Part I of L-values-9. == on Rat is equality of rationals (lowest terms with positive denominator).
  • parse_numeral, DecimalValue::of_numeral: the reference definitions; val(d)=(−1)negative⋅digits⋅10exponent for d = DecimalValue { negative, digits, exponent }.

Proof

  1. If the reading holds, then q∈VF​. By the definition of holds_exactly, a true result requires round_to(F, q, false) to be Finite(bits) and decode(F, bits) to be Finite { value, .. } with value == q. Then bits is a pattern of F whose finite value is q, so q∈VF​ by the definition of VF​.
  2. If q∈VF​ and q=0, the reading holds. Item R1 of L-values-9 with z false gives Finite(0), and decode(F, 0) is Finite { value: 0, .. } (E=0, f=0), which equals q.
  3. If q∈VF​ and q=0, the reading holds. By item R4 of L-values-9, ∣q∣≤maxVF​=2emax​+1−2emax​−p+1<2emax​+1−2emax​−p=MF​, so item R3 of L-values-9 applies: round_to(F, q, false) is Finite(b) with decode(F, b) equal to Finite { value: v, .. } and ∣v−q∣≤∣t−q∣ for every t∈VF​. Taking t=q gives ∣v−q∣≤0, so v=q and the comparison value == q is true.
  4. Steps 2 and 3 cover every q∈VF​, and step 1 covers every true result, so exact_reading(F, q) holds if and only if q∈VF​.
  5. Numerals. For an accepted numeral the operation is applied to the rational val(d), so step 4 applies to it. A rational with ∣q∣≥MF​ exceeds maxVF​ (step 3) and is not in VF​, so the reading is false, in agreement with item R2 of L-values-9 (the Overflow arm). A zero numeral, written 0 or -0, has val(d)=0∈VF​, so the reading is true by step 2; the exact reading takes the rational alone, and the written sign of a zero does not affect it.
  6. Production binary16 membership. Let x be finite, and let its binary64 decoding be the exact rational qx​. The cases in binary16_bits are precisely the binary16 grid: signed zero; normal values with exponent from −14 through 15 and no non-zero binary64 fraction bit below the binary16 precision; and subnormal values down to 2−24 whose discarded bits are all zero. These are exactly the finite values of V16​ in item R4 of L-values-9. Hence binary16_bits(x).is_some() if and only if qx​∈V16​. Because qx​ comes from one finite binary64 pattern, it satisfies Premise P.
  7. The registered clause. coerce reaches coerce_float(t°, F, Exact) for this specification and class by rows 3 and 4 of L-values-2 (the dialect step of L-values-23 first replacing t by t∘), and t∘ is not a non-finite spelling, so parse_non_finite is None. coerce_float then returns Err(NotANumber) when parse_numeral refuses, which is item 1. Otherwise it forms d and rounded = nearest(F, d); the nearest-keeping-lexeme return is not taken under Exact; Overflow gives Err(Overflow); and a finite pattern π gives Ok(Float(widen_bits(F, π))) exactly when canonical || denotes_exactly(F, d, π), else Err(PrecisionExceeded { max: F.max_significant_digits() }), and max_significant_digits is 5, 9, 17. Here canonical is the test that shortest(F, π) exists and dec_equals it with d, the numeric equality of the closest-shortest text with x. denotes_exactly(F, d, π) holds exactly when d.scaled is Value(q) and the value of π equals q. When scaled is Value(q), q=x and π = round_to(F, q, ·), whose value equals q exactly when q∈VF​ (steps 1 to 4, through items R1 and R3 of L-values-9); when it is BelowLo, 0<∣x∣<10−400 lies below the least positive value of every format, and when it is AtLeastHi, ∣x∣≥10400>MF​, so in both x∈/VF​ and denotes_exactly is false. Hence acceptance is LF​(x)=x or CF​(LF​(x))=x, with the value LF​(x), which is item 2. For "0.1" at binary64, π = 0x3fb999999999999a and shortest of it is 0.1, so canonical holds while 1/10∈/V64​ (its denominator is not a power of two).

Decimal numeric comparison is a total preorder

Statement

Under Assumption W of L-values-10, Decimal::cmp_numeric is a total preorder on all decimal values, finite and special. That is, for all a,b,c of type Decimal:

  1. (totality) a.cmp_numeric(&b) is one of Less, Equal, Greater;
  2. (reflexivity) a.cmp_numeric(&a) is Equal;
  3. (reversal) b.cmp_numeric(&a) is the reverse of a.cmp_numeric(&b);
  4. (transitivity) if a.cmp_numeric(&b) and b.cmp_numeric(&c) are both Less or Equal, then a.cmp_numeric(&c) is Less or Equal, and it is Less when either of the two is Less.

Its equivalence classes (pairs comparing Equal) are exactly: the finite decimals denoting one rational number; the two infinities, each alone; and, for each sign and signalling flag, the NaNs of that sign and flag, whatever their payloads. The same four properties hold for DecimalValue::cmp_numeric on finite decimals. The production DecimalValue::cmp_numeric is required to equal this definition exactly.

Outside the domain

Subject to Assumption W, every value of the reference type Decimal is in the domain: a finite payload is a DecimalValue built from canonical Nat and Int fields, an infinity is a sign, and a NaN is a sign, a flag and a Nat payload, so no ill-formed decimal can be written. A target that violates Assumption W’s pointer-width condition, or a held value that violates its limb bound, is outside the proved domain. In production, a DecimalValue with noncanonical finite digits, or a special value whose digits are not "0", whose exponent is not zero or whose payload is not canonical digits, is outside the domain: deserialization refuses each with ExactParseError of reason FidelityReason::NotANumber, DecimalValue::new refuses noncanonical finite digits with the same reason, and a value built from the public fields in violation of these invariants is not a decimal the law speaks about.

Definitions used

  • ν(d)∈Q is the number a finite decimal denotes, as defined in L-values-10.
  • class_rank(d) is 0 for a negative quiet NaN, 1 for a negative signalling NaN, 2 for −∞, 3 for every finite decimal, 4 for +∞, 5 for a positive signalling NaN and 6 for a positive quiet NaN; these seven arms cover every Decimal.
  • Decimal::cmp_numeric(a, b) returns x.cmp_numeric(y) when a = Finite(x) and b = Finite(y), and class_rank(a).cmp(&class_rank(b)) otherwise. This is the reference panproto_reference::exact::Decimal::cmp_numeric, whose rustdoc states it as its definition: two finite values by DecimalValue::cmp_numeric (every zero Equal), and otherwise by class rank, lowest first, negative quiet NaNs, negative signalling NaNs, the negative infinity, every finite value, the positive infinity, positive signalling NaNs and positive quiet NaNs, payloads ignored.
  • The numeric key of d is K(d)=(class_rank(d),q(d))∈N×Q, with q(d)=ν(x) when d = Finite(x) and q(d)=0 otherwise. N×Q carries the lexicographic order: compare first components, and second components when the first are equal.

Proof

Assume Assumption W throughout.

  1. The lexicographic order on N×Q is a total order: each component order is total, so for two pairs either the first components differ and decide, or they are equal and the second components decide; it is reflexive, its comparison reverses when the pair is exchanged, and it is transitive, by the same three properties of each component taken in order.
  2. For all a,b: a.cmp_numeric(&b) =cmp(K(a),K(b)). Case both finite, a = Finite(x), b = Finite(y): the first components of K are both 3, so cmp(K(a),K(b))=cmp(ν(x),ν(y)), which is x.cmp_numeric(y) by L-values-10, the value the first arm returns.
  3. Case not both finite, with class_rank(a)=class_rank(b): the second arm returns cmp(class_rank(a),class_rank(b)), which is cmp(K(a),K(b)) since the first components differ.
  4. Case not both finite, with class_rank(a)=class_rank(b): the rank is not 3, because rank 3 belongs to finite values only and equal ranks of 3 would make both finite. So neither is finite, q(a)=q(b)=0, K(a)=K(b), and both the second arm and cmp(K(a),K(b)) give Equal. Steps 2 to 4 cover every pair.
  5. By step 2, cmp_numeric is the pullback of the total order of step 1 along K. Totality holds because the function returns a value of Ordering on every pair (step 2 has a value for every pair). Reflexivity: K(a)=K(a). Reversal: cmp(K(b),K(a)) is the reverse of cmp(K(a),K(b)). Transitivity: K(a)≤K(b)≤K(c) gives K(a)≤K(c), strictly when either step is strict, by step 1.
  6. The equivalence classes are the fibres of K. For finite a,b, K(a)=K(b) exactly when ν agrees. For non-finite values, K(a)=K(b) exactly when the class ranks agree, and the seven ranks separate −∞, +∞ and the four (sign, flag) classes of NaNs, while no rank reads the payload.
  7. For DecimalValue::cmp_numeric, L-values-10 gives a.cmp_numeric(&b) =cmp(ν(a),ν(b)), the pullback of the total order of Q along ν, so the four properties follow as in step 5.

Decimal special values have fixed numeric placement

Statement

Under Decimal::cmp_numeric, the infinities and NaNs occupy fixed classes around the finite decimals. For every finite decimal f and all payloads p,p′, writing a≺b for a.cmp_numeric(&b) == Less and a∼b for a.cmp_numeric(&b) == Equal:

−NaNp​≺−sNaNp′​≺−∞≺f≺+∞≺+sNaNp​≺+qNaNp′​,

where ±NaNp​ (also written ±qNaNp​) is NaN { negative, signalling: false, payload: p } and ±sNaNp​ is NaN { negative, signalling: true, payload: p }, with negative true for the sign −. Moreover each infinity is ∼ only to itself, and two NaNs are ∼ exactly when they agree in sign and signalling flag, whatever their payloads. Precisely: whenever a and b are not both finite,

a.cmp_numeric(&b)=cmp(class_rank(a),class_rank(b)),

with the ranks listed under Definitions used. The production DecimalValue::cmp_numeric is required to equal this definition exactly.

Outside the domain

Every value of the reference type Decimal is in the domain, as in L-values-35. In production, a special DecimalValue whose digits are not "0", whose exponent is not zero or whose payload is not canonical digits is outside the domain; deserialization refuses it with ExactParseError of reason FidelityReason::NotANumber.

Definitions used

  • class_rank(d) is defined by seven match arms covering every Decimal: a NaN with negative: true, signalling: false has rank 0; negative: true, signalling: true, rank 1; Infinite { negative: true }, rank 2; Finite(_), rank 3; Infinite { negative: false }, rank 4; a NaN with negative: false, signalling: true, rank 5; negative: false, signalling: false, rank 6. No arm reads a payload.
  • Decimal::cmp_numeric(a, b) returns x.cmp_numeric(y) when both are finite (Finite(x), Finite(y)), and class_rank(a).cmp(&class_rank(b)) in every other case. This is the reference panproto_reference::exact::Decimal::cmp_numeric, whose rustdoc states it as its definition: two finite values by DecimalValue::cmp_numeric (every zero Equal), and otherwise by class rank, lowest first, negative quiet NaNs, negative signalling NaNs, the negative infinity, every finite value, the positive infinity, positive signalling NaNs and positive quiet NaNs, payloads ignored.

Proof

  1. Let a,b be decimals that are not both finite. The first arm of Decimal::cmp_numeric matches only the pair (Finite(_), Finite(_)), so the second arm applies and returns cmp(class_rank(a),class_rank(b)). This is the displayed equation.
  2. The chain has exactly one finite term, f, so every pair of distinct terms has a non-finite side and step 1 applies to it. By the definition of class_rank the seven terms have ranks 0,1,2,3,4,5,6 in order, for every payload and every finite f (the finite arm has rank 3 whatever its fields). So every term compares Less against every later term, which is the chain.
  3. An infinity ±∞ compared with any b: if b is finite, step 1 gives rank 2 or 4 against 3, not Equal; otherwise step 1 gives Equal exactly when b has the same rank, and ranks 2 and 4 are each held by one value only (Infinite { negative: true } and Infinite { negative: false }). So each infinity is ∼ only to itself.
  4. A NaN compared with any b: if b is finite, step 1 gives a rank in {0,1,5,6} against 3, not Equal. Otherwise step 1 gives Equal exactly when the ranks agree. The ranks 0,1,5,6 are held exactly by the NaNs of the four (sign, flag) pairs, and no arm of class_rank reads the payload, so two NaNs are ∼ exactly when sign and flag agree, whatever p and p′ are.

Compare-total refines decimal numeric comparison

Statement

Under Assumption W of L-values-10, compare-total refines the numeric preorder on all decimals, finite and special. For all a,b of type Decimal:

  1. if a.cmp_numeric(&b) is not Equal, then a.compare_total(&b) equals a.cmp_numeric(&b); in particular a strict numeric comparison Less (or Greater) is preserved as Less (or Greater);
  2. if a.compare_total(&b) is Equal, then a.cmp_numeric(&b) is Equal.

So compare-total is a linear extension of cmp_numeric: it keeps every strict numeric comparison, and the only pairs it orders that cmp_numeric does not are pairs inside one numeric equivalence class, which it splits by representation. The production DecimalValue::compare_total and DecimalValue::cmp_numeric are required to equal these definitions exactly.

Outside the domain

Subject to Assumption W, every value of the reference type Decimal is in the domain, as in L-values-35. A target that violates Assumption W’s pointer-width condition, or a held value that violates its limb bound, is outside the proved domain. In production, a DecimalValue that violates the field invariants is outside the domain, with the refusal ExactParseError of reason FidelityReason::NotANumber named in L-values-11.

Definitions used

  • ν(x), the number a finite decimal denotes, as in L-values-10.
  • class_rank and Decimal::cmp_numeric, as in L-values-36: two finite values compare by DecimalValue::cmp_numeric, every other pair by class_rank, whose values are 3 for a finite decimal and, for the clear sign flag, 4,5,6 for the infinity, signalling NaNs and quiet NaNs, and for the set flag 2,1,0 for the same three classes.
  • compare_total, cmp_total_positive and its rank (0 finite, 1 infinity, 2 signalling NaN, 3 quiet NaN), as in L-values-11.
  • From the two rank tables, for every decimal d with the flag clear, class_rank(d)=3+rank(d), and with the flag set, class_rank(d)=3−rank(d). Both identities are checked on the four classes finite, infinity, signalling NaN and quiet NaN: 3,4,5,6 and 3,2,1,0.

Proof

Assume Assumption W throughout.

  1. Property 2 follows from two earlier laws: by L-values-11, a.compare_total(&b) is Equal only when a=b, and by L-values-35 (reflexivity), a.cmp_numeric(&a) is Equal.
  2. For property 1 we split on the sign flags of a and b and on finiteness. Case the flags differ, a with the flag set and b with it clear. compare_total returns Less. We show a.cmp_numeric(&b) is Less or Equal, so property 1 holds whenever it is not Equal. If both are finite, ν(a)≤0≤ν(b) (the set flag gives a nonpositive number and the clear flag a nonnegative one), so by L-values-10 the comparison is Less or Equal. Otherwise cmp_numeric compares class ranks; a has rank in {0,1,2,3} and b in {3,4,5,6}, and the ranks are both 3 only when both are finite, which is excluded, so the result is Less.
  3. Case the flags differ, a with the flag clear and b with it set. Exchanging the arguments reverses both comparisons, by L-values-35 for cmp_numeric and by L-values-11 for compare_total. Step 2 applied to (b,a) gives b.compare_total(&a) = b.cmp_numeric(&a) whenever the latter is not Equal, and reversing both sides gives the same equality for (a,b).
  4. Case equal flags, both finite. compare_total returns a.cmp_numeric(b) whenever that is not Equal, and Decimal::cmp_numeric on two finite values is the same DecimalValue::cmp_numeric, so the two agree.
  5. Case equal flags, not both finite. Here Decimal::cmp_numeric returns cmp(class_rank(a),class_rank(b)), and property 1 concerns only the pairs with different class ranks. By the identities under Definitions used, different class ranks with equal flags mean different values of rank, so the pair is not two NaNs of one signalling flag (those share a rank), and not two finite values; hence cmp_total_positive takes its third arm and returns P=cmp(rank(a),rank(b)).
  6. Within step 5, if the common flag is clear, compare_total returns P=cmp(3+rank(a),3+rank(b))=cmp(class_rank(a),class_rank(b)). If the flag is set, compare_total returns the reverse of P, which is cmp(3−rank(a),3−rank(b))=cmp(class_rank(a),class_rank(b)). In both subcases it equals a.cmp_numeric(&b).
  7. Steps 2 to 6 cover every combination of flags and finiteness, which proves property 1. Together with property 2, compare_total agrees with cmp_numeric on every pair that cmp_numeric separates and orders strictly only pairs that either cmp_numeric separates or that lie in one of its equivalence classes and are distinct representations.

Special decimals have injective canonical bytes

Statement

Under Assumption W of L-values-10, for every decimal d of type Decimal, finite or special:

  1. decimal_bytes(&d) is Some of the byte 13 followed by the write_decimal layout of d; it is never None;
  2. for all a,b, decimal_bytes(&a) == decimal_bytes(&b) implies a=b under the derived ==, so the canonical bytes separate any two representations that differ in variant or in any field: the sign of a zero or of any finite value, the digits, the exponent (hence the scale, as for 1.50 and 1.5), the sign of an infinity, and the sign, signalling flag or payload of a NaN (NaN, -NaN, sNaN and NaN1 have four different byte strings, while NaN and NaN0 are one value and have one byte string);
  3. decode_value(&decimal_bytes(&d).unwrap()) is Some(Value::Decimal(d)).

The production canonical bytes of a decimal are required to equal this definition exactly.

Outside the domain

A target that violates Assumption W’s pointer-width condition, or a held value that violates its limb bound, is outside the proved domain. Subject to that assumption, every value of the reference type Decimal has canonical bytes, by property 1, and the reference type cannot hold a noncanonical digit string, exponent or payload (facts N1 and N3 of L-values-10). In production, a DecimalValue that violates its field invariants is outside the domain; deserialization refuses it with ExactParseError of reason FidelityReason::NotANumber.

Definitions used

  • decimal_bytes(d) is value_bytes(&Value::Decimal(d.clone())).
  • The writer primitives tag, str and write_digits, as in L-values-13, and facts N1 to N3 on Nat and Int, as in L-values-10.
  • write_decimal(d): for Finite(v), the byte u8::from(v.negative), write_digits(v.digits), the byte u8::from(v.exponent.is_negative()) and write_digits of the exponent’s magnitude; for Infinite { negative }, the bytes 2 and u8::from(negative); for NaN { negative, signalling, payload }, the bytes 3, u8::from(negative), u8::from(signalling) and write_digits(payload).
  • read_decimal is the reader of that layout, as defined in the reference canonical module.

Proof

  1. Property 1. write_value on Value::Decimal(d) writes the tag 13 and calls write_decimal, which has no failing branch, and the arm returns Some(()); so value_bytes returns Some of those bytes.
  2. Property 2, the first byte. After the common byte 13, the first byte of write_decimal is 0 or 1 for a finite value (its sign flag), 2 for an infinity and 3 for a NaN. Equal bytes thus give the same variant and, for finite values, the same sign flag.
  3. Finite values. Write c(n) for the bytes of write_digits(n): the 8-byte little-endian length of the numeral n.to_string() followed by the numeral. If c(n)⋅s=c(n′)⋅s′, the first 8 bytes give equal lengths (to_le_bytes is injective, and the length’s conversion from usize to u64 is injective under Assumption W of L-values-10), the next bytes give one numeral, so n=n′ by N1 and N2, and the remaining bytes give s=s′. After the sign byte, a finite value writes c(digits), the exponent’s sign byte and c of the exponent’s magnitude; applying the previous sentence twice, equal bytes give equal digits, equal exponent sign flags and equal magnitudes, hence equal exponents, because an Int is the pair of its sign flag and magnitude (N3). A DecimalValue is the triple of flag, digits and exponent, so equal bytes give equal values.
  4. Infinities and NaNs. An infinity’s bytes are 2 and its sign byte, so equal bytes give equal signs. A NaN’s bytes are 3, its sign byte, its signalling byte and c(payload), which determines the payload by step 3. Steps 2 to 4 cover every pair of variants and prove property 2. The listed examples differ in the field named, and NaN and NaN0 are both NaN { payload: 0 } by parse_decimal, which reads an empty payload and the payload 0 as zero.
  5. Property 2 is also the instance of L-values-13, property 2, at the values Value::Decimal(a) and Value::Decimal(b), which lie in that law’s domain because they have no temporal component; the variant Value::Decimal is injective, so a=b.
  6. Property 3. Value::Decimal(d) has no temporal and no big-integer component, so it satisfies the hypothesis of L-values-13, property 3, which gives decode_value(&decimal_bytes(&d).unwrap()) == Some(Value::Decimal(d)).

Unwritten YAML UTC remains a distinct representation

Statement

Let T be the set of values v: Temporal with v.well_formed(), and let v∈T have the offset Zulu(Unwritten), the representation a YAML timestamp without a zone receives. For an offset o write v[o] for v with its offset replaced by o. Let Zw​ be the set of written zero offsets Zulu(Upper), Zulu(Lower), Fixed(0, f) for f∈{Extended, Basic, HourOnly, ExtendedSeconds} and NegZero(f) for the same four forms, and let Zu​={Fixed(0, Unwritten)}. Every v[o] with o∈Zw​∪Zu​∪{Local} lies in T, and:

  1. (zero offset) for every o∈Zw​∪Zu​ and every c∈T, cmp_chronological(v, c) == cmp_chronological(v[o], c), cmp_chronological(c, v) == cmp_chronological(c, v[o]) and cmp_chronological(v, v[o]) == Some(Equal); and v is zoned, so cmp_chronological(v, v[Local]) and cmp_chronological(v[Local], v) are None;
  2. (the marker) unwritten_zulu(w) is true exactly when w.offset == Zulu(Unwritten), so it holds for v and fails for every v[o] above;
  3. (equality, descriptor and bytes) for every w∈T with w=v, canonical_bytes(w) != canonical_bytes(v); in particular v differs from every v[o] above under ==, under lexical_form (whose offset component is v.offset) and under canonical_bytes, and the offset of v is encoded as the bytes 1, 2 of the new layout, never the historical layout;
  4. (display) when v is finite, v.to_string() differs from the displays of v[Zulu(Upper)] and v[Zulu(Lower)], which are v.to_string() followed by Z, respectively z, and likewise from v[o].to_string() for every other o∈Zw​; and v.to_string() equals v[Local].to_string() and v[Fixed(0, Unwritten)].to_string(). When v is an infinity, v and every v[o] display as the same infinity spelling;
  5. (round trip) parse_as(v.lexical_form().unwrap(), &v.to_string()) == Some(v), so the marker survives display followed by parsing under the value’s own descriptor, while the same text under the descriptor of v[Local] reads v[Local];
  6. (no standard reading yields it) no value returned by parse_candidates, and so none returned by parse, parse_union or parse_any, has the offset Zulu(Unwritten); parse_as returns it only under a descriptor whose offset is Zulu(Unwritten);
  7. (dates may carry it) for every well-formed date d (finite or infinite, any date shape), d[Zulu(Unwritten)] is well formed.

The derived Hash of Temporal reads the same fields as ==, so it is consistent with clause 3; distinct values may still share a hash value, and no claim beyond that consistency is made.

Outside the domain

  • unwritten_zulu is total and has no refusal.
  • A value with well_formed() false is outside the carrier; it can be built only by assigning public fields, lexical_form and canonical_bytes return None for it, and production deserialization refuses it.

Definitions used

  • unwritten_zulu(v): matches!(v.offset, Offset::Zulu(ZuluCase::Unwritten)).
  • well_formed, cmp_chronological, lexical_form, parse_offset, parse_candidates, parse, parse_union, parse_any, parse_as and Display as defined in the reference module temporal; canonical_bytes, complete_layout and write_offset_form as defined there and in the module canonical.
  • Written-form variants ≈ and clauses 1 and 2 of Chronological equality ignores written temporal form.
  • Clause 2 of Extended temporal forms have distinct canonical bytes and the statement of Temporal display parses to the same value.

Proof

  1. Admission of the replacements. In well_formed the offset enters only through offset_ok, which admits Local and every Zulu(_), admits Fixed(0, f) for every form (the hour-only condition 0mod60=0 holds), and admits NegZero(f) for every form except Unwritten. The other conditions do not read the offset, so every listed v[o] is in T.
  2. Clause 1. For o∈Zw​∪Zu​, v and v[o] have the same infinity, shape, fields and fraction, both offsets are zoned, and seconds() is 0 for Zulu(_), NegZero(_) and Fixed(0, _). Hence v≈v[o], and clauses 1 and 2 of L-values-19 give the three equalities. Zulu(Unwritten) is zoned and Local is not, so the zoning test of comparable fails in both orders and both results are None.
  3. Clause 2 is the definition of unwritten_zulu; every v[o] listed has an offset other than Zulu(Unwritten).
  4. Clause 3. v=v[o] because the offsets differ. By clause 2 of L-values-21, distinct well-formed values have distinct canonical bytes. lexical_form copies the offset into its offset field, so the descriptors differ. complete_layout returns false for the offset Zulu(Unwritten), so write_temporal uses the infinity layout or the new finite layout, both of which end with write_offset_form, which writes Zulu(Unwritten) as the tag 1 followed by the case byte 2.
  5. Clause 4. Display for Temporal writes the offset last. Display for Offset writes nothing for Local and Zulu(Unwritten) (one arm), and nothing for Fixed(0, Unwritten) because numeric writes nothing for OffsetForm::Unwritten; so the three displays are equal. For o∈Zw​ it writes, respectively, Z, z, +00:00, +0000, +00, +00:00:00, -00:00, -0000, -00 or -00:00:00, each nonempty, so for a finite v the display of v[o] is the display of v followed by that text and is longer. For an infinite v every display is the infinity spelling, so the displays of v and v[o] agree, as clause 4 states.
  6. Clause 5 is L-values-16 applied to v and to v[Local], both in T by step 1, which have the same display by step 5.
  7. Clause 6. parse_offset returns only Local, Zulu(Upper), Zulu(Lower), Fixed(_, f) and NegZero(f) with written forms f, and FixedSeconds(_); the infinity candidates of parse_candidates carry Local. So no candidate has the offset Zulu(Unwritten); parse returns the first candidate, and parse_union and parse_any return a candidate or a refusal. parse_as changes a candidate’s offset only by replacing Local with the descriptor’s offset when that offset is unwritten, and its infinity branch uses the descriptor’s offset, so a result with offset Zulu(Unwritten) requires a descriptor with that offset.
  8. Clause 7. By step 1, replacing the offset of a well-formed value by Zulu(Unwritten) keeps it well formed; well_formed imposes no condition tying a date’s offset to its form.

Latin-1 encoding followed by decoding is identity

Statement

Call a string t=c1​⋯cn​ (n≥0) admitted when every code point of t is at most U+00FF. For every string t, latin1_encode(t) is Ok exactly when t is admitted, and for every admitted t, latin1_encode(t) = Ok(b) with latin1_decode(&b) = t; equivalently, latin1_encode_decode(t) is true exactly when t is admitted. For a lexeme of class LexClass::Bytes and a ValueSpec whose kind is ScalarKind::Bytes(BytesText::Latin1), production reading is required to equal the reference coercion reading coerce::decode_bytes, which for this form is bytes::latin1_encode(text).ok(), with None reported as FidelityReason::InvalidEncoding; it thus accepts exactly the admitted strings and returns the bytes whose Latin-1 decoding is t.

Outside the domain

A string that is not admitted contains a character whose code point exceeds U+00FF; latin1_encode returns Err(NonLatin1) for it and latin1_encode_decode returns false. For a lexeme of class LexClass::Bytes under a ValueSpec whose kind is ScalarKind::Bytes(BytesText::Latin1), production reading returns FidelityReason::InvalidEncoding; no other refusal can arise under that class and specification.

Definitions used

  • A string is a finite sequence of Unicode scalar values, read in order by chars(); its code points are the values u32::from(c).
  • latin1_encode(t) maps each character c of t, in order, to u8::try_from(u32::from(c)): the byte equal to the code point of c when that code point is at most 255, and the refusal NonLatin1 otherwise. Collecting into a Result returns Ok of the bytes in order when every character maps to a byte, and the first refusal otherwise.
  • latin1_decode(b) maps each byte bi​ to char::from(b_i), the scalar value with code point bi​, collected in order into a string.
  • The reference coercion reading coerce::decode_bytes, the function every coercion differential compares with production, reads BytesText::Latin1 text as bytes::latin1_encode(text).ok(); its caller reports None as FidelityReason::InvalidEncoding.
  • latin1_encode_decode(t) is latin1_encode(t).is_ok_and(|bytes| latin1_decode(&bytes) == t).

Proof

  1. Let t=c1​⋯cn​ and let pi​= u32::from(c_i). By the definition of u8::try_from on a u32, the per-character map in latin1_encode sends ci​ to the byte pi​ when pi​≤255 and to NonLatin1 when pi​>255.
  2. Case t is not admitted. Some pi​>255, so by step 1 at least one character maps to NonLatin1; by the definition of collecting into a Result, latin1_encode(t) is Err(NonLatin1), the only refusal the map produces. Then is_ok_and returns false by its definition.
  3. Case t is admitted. Every pi​≤255, so by step 1 every character maps to the byte pi​, and by the definition of collecting into a Result, latin1_encode(t) = Ok(p1​⋯pn​). This includes n=0, where the result is Ok of the empty sequence. Steps 2 and 3 together show that latin1_encode(t) is Ok exactly when t is admitted.
  4. In the admitted case, by the definition of latin1_decode, latin1_decode(p1​⋯pn​) is the string whose i-th character is the scalar value with code point pi​. A scalar value is determined by its code point, so that character is ci​, and the string is c1​⋯cn​=t.
  5. By steps 3 and 4, is_ok_and evaluates its predicate on p1​⋯pn​, which holds by step 4, so latin1_encode_decode(t) is true; by step 2 it is false when t is not admitted.
  6. For a lexeme of class LexClass::Bytes and a ValueSpec whose kind is ScalarKind::Bytes(BytesText::Latin1), production reading is required to equal the reference coercion reading coerce::decode_bytes, which for this form is bytes::latin1_encode(text).ok(), with None reported as FidelityReason::InvalidEncoding. By steps 2 and 3, latin1_encode(t) is Ok exactly when t is admitted, so the reference reading, and with it the production reading under that class and specification, accepts exactly the admitted strings, returning the bytes p1​⋯pn​, whose Latin-1 decoding is t by step 4, and FidelityReason::InvalidEncoding otherwise.

Padded base64 encoding followed by decoding is identity

Statement

For every byte string b, decode_base64(&encode_base64(b), true) = Ok(b); equivalently, padded_bytes_decode_encode(b) is true. Production reading under each base64 form is required to equal the reference coercion reading coerce::decode_bytes, with None reported as FidelityReason::InvalidEncoding. That reading is bytes::decode_base64(text, false) for BytesText::Base64 and bytes::decode_base64(text, true) for BytesText::Base64Padded; for BytesText::Base64Url and BytesText::Base64UrlPadded it refuses a text that contains + or / and otherwise is bytes::decode_base64(τ(text), r) with r false and true respectively, where τ replaces each - by + and each _ by /. Consequently the BytesText::Base64Padded reading returns b from encode_base64(b), and the BytesText::Base64UrlPadded reading returns b from the URL-safe canonical padded encoding υ(encode_base64(b)).

Outside the domain

The domain is every byte string, so no input lies outside it. No refusal can arise on the canonical padded encoding: the InvalidPadding of the required-padding comparison is excluded by step 2 below, the refusals of optional and of the quantum loop are excluded by the optional-padding decoding law, and NonLatin1 is never returned by a base64 operation. The unpadded form of a canonical encoding whose padding is nonempty lies outside the domain and is refused with InvalidPadding (step 4), and production reports FidelityReason::InvalidEncoding for it.

Definitions used

  • encode_base64, optional and decode_base64 are as defined in the padded-canonicity law. In particular decode_base64(t, r) computes m= optional(t) (returning its refusal if it refuses), returns InvalidPadding when r holds and m=t, and otherwise runs a quantum loop that reads only m.
  • The reference coercion reading coerce::decode_bytes, the function every coercion differential compares with production, reads BytesText::Base64 as bytes::decode_base64(text, false) and BytesText::Base64Padded as bytes::decode_base64(text, true). For BytesText::Base64Url and BytesText::Base64UrlPadded it returns None when the text contains + or /, and otherwise bytes::decode_base64(τ(text), r) with r false and true respectively; its caller reports None as FidelityReason::InvalidEncoding.
  • τ replaces each byte - of a text by + and each _ by /; υ replaces each + by - and each / by _. All four are single ASCII bytes, and no byte of a UTF-8 encoded character above U+007F is ASCII, so both maps preserve byte length and every other byte. Hence υ(τ(s))=s for a text s without + or /, and τ(υ(x))=x with υ(x) free of + and / for a text x without - or _. The URL-safe canonical padded encoding of b is υ(encode_base64(b)).
  • padded_bytes_decode_encode(b) is decode_base64(&encode_base64(b), true).as_deref() == Ok(b).
  • For t= encode_base64(b), t∘ is t with its trailing = bytes removed, as in L-values-26.

Proof

  1. Let t= encode_base64(b). By claim (i) of L-values-26, optional(t) = Ok(t), so m=t.
  2. Since m=t, the required-padding comparison m=t is false, and decode_base64(t, true) does not refuse there.
  3. By the definition of decode_base64, the only use of r is the comparison of step 2, so after it the computation for r true is the quantum loop on m=t, which is the computation for r false. By claim (iii) of L-values-26 that loop returns Ok(b). Hence decode_base64(t, true) = Ok(b), and padded_bytes_decode_encode(b) is true by its definition.
  4. For the unpadded form: by claim (ii) of L-values-26, optional(t∘) = Ok(t). By the definition of encode_base64, its output ends in = exactly when the last chunk of b has fewer than three bytes, that is, when ∣b∣mod3=0. In that case t∘=t, so the comparison of step 2 is true and decode_base64(t∘, true) returns InvalidPadding; when ∣b∣mod3=0, t∘=t and step 3 applies. These two cases are exhaustive.
  5. Production. Under BytesText::Base64Padded the reference coercion reading is decode_base64(·, true), which returns b from t by step 3 and refuses t∘ by step 4 when ∣b∣mod3=0. Under BytesText::Base64UrlPadded: t consists of bytes of the standard alphabet and = (claim (i) of L-values-26 and the definition of encode_base64), so it contains no - or _; by the translation identity of the definitions, υ(t) contains no + or / and τ(υ(t))=t, so the reading of υ(t) is decode_base64(t, true), which returns b by step 3. Production reading is required to equal this reference reading, with None reported as FidelityReason::InvalidEncoding, so it returns b in both cases and refuses t∘ under BytesText::Base64Padded when ∣b∣mod3=0.

Exact binary rounding uses ties to even

Statement

For every format F∈{Format::B16, Format::B32, Format::B64} (all three widths 16, 32 and 64), every rational q satisfying Premise P of L-values-9 and every boolean z, the reference operation round_to(F, q, z) returns a result, and the result satisfies the following six items, with S, VF​, MF​ and “even” as defined below.

  1. (Signed zero.) If q=0, the result is Finite(S) when z holds and Finite(0) otherwise.
  2. (Signed overflow.) If ∣q∣≥MF​, the result is Overflow { negative } with negative true exactly when q<0.
  3. (Nearest, ties to even.) If 0<∣q∣<MF​, the result is Finite(b), where the sign bit of b is set exactly when q<0, decode(F, b) is Finite { negative, value: v } with negative true exactly when q<0, and ∣v−q∣≤∣t−q∣ for every t∈VF​. If moreover some t∈VF​ with t=v has ∣t−q∣=∣v−q∣, then t is the only such element, b is even, and the pattern whose sign bit equals that of b and whose value is t is odd. In particular a non-zero q whose nearest value is zero gives the zero of the sign of q.
  4. (Grid.) The non-negative elements of VF​ are exactly the numbers n⋅2emin​−p+1 with 0≤n<2p−1 and n⋅2m−p+1 with emin​≤m≤emax​ and 2p−1≤n<2p. The map from the patterns 0,1,…,bmax​ to their values is strictly increasing, where bmax​=(2w−1)2p−1−1 is the largest pattern with a clear sign bit that decodes as finite, and maxVF​=2emax​+1−2emax​−p+1. For a finite pattern b<S, the pattern b+S decodes to the negation of the value of b and has the same lowest bit.
  5. (Sign symmetry.) For every rational r>0 and booleans z,z′: round_to(F, -r, z) is Finite(S + b) when round_to(F, r, z') is Finite(b), and is Overflow { negative: true } when round_to(F, r, z') is Overflow { negative: false }.
  6. (Round trip.) For every pattern b<2W with decode(F, b) equal to Finite { negative: s, value: v }, round_to(F, v, s) is Finite(b).

Outside the domain

A rational that does not satisfy Premise P is outside the proved arithmetic domain. The implementation still returns a Rounded value because its conversions have fallbacks, but this law makes no claim about nearest-value correctness on that path. Under Premise P the operation never refuses and none of its fallbacks is taken (steps 11 and 26 of L-values-9). Rounded::Overflow { negative } is a result of the operation, not a refusal; the exact float reading turns it into FidelityReason::Overflow, and the nearest reading turns it into the infinity of its sign.

Definitions used

  • The format parameters, pattern, even and odd patterns, decode, S, VF​, MF​, bmax​, floor_log2, Rat arithmetic and round_to(F, q, z): as defined in Part I of L-values-9, whose definitions are those of the reference module float and of num.rs.

Proof

  1. Items 1 to 6 of this statement are, word for word and over the same domain (every format F, every rational q satisfying Premise P, every boolean z), items R1 to R6 of Part I of L-values-9, which are proved there by a complete case analysis of the definition of round_to over q=0, q>0 (with the cases e>emax​ and e≤emax​, and within the latter the significand cases n=0, 1≤n<2p−1, 2p−1≤n<2p and n=2p) and q<0.
  2. Item 1 (signed zero) is R1; item 2 (signed overflow, ∣q∣≥MF​ exactly) is R2; item 3 (nearest value, ties to even, sign of an underflowing q kept) is R3; item 4 (grid and monotonicity) is R4; item 5 (sign symmetry) is R5; item 6 (round trip) is R6.
  3. The claim for the stated domain, that the operation returns and none of its fallbacks is taken, is step 26 of the proof of L-values-9, with the conversions inside floor_log2 covered by step 11 there under Premise P.
